23001-by-the-sea-1887:
Heman White Chaplin sketches a tidy man in By the Sea, a story dated 1887. James, with his easy collar and wristbands, always seemed fresh from the ironing-board. Keeping James clean costs no effort at all, Mrs. Parsons says in her funny little way. He picks his way round like a pussycat and never gets a spot on him, nowhere.

Chaplin wrote of New England coastal folk in dialect as fine as lace. A character like James, neat to a fault, becomes a whole study of village values. Little happens beyond talk, weather, and small errands by the sea. The pleasure is in the voice. Chaplin's ear for shore speech made his stories favorites of the magazines, and this one shows the gift plainly.
23002-saint-patrick-1887:
Heat hangs over the city in Saint Patrick, Heman White Chaplin's story dated 1887. Soulless faces loll in open ground-floor windows. Few customers sit in the barrooms, and policemen stroll listlessly with little to do. At nightfall comes the change, the scrape of fiddles and the stamp of boot-heels from the dance halls.

An Irish saint's day in an American city gives Chaplin his crowd and his music. The story moves between the day's dull weight and the night's release, watching immigrants at leisure. Chaplin usually wrote of fishing villages, and the urban setting stretches his range. Dance halls, saloons, and patrolmen fill the frame. The piece survives as a vivid slice of Irish-American city life in the Gilded Age.
23004-in-madeira-place-1887:
An old street musician carries a war in In Madeira Place, a sketch by Heman White Chaplin dated 1887. Nobody watching her slow round would guess her past. She once marched in Napoleon's armies and stood in the ranks at Waterloo. Since music goes with war, she also bears a worn accordion.

Kneeling by a flagged park path, she lifts a wrinkled, hopeful face. Now and then a passerby drops a copper into her hand. Chaplin builds a whole life from that kneeling figure, glory shrunk to a busker's pitch. His sketches often work this way, one overlooked person, closely seen. The Napoleonic detail startles, and it is meant to. Empires end, this piece says, in old women playing for pennies.
a-professor-of-alchemy-denis-zachaire-18: A Professor of Alchemy, Denis Zachaire, 1887. The alchemy professor. This book preserves that biography. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
appletons-cyclopaedia-american-biography:
James Wilson and John Fiske edited Appletons' work, and Volume One appeared in 1887, covering Aaron to Crandall. The whole set holds more than 15,000 lives. It was America's great national book of lives of the nineteenth century.

Entries sketch presidents, generals, inventors, clergy, and artists from the colonial age to the editors' own day. Portraits and facsimile signatures enliven the pages. The editors aimed for a complete record of notable American lives in one alphabet. Family historians and scholars still consult Appletons' for people found in no other reference work of the period. The entries run short, plain, and full of dates that are hard to find elsewhere now.
arxiv-2512-00187:
Simulating how particles shower through a detector is essential in high-energy physics, but it is also a bottleneck. Lorenzo Valente studies fast electromagnetic shower simulation in a 2025 study, focusing on transfer learning across detector geometries. Standard Monte Carlo tools such as Geant4 are accurate but computationally prohibitive.

Machine learning surrogates are faster, yet most are tied to one geometry and need full retraining for each design change. Valente examines whether a model can carry knowledge from one geometry to another. If transfer works, detector designers could test new layouts quickly instead of rebuilding simulations from scratch each time. Particle detectors are redesigned often, which makes reusable simulation especially valuable. The point lands for teams who plan the next round of test beams. Each new plan can reuse what was learned from the last one in the lab.
arxiv-2512-00587:
Mean field games model crowds of rational agents, each reacting to the average behavior of all. Antonio Siconolfi investigates first-order mean field games in a generalized form in 2025, comparing differential and variational approaches. The games play out on a torus, a periodic domain.

The classical formulation couples a Hamilton-Jacobi equation for optimal choices with a continuity equation for the crowd's density. The variational approach instead uses fixed points of a multivalued map on probability measures over trajectories. Showing how the two views relate strengthens the theory behind models of traffic, economics, and crowd motion. The torus removes boundary effects, letting the comparison focus on the equations themselves. The work is pure math, and its worth is in the bridge it builds. Two ways to pose the same crowd game are shown to be two sides of one coin.
arxiv-2512-00687:
Ruofan Jiang wrote a 2025 paper in arithmetic geometry on p-adic monodromy and unlikely intersections. The setting is ordinary abelian schemes in characteristic p, a world where numbers are measured by divisibility by a prime p. Their moduli spaces catalog whole families of these objects at once.

Jiang studies these spaces through three conjectures from characteristic p geometry, tied to Mumford-Tate groups, Ax-Lindemann type results, and André-Oort type results. Unlikely intersections are special overlaps that should happen only for good reasons. Results at this level help map the hidden order inside families of geometric objects.
arxiv-2512-01387:
Sanjeeva Rao Prattipati, Reetanjali Moharana, and Sourav Dutta hunt for bursts like a famed 2017 event. That event paired gravitational waves with a short gamma-ray burst. It came from two neutron stars merging. Wave rates hint more such bursts hide in past records.

The team scans Fermi-GBM records for bursts with traits like that event. They look in both mega and giga energy ranges. Finds would add cases where light and waves came from one merger. More cases sharpen rates for mergers and for the heavy elements they forge. Each added case also helps separate true merger bursts from look-alike bursts made by other violent events in deep space.
arxiv-2512-02587:
Marcelino Agúndez asks how much trust to place in computed air compositions for distant planets. Chemical models predict what exoplanet atmospheres hold, and telescopes check those predictions against real spectra. How wrong the model abundances might be has rarely been measured.

Agúndez runs a sensitivity analysis with a state of the art atmosphere model. Six well observed planets serve as test cases, from hot giants to a small sub-Neptune world. Knowing the uncertainty on each gas helps astronomers judge whether a claimed detection, or a mismatch, means new chemistry or just model noise. Error bars of this kind turn a bold claim about a far world into a claim that can be checked.
arxiv-2512-03287:
Wearable sensors can track what a person is doing. Dario Fenoglio and co-authors study activity recognition with head-worn sensors in this 2025 work. Such tracking helps in health and elderly care, where daily habits matter.

Classic systems send user data to a central server, which raises privacy concerns. The authors use federated learning, where models train on each device and share only updates. They also use signals at several frequencies. Private, on-device learning could let health tools work without gathering raw personal data. Head-worn sensors suit daily life, since glasses and earbuds already sit where motion is rich.
arxiv-2601-07087:
Dylan Sam and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers when should we introduce safety interventions during pretraining?. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Ensuring the safety of language models in high-stakes settings remains a pressing challenge.

As aligned behaviors are often brittle and easily undone by adversarial pressure or downstream finetuning. Prior work has shown that interventions applied during pretraining, such as rephrasing harmful content, can substantially improve the safety of the resulting models. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07387:
F. Bolis, E. Sobacchi, and F. Tavecchio wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on jets from blazars. A blazar is a galaxy whose jet points near our line of sight. The jet shines by synchrotron radiation, light from fast charges that spiral in a magnetic field. That light is polarized, which means its waves lean one way more than others.

The team asks how that lean shifts over time. Data at many bands show the lean angle swing by large amounts. The angle is called the electric vector position angle, or EVPA. Swings show up in light we can see and in X-rays. More often, both the strength of the lean and the EVPA jump in a way that looks random. The paper weighs what such jumps tell us about the jet. Shifts in the lean can trace how the field in the jet twists and churns.
arxiv-2601-07487:
J. W. Moffat examines a puzzle in cosmology in this 2026 preprint: radio galaxies seem unevenly spread across the sky. Wide-area surveys report a number-count dipole, an excess in one direction, larger than expected. The measured amplitude is three to four times the purely kinematic value predicted by the standard cosmology model. Reported significance reaches up to 5.4 sigma.

An effect that strong demands an explanation, either in the data or in theory. Moffat turns to modified gravity, a family of theories that change Einstein's gravity rules. He asks whether such a change can produce the observed excess. Readers get a compact case study in how an odd survey result can test the foundations of cosmology.
arxiv-2601-08087:
Kristen Dage and twelve co-authors look inside three nearby open star clusters. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses observations across many wavelengths to find results of close stellar encounters. Dense clusters force stars to interact, and those interactions leave unusual products behind.

The three clusters span very different ages. IC 2602 is about 30 million years old, NGC 2632 is about 750 million years old, and M67 is about 4 billion years old. Comparing young, middle-aged, and old clusters shows how interaction products change over time. Readers get a tour of hidden cluster life, from fresh systems to ancient ones.
arxiv-2601-08287: Jiaman He and co-authors link personality traits to eye movements during interactive search. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that personality shapes how people engage, behave, and decide while seeking information. Few studies have tied personality to observable search behavior, though. The team builds a multimodal time-series model that joins eye-tracking data with gaze missingness. Missingness means periods when the user's gaze is not captured at all. Treating absence as signal may reveal traits that gaze position alone would miss, with uses in adaptive search design.
arxiv-2601-08687:
Marco Tonnarelli and three co-authors present Data Product MCP for chatting with enterprise data. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from computational data governance, which aims to enforce policies and legal duties efficiently. Natural language processing and agentic AI offer ways to improve how organizations share and use data.

Many barriers remain in current practice. Today's tools demand technical skills and multiple roles to discover, request, and query data. A chat interface over governed data products could let staff ask in plain language. Governance rules would still gate what can be shared. The work targets firms where data access delays, not data scarcity, slow decisions.
arxiv-2601-08787:
F. Dai and V. Temlyakov survey how to rebuild a smooth curve or field from a few sample points. Such rebuild work sits at the heart of data squeeze, signal work, and learn theory. A good rebuild uses few points, yet stays close to the true field at all points. The survey maps what is known on how close we can get.

They tie best rebuild error to two known gauges. One is how well short sparse sums can near the field. The next is the width of the class the field comes from. Those ties tell us when a rebuild plan is as good as it can be. A reader gets a map of a wide field in one place, with the key open asks marked.
arxiv-2601-08987:
Mohammad Waquas Usmani, Susmit Shannigrahi, and Michael Zink guard 3D video streams with a rights lock that is light to run. A 3D stream sends point clouds, vast sets of dots that form a scene. Locking all dots costs much time and power. Pirates need just a clear view to steal worth, so a light lock may still block them.

Their frame is called ABE-VVS. It locks just a picked set of dot places, based on who may view the stream. The rest of the dots flow free, so lag stays low. The locked dots blur the view past use for a thief. A reader in stream work gets a rights plan that trades full lock for speed.
arxiv-2601-09087:
Schuyler Van Dyk and nine co-authors name the star that blew up as the supernova SN 2025pht. The burst was of Type II-Plateau, a class from huge red stars. The host galaxy is NGC 1637, near by space scale. Old sky shots from two space scopes caught the star long past its death, in a span of more than two decades.

The star looks to be a red supergiant, huge and bright. It was wrapped in much dust, the most dust the team has seen for such a case. Dust hid part of its light, so its true size took care to gauge. A reader in star death work gets a rare pre burst view of the star that died.
arxiv-2601-09287:
Dafne Lozano-Paredes and four co-authors build a warn tool for a fast grid talk rule with no built in guard. The rule is the GOOSE protocol, used in power sub stations. It sends trip and state notes in a flash, to guard gear. A foe who can join the net can send fake GOOSE notes that look rule true. Old guards miss such fakes, and marked attack data is thin.

Their tool learns the shape of sound GOOSE talk with an auto code net. Talk that breaks that shape is flagged. They add a why layer, so staff can see what trait set off the flag. A reader in grid safety gets a guard that can learn with few attack marks.
arxiv-2601-09587:
Samuel A. Federman and a large team peer at jets from newborn stars with the James Webb Space Telescope. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports observations within 2,000 astronomical units of three deeply embedded protostars. The targets are the low-mass Class 0 protostars B335 and HOPS 153, plus the intermediate-mass HOPS 370.

Webb's infrared eyes, from 2.9 to 27 microns, show the jets' shapes and motions. Class 0 is the youngest phase, when the star is still wrapped in its birth cloud. Jets this close to the source reveal how infalling material gets expelled. Those flows shape the mass the star finally keeps.
arxiv-2601-09687:
Yi Huang and Sankar Das Sarma explain a striking experiment on electrons in bilayer graphene. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats strong localization in two-dimensional systems under a strong magnetic field. A scanning tunneling study had found three distinct quantum phases in the lowest Landau level.

The three phases are a fractional quantum Hall liquid, a hexagonal Wigner crystal with long-range order, and a random localized solid with no order. Which phase appears depends on the filling factor. Disorder, often treated as a nuisance, helps create the localized phase. The paper works out how strong fields and disorder together produce this strong localization.
arxiv-2601-09887:
Rostyslav Hnatyshyn and four co-authors help materials scientists see atoms move. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents LAMDA, a visual tool for atomic displacements in molecular dynamics simulations. Modern materials research runs in silico, generating huge simulations of atomic motion.

Listing the basic patterns in how atoms shift is key to knowing how a material's traits will change. The space of possible transitions is vast, and high-throughput runs flood experts with data. LAMDA supports visual exploration of the movement patterns. Better tools for seeing atomic shifts could speed the design of new materials for real use.
arxiv-2601-09987:
Guglielmo Grimaldi, Matthew Headrick, Veronika Hubeny, and Pavel Shteyner study bounds on how much parts of a system can share. In holography, shared load can be read from cuts on a weighted graph. The least cut sets the bound. Bounds of this type are called HEIs.

The team built a new frame to sort these bounds. They use it to prove traits that all such bounds share. Two traits deal with which bounds beat which. One trait gives a full test for when a bound counts at all. The frame turns a loose set of bounds into a clear class.
arxiv-2601-10387:
Christina Lu and co authors map the role space of language models. A model can play many roles. Yet it slips back to one base role: the helpful Assistant. That role is set by late train steps. The team ask how that role sits in the model's state space.

They pull out state paths for a range of role types. Each path marks one stock role, from sage to rogue. The base role sits at a set place in that map. The team then test ways to keep it there. Shifts in role can change how a model acts. A firm base role is a safety aim.
arxiv-2601-10687:
S M Rayeed and a large team of co-authors built a dataset of ground beetles that spans a continent. Trait databases for ecology lean hard toward vertebrates and plants. Groups like ground beetles, rich in species, are left thin. Yet these beetles are trusted signs of ecosystem health, since their numbers shift with changes in the land.

The dataset pairs high-resolution images of the beetles with checked measurements of their body traits. Such traits let ecologists compare species and sites on equal terms. With images and traits together, the data can train vision models as well as serve field studies. It helps close a data gap that has limited work on insect diversity.
arxiv-2601-11287:
Markus Bink, Marten Risius, Udo Kruschwitz, and David Elsweiler demo a search helper. Their 2026 preprint was made for the ACM SIGIR meeting. Many users search poorly and judge sources with weak care. The risk is worst in high-stakes fields such as health.

Users also tend to rate their own digital skill too high. The team's helper sits inside normal search result pages. It weaves expert search moves into the page flow itself. No separate app or new habit is asked of the user. The design is then put to a test with real users. The aim is better queries and sharper checks on what is found.
arxiv-2601-11387:
Greta Warren, Jingyi Sun, Irina Shklovski, and Isabelle Augenstein test AI fact-check help. Their 2026 preprint asks what evidence does for such help. Much past work honed the explanations AI gives users. The role of the evidence itself is oddly under-studied.

The team varies three things in a study with non-experts. One is the type of explanation shown with a claim. One is how sure the AI says it is. The third is whether the AI advice is right or wrong. Users then judge the truth of claims themselves. They also judge the AI system's calls on those claims. The design shows when evidence earns its place in the loop.
arxiv-2601-11587:
Yuyan Huang and five coauthors support city carbon planning with grounded AI. Their 2026 preprint joins multi-agent planning with retrieval. Urban carbon governance needs many kinds of evidence at once. Emission inventories and statistical yearbooks are two such kinds.

Policy texts, technical measures, and academic findings add more. Planners must merge them into cross-departmental action plans. LLMs can assist, but factual reliability is a barrier. Evidential traceability is the other barrier in pro use. The team's support grounds each claim in retrieved sources. Multi-agent planning splits the governance task by role. Plans that cite their evidence are easier to defend.
arxiv-2601-11987:
Berkani Khaled presents a graph method for chest X-ray diagnosis that can explain its calls. Feature maps from a convolutional net are recast as graphs of image patches. Each node holds both look and place data, and edges link near patches.

Anatomical priors, facts about chest form, guide the graph. That guide should make the calls more clear to a doctor. A tool that shows its grounds can earn more trust in clinics. The work joins graph thought with known body form for X-ray reads.  Clear grounds help a doctor judge each call with care.
arxiv-2601-12187:
Rafał Filipów, Adam Kwela, and Paolo Leonetti study sets of Ramsey-limit and IP-limit points for sequences. They work in an uncountable Polish space. The Hindman ideal holds all sets of whole numbers that are not IP sets.

For each sequence, they define its set of IP-limit points via finite sums. Ramsey-limit points add a second, stricter notion. The team sort how these sets can look. Such sorts link combinatorics on numbers to topology of limit sets.  The sets are tied to sequences in the space X.  Such limit sets show how wild a sequence can act in a space.
arxiv-2601-12287:
Bijun Fan, Chao Zhang, Liang Zheng, and Shusu Shi model open charm hadron output in proton and gold crashes at RHIC. The crashes run at a nucleon pair energy of 200 GeV. They use an improved multi-phase transport model for the work.

They give momentum spectra and nuclear modification factors for D0 mesons and Lambda_c baryons. They also give the ratio of the two in both crash kinds. That ratio tests how charm quarks form baryons in hot matter. The work aids heavy-ion physics at RHIC.  The ratio is the key test in their model runs.
arxiv-2601-12387: Jihang Zhu and Chunli Huang study chiral superconductors, a phase that breaks time reversal symmetry. Such phases draw wide interest in physics. One hope is that they could host platforms for topological quantum computation. When time reversal breaks, a clear effect should follow. That effect is orbital magnetization, a magnetic response tied to the motion of electrons.
arxiv-2601-12487:
Caden Drover, R. L. Irvine, and Rachel Wortis study a double quantum dot, a pair of tiny electron traps. Strong Coulomb repulsion in such systems gives rise to a zero bias anomaly. That is a feature in the single particle density of states near zero energy. Its shape and its shifts with settings act as signs of the underlying electronic state.

Disorder plus interactions shape that feature in many systems at once. The team ask a pointed question: how do the leads attached to the dots affect the signs? Leads are needed to measure the dots, but they may distort what they measure. Knowing that effect helps readers trust the anomaly as a probe. It bears on mesoscopic physics and quantum device design.
arxiv-2601-12787:
Ning Sun and Pengfei Zhang connect two measures of quantum chaos in thermofield double states. Under unitary evolution, chaotic systems begun in simple states grow complex very fast. That growth soon blocks any efficient classical description. Chaos is traditionally characterized by spectral traits of the Hamiltonian, most notably the spectral form factor.

A second lens is quantum magic, the hardness of simulation in the stabilizer formalism. Magic can be quantified by the stabilizer Renyi entropy. The team link magic dynamics in these special states to spectral form factors. A bridge between simulation hardness and spectra would unify two views of chaos. It could also guide tests on near term quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-12987:
Evangelos Ntouros and Ewoud J. J. Smeur develop guidance for a tailsitter aircraft under wind disturbances. A tailsitter sits on its tail and flies like a plane, mixing drone and aircraft traits. Their control law is based on a parametric guiding vector field. A vector field approach steers the craft along a path rather than chasing a moving target point.

They integrate the law with a state of the art acceleration and attitude control architecture. The framework enables direct comparison of trajectory tracking and path following guidance. Tests use a realistic tailsitter model under windy conditions. Wind is where elegant guidance laws often fail, so the test is stern. The work serves vertical takeoff aircraft design.
arxiv-2601-13887:
Hong Su sets out a human-inspired frame for AI systems that adapt in 2026. Large language models show strong skill with knowledge and reasoning from text. But text alone limits how they adapt to new settings. It also limits how they verify their own reasoning. Open, dynamic real-world settings expose those limits fast.

Su calls the frame Human Simulation Computation. It aims to mimic how humans sense, check, and adjust in the world. Adaptive systems need feedback loops that text-only models lack. A human-like loop could help AI act with more care outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-14187:
Yaling Ke studies how strong light fields can steer chemical reactions in optical cavities in 2026. Harnessing strong light-matter interactions to control reactions is a promising route. It could deepen our grasp of chemical dynamics at the collective quantum level. It also holds implications for future chemical synthesis paradigms.

Cooperative reactions in cavities show a complex interplay of effects. Mode hybridization, timescale balance, and pathway interference all play roles. A mechanistic understanding of the dynamics is required to reach control. Cavity chemistry may one day let light pick which product forms. The three effects must be read as one play, not as lone parts. That joint read is the hard core of the work.
arxiv-2601-14387:
Songela W. Chen and David T. Limmer study the energy cost of erasing a bit in this 2026 paper. Energy costs of information processing are growing fast. Bit erasure sits at the heart of that cost. Past work set key links between thermodynamic cost and memory storage.

Modern systems, though, work far from equilibrium, where those classic links strain. The authors take on optimal control of bit erasure in stochastic random access memory. Stochastic means the device is subject to random thermal kicks. Their aim is control schemes that erase bits at the lowest true cost in a real, noisy device.
arxiv-2601-14487:
Mrigank Dhingra and Omer San work on forecasting chaotic systems in this 2026 paper. Long-horizon autoregressive forecasting of chaotic dynamics is hard for two reasons. Small one-step errors amplify fast. Rollouts also drift off distribution, so predictions collapse into physically inconsistent states with wrong large-scale statistics.

The team introduces MSR-HINE, a hierarchical implicit forecaster. It augments multiscale latent priors with multi-rate recurrent modules. Those modules run at distinct temporal scales, fast and slow. The design aims to stabilize long rollouts. The point is trust. A long run that stays true to the real system is worth more than a short one that drifts. Readers get a forecaster built to keep the broad statistics of a chaotic system intact over long runs.
arxiv-2601-14787:
Yu Pan leads a team of seventeen authors on a small black hole in this 2026 paper. NGC 4395 is a nearby dwarf spiral galaxy hosting an active galactic nucleus. That nucleus is powered by an intermediate-mass black hole, with a mass of about ten thousand to one hundred thousand suns. Such mid-size black holes are rare finds and key missing links.

The project is the Intermediate-Mass Black Hole Reverberation Mapping Project. Reverberation mapping times how light echoes through gas near the black hole to weigh it. The team reports stable optical continuum lags for the NGC 4395 black hole over years. Stable lags mean the echo delay held steady across long monitoring. Readers get a long-baseline check on a prized small black hole.
arxiv-2601-14887:
Itzhak Goldman looks at turbulence inside a far-off galaxy that is forming stars. His 2026 arXiv paper studies CSWA13, a galaxy stretched by gravitational lensing. The galaxy sits at a redshift near 2, so its light left it long ago.

Earlier work by Goldman found signs of large-scale turbulence in the galaxy's gas. That flow was compressible and of the Burgers type. The new work asks if small-scale turbulence runs alongside the large flow. He probes both scales with multi-point structure functions, a tool that compares the moving gas at set spatial gaps.
arxiv-2601-15087:
Dario Benedetti, Fanny Eustachon, and Omar Zanusso study exotic fixed points of a scalar field theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the Lee-Yang universality class and its multicritical kin. The theory has a complex interaction term, an odd power of the field times an imaginary factor.

These fixed points come from the renormalization group, the tool that tracks a theory across scales. The team works just below the upper critical dimension. They use the local potential approximation to chart critical and multicritical points. The results extend what is known about this odd family.
arxiv-2601-15187:
Noam Soker compares seven rival stories for where the heaviest elements were first forged. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with the r-process, a chain of reactions that builds heavy nuclei in extreme settings. The question is which sites did this work in the early universe.

Soker tests each scenario against the observed traits of r-process elements from that era. He concludes that two sites split the job. A magnetorotational process likely made the elements below the third peak. A common envelope jets supernova likely made the third peak itself in full.
arxiv-2601-15487:
Chandan Kumar Sahu, Premith Kumar Chilukuri, and Matthew Hetrich build a test set for search systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework is called MiRAGE. It targets retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, as it moves toward multimodal, high-stakes use. Evaluation tools have not kept pace with that shift. Most datasets use general text or plain documents.

Real enterprise files are harder than that. Key facts hide in tables, figures, and text together. Answering often means joining disjoint pieces of evidence. MiRAGE uses multiple agents to build such questions and answers. The questions are multimodal and multihop by design. For teams that ship RAG systems, a harder, more honest test set is the point.
arxiv-2601-15887:
Piotr Salabura searches for hypothetical particles in a rare decay in a 2026 arXiv paper. Dark matter and new particles may explain effects the Standard Model cannot. Axion-like particles are one candidate family. Their masses may run from MeV to GeV scales. Some versions carry an extra Peccei-Quinn breaking contribution. They couple to Standard Model matter in specific ways. Those couplings make certain decays worth watching.

The search uses the eta meson decay into two pions and an electron pair. The HADES detector collects the data. A rare decay is a clean place to hunt: backgrounds are low, and a new particle could appear as a bump. Null results still matter. They narrow the space where such particles can hide.
arxiv-2601-15987:
Nguyen N. Hung, Gabriel Navarro, and Pham Huu Tiep study character values in finite group theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Characters are functions that summarize a group's representations. Their fields of values collect the numbers characters can take. The authors fix a prime p. For p equal to two, the fields are classified for characters whose degrees avoid p. For odd primes, a conjectural classification has been proposed.

The paper works on that open side of the problem, per its title. Primes enter because degree divisibility shapes character behavior. Classifications of value fields constrain what groups can exist. Group theorists use such constraints in the broader program of understanding finite groups. Incremental progress on a sharp conjecture is how that program advances.
arxiv-2601-16287:
Ryan Lopez and three coauthors use live choice to speed band gap guesses for light crystals. Their 2026 preprint joins a last layer Bayes net with choice by doubt. Light crystals guide light by their gap traits. Guessing gaps by full sums is slow and costs much. A net can guess fast, but needs good train picks to stay true.

Doubt led choice picks the next sums that teach most. An exact form of the net gives doubt marks with no fake draws. Good doubt marks make each new sum count more. Fast, true gap guesses aid design of light gear. The work blends net maths with sum choice.
arxiv-2601-16387:
Hyun-Myung Chun and three coauthors set one law for waver and reply in Langevin flows. Their 2026 preprint deals with flows bent by chance heat noise. Past laws link waver size to reply size at rest. Far from rest, that old link no longer holds in plain form. The team seeks one law that holds in both zones.

They use shared maths in the waver of mass and flow counts. From it they draw one tie that spans rest and non rest. A wide law lets teams read drive from waver in real flows. It also tests if a flow is at rest from data. The work firms up non rest flow maths.
arxiv-2601-16487:
Remi Chierchia and coauthors give wound cuts that stay same across views with field nets. Their 2026 preprint deals with wound care cost and strain. Wards and homes face high cost to track wounds by hand. Pic tools can cut wound zones to track size and heal. One view cuts can clash when the same wound is shot anew.

Field nets hold the wound in a 3D like form from all views. Cuts from that form stay same view to view. Same cuts let teams trust size tracks through time. The work seeks wound tools that cut hand work. It tests field nets on real wound pic sets.
arxiv-2601-16587:
Léonard Polat shares a fresh fine count of a key clash rate for the muon test. His 2026 preprint comes from the BABAR team work. The rate is for electron plus positron to two pions. That rate feeds the sum for the muon odd spin mark. The muon mark is a hot test of the known grain model.

Fine rate counts cut the doubt in that sum much. BABAR data gives one of the most sharp counts to date. Sharp counts let teams tell if the muon mark truly clashes. A true clash would point to new grains past the model. The work is a key part of that long test.
arxiv-2601-16687:
Felix Stoehr and a team of co-authors gauge the reach of the ALMA scope array. ALMA is a set of radio dishes high in Chile. It maps cold gas and dust in space. A space tool proves its worth in part through print. Papers in strong journals show what the data gave. Their 2026 preprint counts and weighs that print record.

The team tracks how many papers rest on ALMA data. They also look at how oft those papers get cited. Trends by year and field come into view. Such counts help funders judge the worth of big tools. They also help the field plan its next grand scopes.
arxiv-2601-16787:
A review sums fresh gauges of a deep split in how matter and antimatter act. When a bit and its anti-twin decay in unlike rates, that split shows. Such splits, timed over full decay spans, test the base theory. The 2026 talk text pulls news from two big labs. LHCb and Belle II both feed the pool.

News spans the CKM angle gamma, a key weak-force mark. It also marks the first clear split seen in baryon decays. Charm meson decays add more fresh cases. These gauges bound how the cosmos kept matter over antimatter. They also point to where new physics may hide.
arxiv-2601-16887:
Oleksii Yanchyshen, Eva Hackmann, and Claus Lämmerzahl track orbits near a black hole with fresh math. Orbits there bend by strong gravity's pull. Small extra forces then nudge the path bit by bit. Gauss-style rules track how path traits shift. Their 2026 preprint builds those rules for Schwarzschild space-time.

No curbs are set on the nudge force's form. Path traits, called osculating elements, shift per the rules. The rules hold in the strong field near the hole. Such math aids probe paths near black holes. It also aids tests of gravity's tale in deep fields.
arxiv-2601-17087:
Preethi Seshadri and a team of four co-authors test fake users in chatbot grades. Bench tests now use chatbot-made users to save cost. Those fake users chat with the bot on test tasks. No one had checked if fakes stand in well for folks. Their 2026 preprint runs a user study on four lands' folk. The lands are the US, India, Kenya, and Nigeria.

Real users did shop-type tasks from a known bench set. Their acts were set next to fake users' acts. Gaps in grade, truth, and fair marks then show. Fake users may grade bots in skewed ways. Bench teams need that truth to trust their scores.
arxiv-2601-17187:
Or Ordentlich and Yury Polyanskiy study fast, compact matrix multiplication. Big language models lean on matrix products for most of their work. Shrinking numbers to fewer bits cuts memory and speeds runs. That shrink is called quantization. The authors study high-rate forms of it, where more bits stay in play.

They cover two cases. In one, both matrices must be shrunk. In the other, only the weights shrink, and the second matrix is known through its covariance. They give both theory and practice for these cases. The work helps teams weigh speed gains against loss of care. It points to where high-rate shrinking is safe to use.
arxiv-2601-17587:
Azza Fadhel and five co-authors use AI to find workable 3D printing settings for metal alloys. Printing quality hinges on inputs like laser power and scan speed. Their links to output quality are complex. Trial and error is the standard hunt, and it is slow and costly. The team uses AI-driven adaptive experimental design.

Adaptive design picks each next test from past results. That steers the hunt toward feasible settings fast. Fewer failed prints save powder, time, and machine wear. Metal printing serves aerospace and medical parts. A smart hunt widens who can print well. The work turns a craft skill into a guided search.
arxiv-2601-17787:
Wei-Ning Chiu, Chuan-Ju Wang, and Pu-Jen Cheng work on teaching recommender systems what matters most in a user history. Their 2026 preprint is about generative recommenders. These systems treat the task of picking the next item as a step-by-step text task. Items are named by semantic codes, and the model writes the code of the item it predicts.

Most training treats each piece of the code as worth the same. The authors say that is a poor match for how the codes carry meaning. They propose two ways to weight the pieces by the information each one adds. A staged training plan, called curriculum learning, supports the scheme. The aim is a model that learns the key signals first.
arxiv-2601-17987:
Ziwei Zheng and co-authors hunt for the smallest neural networks that still do their job well. Their 2026 preprint gives a unified study of minimal deep learning designs. Neural networks excel at classification, yet no one has a clear map of how small a network can be for a set task. The team builds a method to explore that space in a systematic way. They study how three forces interact: convergence, pruning, and quantization.

Pruning cuts parts of a network away. Quantization stores its numbers with less precision. Both shrink a model, but each can break its training. Knowing how the three forces trade off guides lean design. Small, sound models matter for phones, sensors, and low-cost devices.
arxiv-2601-18187: Mabud Ali Sarkar studies the image of the p-adic logarithm on rings of principal units. His 2026 preprint works over a finite extension of the p-adic numbers, with its maximal ideal. The group of principal units, one plus that ideal, plays a key role in number theory. Sarkar examines where the logarithm sends annuli of these units, a question with uses across local field theory.
arxiv-2601-18787:
Saul Baltasar and seven colleagues build a fast path to fit the bent light of far points that pass near a heavy mass. The mass acts as a lens: it splits one point of light into a ring of shots. From the shots, staff can read the lens's mass and the gaps in time between the shots. Those gaps can set the scale of space it-self. Past fits were slow and could miss the true best fit.

Their path runs on graphics chips with a famed lens frame. In tests on made-up shots it reads back the spots, the glow, and the time gaps with care. It also reads the slope of the lens's mass, a hard trait to pin. A fast, true fit could open lens work to far more cases. Bright points like burst stars make the best lens probes of all.
arxiv-2601-19087:
Mohammed E. Eltayeb steers millimeter waves indoors with printed reflectors that use no power at all. Millimeter wave signals are fast but easily blocked, so rooms have dead zones. His reflectors are flat panels whose parts bounce the signal toward a chosen spot, like a mirror shaped for radio.

Each part's bounce is set by the angles of the incoming and wanted outgoing waves, a model the paper works out in full. A switchable pattern of parts, called binary aperture control, aims the beam. Passive panels could stretch indoor coverage without the cost and power draw of active relays.
arxiv-2601-19187:
Aman Desai, Amelia Lovison, and Paul Jackson hunt for a bound pair of top quarks at the Large Hadron Collider. Fresh results from the ATLAS and CMS experiments hint that top and antitop quarks can briefly bind near the energy threshold where they are born. Such a state is called toponium.

The team presents a way to rebuild that state from the debris of collisions, using a method called recursive jigsaw reconstruction. Top quarks decay almost at once, so any bound state hides in fine patterns. A sound rebuild method could turn a hint into a firm find at the collider.
arxiv-2601-19287:
Md. Asif Haider and Thomas Zimmermann study how human reviewers react to code written by AI agents. Past work graded how well agents generate code, but little was known about the review side of real practice. Their large scale study reads code review on pull requests that agents authored.

They map the dominant themes in what reviewers say and ask for. Review is where agent code meets human judgment, trust, and standards. Knowing what reviewers balk at tells agent builders what to fix. It is not just whether the code runs. A human must also accept it into the project.
arxiv-2601-19387:
Lekshmi Murali Rani, Richard Berntsson Svensson, and Robert Feldt study the human side of working with AI coders. Generative tools now support software engineers and their teams day to day. Getting the tools to work well with people, though, is not just a matter of code quality.

The team focuses on the socio-emotional gap: trust, tone, frustration, and the feel of teamwork with a machine partner. Their functional view asks what such collaboration must do for the humans in it. Ignoring that side risks tools that are sharp on paper and draining in practice.
arxiv-2601-19487:
Haonan Zhang and four co-authors untangle the trade between letting attacks through and refusing harmless asks. Safety aligned models fail two ways: jailbreaks that answer harmful inputs, and over refusal that declines benign ones. Past steering methods turn one knob, the size of an answer vector, and trade one failure for the other.

Their method, LLM-VA, aligns vectors in direction instead of just scaling them. A directional fix could cut both failures at once, escaping the seesaw. Models that are both safer and less skittish would serve users better on both sides of the line.
arxiv-2601-19687:
Daniel L. Clarkson and Eduard P. Kontar read the radio static of the Sun for clues about its magnetic field. Type III radio bursts come from beams of fast electrons racing outward along magnetic field lines. The burst's frequency drifts as the beam climbs into thinner plasma. From that drift, scientists infer the beam's speed and path.

The inferred motion does not fit a smooth, straight climb through steadily thinning plasma. Something disturbs the path. The authors argue the bursts carry signatures of large-scale magnetic disturbances and switchbacks, kinks where the field folds back on itself. Reading these signatures turns routine bursts into probes of the solar wind. That helps forecast the space weather that reaches Earth.
arxiv-2601-19787:
Elena Masserini, Diego Clerissi, Daniela Micucci, and Leonardo Mariani build resources for studying task-based chatbots. Chatbots now serve users around the clock in many domains. Yet research on their quality is held back by a lack of large, curated datasets. The authors set out to fix that for chatbots built with Dialogflow, a popular platform.

They present TOFU-D, a snapshot of close to two thousand Dialogflow chatbots gathered from GitHub. From it they curate COD, a validated subset of under two hundred chatbots. A snapshot shows what builders actually ship, flaws included. A curated subset gives researchers a clean base for experiments. Both resources support work on testing and improving conversational software.
arxiv-2601-19887:
Dominic Maggio and Luca Carlone present a system that rebuilds scenes in three dimensions from ordinary colour video, in real time. SLAM systems map a space while tracking the camera through it. Their system builds on VGGT, a feed-forward model that estimates scene geometry directly. Version 2.0 substantially improves how incremental submaps are aligned.

Two fixes headline the upgrade. A new factor graph design removes a fifteen-degree-of-freedom drift that plagued the earlier system. It also removes a planar degeneracy, a failure mode on flat scenes. The system still handles the ambiguity that arises when camera settings are unknown. Dense, real-time reconstruction serves robots and augmented reality alike.
arxiv-2601-20087:
A. Tayebi and B. Najafi prove a rigidity result in Finsler geometry. Berwald spaces are a tame class of Finsler manifolds, where distances can depend on direction. Flag curvature measures how those spaces bend. The authors prove that every Berwald manifold with nonzero flag curvature is actually Riemannian, the simpler direction-independent kind.

The result extends classical rigidity theorems of Numata and Szabó. They also show that positively curved constant isotropic Berwald manifolds are Riemannian or locally Minkowskian. Compact cases with strictly positive or negative curvature reduce further. Rigidity theorems are prized because they collapse a wide class to a familiar one. The work sharpens the map of Finsler geometry's landscape. The class looks wide at first sight.
arxiv-2601-20187:
Dingxin Zhang gives a new proof of the Riemann hypothesis part of the Weil conjectures. That landmark result counts points on varieties over finite fields. The proof covers smooth projective varieties. It works by reducing the general case to the case of a hypersurface, using deformation.

The main tool is Artin's vanishing theorem, together with basic facts about perverse sheaves. Shorter or clearer proofs of deep results still matter, since they can expose new links between fields. This route ties arithmetic geometry to sheaf methods in a direct way, and it may help readers who found earlier proofs hard to enter.
arxiv-2601-20287:
Francesco Caravelli presents a framework for memory in classical and quantum systems, seen through hysteresis, where a system's state depends on its past. In his setup, the Hamiltonian at each moment depends on past values of a control Hamiltonian through a causal kernel. This structure fits finite-bandwidth or filtered control channels well.

The framework separates memory that lives in the control signal from true non-Markovian dynamics of the state itself. That distinction matters in experiments, where an apparent quantum memory effect may just be lag in the equipment. The paper gives researchers a clean way to tell the two apart.
arxiv-2601-20487:
Nico Mutzner, Taha Yasseri, and Heiko Rauhut study cooperation when AI agents join small human groups. Most earlier work on human-AI cooperation looked at pairs, one person and one agent. Little is known about how agents affect the rise and upkeep of cooperative norms in groups.

Their title states the headline finding: behavior, not identity, drives cooperation in mixed groups. In other words, what an agent does matters more than the fact that it is an agent. That result shapes how teams should introduce AI members: norms follow conduct, whoever or whatever shows it.
arxiv-2601-20587:
Saifian Farooq Bhat and four colleagues build a hybrid jump-diffusion model for controlling quantum emitters in hexagonal boron nitride. This two-dimensional material is a promising host for stable single-photon emission, thanks to its wide bandgap, high photostability, and fit with nanophotonic devices. The authors study an emitter that is mechanically decoupled from its host.

Their simulation covers temperature-dependent spectral dynamics and optical coherence. Modeling both helps design coherent optical control of the emitter. Reliable single-photon sources are building blocks for quantum communication, so sharpening their control matters. All of this is worked out in a model on a screen, not in a lab test. That keeps the cost low while the team learns what to build next.
arxiv-2601-20787:
G. Chacon-Acosta and two co-authors study a quantum particle that must live on a sphere. Their 2026 paper builds a semi-classical picture of this system. The particle moves on a curved surface. It also feels a force that does not pull toward the center. The team uses a method that adds quantum spread to the classical phase space. The added terms are called moments.

They derive corrected Hamiltonians and paths for the sphere. The new terms show how the particle's own quantum spread pushes back on its motion. Classical theory misses that push. The goal is to keep the ease of classical paths while adding key quantum effects. The work serves studies of particles bound to curved surfaces.
arxiv-2601-20987:
Md Muhtasim Munif Fahim and Md Rezaul Karim bring pretrained AI to child development screening. Their 2026 paper concerns transfer learning in data-scarce settings. Many children face preventable developmental delays each year. Machine learning could flag risk early. Deployment in new countries, though, hits a data bottleneck. Reliable models need thousands of samples. New programs often begin with fewer than one hundred.

The authors use pre-trained encoders to bridge that gap. An encoder first learns from large existing data. It then transfers to the new country with little local data. That transfer enables deployment where training from scratch would fail. The paper targets global child development programs. It offers a path to early screening that does not wait for big local datasets.
arxiv-2601-21187:
Chenyu Huang and six co-authors inject reasoning skill into vision-language models with a finer touch. Their 2026 paper presents FRISM, a model merging method. Enhancing the reasoning of vision-language models by merging them with large reasoning models is a promising direction. Existing methods operate at a coarse, layer-wide level. That often forces a trade-off. Injecting reasoning can erode visual capability. The authors aim to break that trade-off.

FRISM merges at the subspace level instead. Fine-grained reasoning injection targets only the parts of the model that carry reasoning. Visual strengths elsewhere are left intact. The name spells out the recipe: fine-grained reasoning injection via subspace-level merging. Cheaper than retraining, merging reuses models that already exist. The work helps builders who want smarter multimodal systems without starting over.
arxiv-2601-21587:
Abderrahmane Issam, Yusuf Can Semerci, Jan Scholtes, and Gerasimos Spanakis use language models as stand-in learners to study how one language shapes another. Crosslinguistic influence is central to research on bilingual minds. Human studies, though, often clash because no two groups of learners match.

Models offer a controlled learner that can be rerun at will. The authors simulate the influence in a systematic way and isolate its drivers. With noise and background held fixed, the true causes stand out. The approach gives language science a lab bench where classic disputes can be rerun cleanly.
arxiv-2601-21687:
Francesco Alessio, Vittorio Del Duca, Riccardo Gonzo, and Emanuele Rosi work on the theory of gravity at very high energies. Their 2026 preprint builds a systematic framework, based on Regge theory, for scattering where two heavy particles collide and emit several gravitons. The setup also keeps track of spin effects.

The authors work in an ultra-fast limit and keep the leading terms in a standard approximation. In that limit, their results for heavy particles reduce smoothly to the known results for particles with no mass. The framework links three views of the same events: waveforms, shock waves, and unitarity cuts. That gives other theorists a shared language for high-energy gravitational scattering.
arxiv-2601-21787:
Chantale Lauer, Peter Pfeiffer, Alexander Rombach, and Nijat Mehdiyev test whether large language models can draw proper business process models. Building a model in the BPMN notation is complex and slow, since it needs both knowledge of the field and command of strict modeling rules.

Recent models can now generate such diagrams directly from plain text descriptions, building on older text-to-process methods. The 2026 study assesses how competent the models really are at this task. The answer matters for companies that hope to draft process documentation automatically. A fluent diagram with wrong logic is worse than none, so measured competence tells managers where human review must stay in the loop.
arxiv-2601-21987:
J. Christopher Mihos and co-authors peer into the faint outskirts of the spiral galaxy M96. Using deep imaging from the Hubble Space Telescope, they study the stars in the galaxy's extreme outer halo. M96 sits in the Leo I group, a dynamically active neighborhood where galaxies disturb each other.

Their fields lie far from the galaxy's center, at a projected distance given in the paper, and reach very faint stars. The mix of star ages and chemistries there records how the halo was assembled, from swallowed smaller galaxies and scattered disk stars. Their 2026 preprint reads that record. Outer halos are galactic archaeology: their faint stars preserve the merger history that brighter inner regions have overwritten.
arxiv-2601-22087:
Qian Zhang and co-authors build a fairer way to credit power resources for keeping the grid reliable. Capacity accreditation decides how much each generator or storage unit counts toward resource adequacy, the grid's ability to meet demand. Probabilistic assessment is the modern standard for that judgment.

Their 2026 preprint develops a gradient-based framework. Accreditation becomes the directional derivative of a reliability metric with respect to a resource's capacity: how much reliability actually improves when the resource grows. That view unifies two widely used accreditation approaches. Fairer credits matter because they steer billions in investment toward resources that genuinely keep the lights on during the hardest hours.
arxiv-2601-22187:
A short mathematics preprint studies a basic task: solving for a root of an equation. The equation considered takes a simple power form, where an unknown raised to a whole-number power must equal a given positive number. Its real solution is the corresponding root of that number.

The author presents a root finding method whose order of convergence can be chosen freely. The order measures how fast the error shrinks at each step; higher orders reach a precise root in fewer iterations. Methods with tunable order are useful in numerical software, where root finding sits inside countless larger computations. The note keeps its focus narrow: one equation family, one method, and its convergence behavior.
arxiv-2601-22387:
Victor Nikhil Antony and a large team look to plants for a new way to design social robots. Plants are calm, low-demand presences, yet they shape a room's mood and a person's day. Their 2026 preprint contrasts this with most robots, which copy people or pets and demand much heed.

Plant-like robots would act through slow rhythms and soft, subtle cues. They could keep company without nagging for response. The team set out design metaphors drawn from plant life. The work opens a quiet path for home robots. It suits care homes and calm work spaces.
arxiv-2601-22787:
Patrick Putzky and five co-authors tackle a trade-off in shrinking large AI models after training. Fast methods need no extra data and work on any model, but they break down when models are squeezed below four bits per weight. Methods that use extra data keep quality better, yet cost far more compute.

Their method, named in the title, uses entropy coding to store weights in a smarter way. The goal is strong compression to about two bits without needing data for tuning. Small, cheap models matter for running AI on phones and small machines.
arxiv-2601-22887:
Yangyan Li proposes a new way to give autoregressive models more memory without more computing cost. These models, which predict one step at a time, power most modern AI for text and images. Normally, adding memory means making the network deeper or wider, which raises the cost of every step.

The proposal, MoVE, mixes many value embeddings to store knowledge in a new dimension of scale. If memory can grow while active compute stays flat, models could know more for the same price. That trade-off matters for serving AI to millions of users.
arxiv-2601-22987:
Salem Lahlou presents ArabicDialectHub, a learning resource that spans six kinds of Arabic. It covers Moroccan Darija, Lebanese, Syrian, Emirati, and Saudi varieties, plus Modern Standard Arabic. The set holds more than five hundred phrases, drafted with language models and checked by five native speakers.

Phrases are sorted by difficulty and grouped by theme on an interactive web platform. Learners often study the standard form, then struggle with the dialect spoken on the street. A side-by-side resource helps bridge that gap for students and travelers. Stratified difficulty and thematic grouping let learners progress from everyday phrases toward harder, situation-specific language.

augustine-of-hippo-against-lying-npnf1-1:
Years after On Lying, Augustine returned to deceit in Against Lying. A new case had arisen among Christians hunting for heretics. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the later treatise in English.

Some believers faked conversion to a heresy to spy on its members. Augustine condemns the tactic without any hesitation at all. The end, he insists, never makes deceitful means acceptable. Even hunting heresy cannot license a lie told in God's name. The protest against noble lies carries real moral force. It comes from a man who knew temptation from the inside and refused to dress it as virtue.
augustine-of-hippo-against-two-letters-o:
After their teaching was condemned, Pelagian writers appealed to Rome with two letters defending their cause. Augustine replied with Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, a reply in four books. The work reaches readers here through the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

He brings scripture, church tradition, and close reasoning together in one sustained attack. Again and again he returns to his core claim: grace, not human will, does the saving. The controversy over Pelagius effectively ended with exchanges like this one. Augustine's view of grace went on to shape the teaching of the Western Church for centuries.
augustine-of-hippo-concerning-faith-of-t:
Augustine asks a plain question in Concerning Faith of Things Not Seen. How can people believe in things they have never laid eyes on? The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the short treatise in English.

Everyday life supplies his answers in case after case. We trust a friend's love though we cannot see it directly. We believe past events on the word of those who report them. Countless unseen things are accepted each day without a second thought. Faith in God, he argues, is no stranger than faith in each other. The great theologian appears here as a philosopher of ordinary trust.
augustine-of-hippo-expositions-on-the-bo:
Over many years Augustine preached his way through all one hundred fifty psalms. The Expositions on the Book of Psalms gather that life's work of sermons and notes. They reach modern readers in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Part commentary, part sermon, part spiritual diary, the expositions find Christ hidden in psalm after psalm. Augustine reads the whole Christian life out of the Church's prayer book. Kings, exiles, and singers of the Old Testament all become voices of the believer's own story. For centuries these volumes stood as the Church's favorite guide to the Psalms.
augustine-of-hippo-of-holy-virginity-npn:
Augustine praises virginity as a high calling in Of Holy Virginity. At the same time he warns virgins sternly against spiritual pride. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the treatise in English.

A humble married person, he says, outranks a virgin who boasts. That sharp reversal keeps the honor from rotting into vanity. Two truths are held together with care across the whole work. Celibacy is honored fully, and marriage is never despised beside it. The balance proved hard for later ages to keep so steady. Readers still profit from his refusal to let a great gift become a ground for pride.
augustine-of-hippo-of-the-work-of-monks-:
Some monks of Augustine's day claimed prayer excused them from manual labor. Of the Work of Monks answers that claim with plain disagreement. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the treatise in English.

Monks should work with their hands, Augustine argues at length. The apostle Paul made tents while preaching, and he sets the pattern. Ordinary work carries a dignity that spiritual pride must not scorn. The practical treatise shaped monastic rules for centuries to come. Its influence runs into the Benedictine pairing of prayer and work. Readers meet Augustine as a defender of common labor against an early form of religious elitism.
augustine-of-hippo-on-care-to-be-had-for:
A fellow bishop asked Augustine whether care for the dead does any good. On Care to Be Had for the Dead answers him with care. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the tender treatise in English.

Do prayers and burials truly help those who have died, he asks. The dead lie beyond our direct help, Augustine replies in sorrow. Prayer, alms, and the Eucharist offered for them still avail, he holds. His answer founded later teaching on praying for the departed. Grief itself receives gentle and thoughtful treatment along the way. Few ancient works console mourners with such calm, reasoned, and humane warmth as this one does.
augustine-of-hippo-on-christian-doctrine:
On Christian Doctrine serves as Augustine's handbook for preachers and readers. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the work in English. Its subject is how to read the Bible and how to teach it well.

Augustine sets rules for untangling hard and figurative passages. He then turns to clear and moving speech for the pulpit. Pagan learning, he argues, can serve God when rightly used. All truth, in his bold claim, belongs to believers already. The book in effect invented the idea of a Christian education. Its influence shaped Western schooling for a full thousand years after his death.
augustine-of-hippo-on-continence-npnf1-1:
Continence, for Augustine, means mastery over every appetite of life. Self-control of the body is only one part of his subject. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the treatise in English.

He presents continence as the virtue that makes other virtues possible. A well-governed soul keeps an inner order that spills into all conduct. Desire itself is not denied, but trained and directed toward good. His insight into the heart grew from his own long struggles. The Confessions tell that story, and this work draws its lessons. Profound reading on the discipline of desire remains on offer here for modern readers.
augustine-of-hippo-on-faith-and-the-cree:
Augustine explains the Apostles' Creed line by line in On Faith and the Creed. He wrote the clear exposition for new converts to the faith. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the work in English.

God the Father opens the articles, in the creed's own order. Christ's birth and suffering receive careful treatment in turn. The Holy Spirit, the Church, and the life to come follow after. Crystal clarity marks every paragraph of the short book. For fifteen centuries it has introduced Christians to their belief. Few teaching texts in any age match its calm and orderly survey of what the creed affirms.
augustine-of-hippo-on-grace-and-free-wil:
Monks troubled by Augustine's teaching on grace asked a fair question: if grace does everything, is free will a fiction? On Grace and Free Will, written for those monks, gives his most balanced answer. The treatise is printed here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Augustine answers no. Grace, he says, works through human willing rather than crushing it, so people still choose and still bear blame. God gives the good will, and the person acts with it. The book is short and unusually clear for so hard a subject. Later debates on freedom and grace have quoted it ever since.
augustine-of-hippo-on-lying-npnf1-1887:
Is it ever right to lie, even to save a life, Augustine asks. His answer in On Lying is absolute: no, never, in any case. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the treatise in English.

Relentless logic defends that hard position against every objection. Lies to shield the innocent get the same firm refusal as the rest. Joke lies and hard passages in scripture itself are faced squarely. Many readers find the argument uncomfortable, and that is the point. Augustine will not bend the rule for even the noblest motive. The book remains the classic statement of moral absolutism on truth-telling in the Western tradition.
augustine-of-hippo-on-man-s-perfection-i:
Can any person in this life reach a state without sin? Augustine takes up that question in On Man's Perfection in Righteousness, another reply to Pelagian claims. The short treatise survives here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, drawn from the Christian Classics Ethereal Library.

His answer is cautious: a sinless life might be possible by God's grace, yet in practice nobody achieves it. That is why, he notes, Christians still pray daily to be forgiven their debts. The tone stays humble and close to scripture throughout. Later debates about human perfection kept returning to the careful balance struck in these pages.
augustine-of-hippo-on-marriage-and-concu:
On Marriage and Concupiscence defends marriage from attacks coming in two directions at once. Some critics despised marriage itself, while the Pelagians denied that human desire had been disordered by sin. Augustine's treatise, in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers version, answers both sides.

He holds that marriage is a genuine good, blessed by God and honored by the Church. Yet the unruly desires felt even inside marriage show, for him, that human nature has fallen. The book is among his most personal pieces of theology. Readers of his Confessions will recognize the same struggles worked out here as doctrine.
augustine-of-hippo-on-nature-and-grace-n:
Pelagius taught that human nature, left to itself, was strong enough to live a righteous life. Augustine answered with On Nature and Grace, a careful reply that goes through his rival's book point by point. The treatise is presented here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Augustine insists that nature is wounded by sin and cannot heal itself. People need grace the way a sick person needs a doctor, not just good advice. Page after page, he presses the claim that no one can save himself by willpower alone. The work states his side of the early Church's greatest debate with unusual clarity.
augustine-of-hippo-on-patience-npnf1-188:
True patience, Augustine argues, is more than grimly bearing pain. The reason for enduring matters as much as the endurance itself. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the sermon-treatise in English.

Love of God must drive Christian patience, not mere stubborn pride. Endurance for show or spite earns no praise in his account. The line between real virtue and tough pretense is drawn with care. His insight into motives shows deep knowledge of the human heart. Short, searching, and quietly demanding, the work rewards slow reading. It asks readers to test not just what they bear, but why they choose to bear it.
augustine-of-hippo-on-rebuke-and-grace-n:
On Rebuke and Grace faces the hardest objection to Augustine's late teaching head-on. If everything rests on God's grace, why bother rebuking anyone for sin? Augustine wrote the treatise near the end of his life, and it appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

His reply is that rebuke itself can be one of the tools grace uses to turn a person around. Being corrected may be the very means by which God rescues someone. The argument is stern, but it comes from a bishop still wrestling honestly with hard mysteries. These pages show his mind working at full stretch in old age.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-catechising-of:
A bored deacon asked Augustine how to teach newcomers the faith. On the Catechising of the Uninstructed was his practical reply. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the guide in English.

How do you explain Christianity to someone who knows nothing at all? Tell the story of salvation simply, Augustine answers at length. Adapt the telling to the listener in front of you, he adds. Let joy in the teacher carry the message to the hearer. The result reads as a master class in the art of teaching. Many judges call it the wisest short book on religious education ever written.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-good-of-marria:
Some critics of Augustine's day despised marriage as a low state. On the Good of Marriage answers them with a firm defense. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the treatise in English.

Marriage is genuinely good, he argues, on three clear grounds. Its goods are children, fidelity between spouses, and the sacred bond itself. Celibate life is honored too, without making marriage a lesser calling. Balance and humanity mark the argument from start to finish. The treatise shaped Christian teaching on marriage for a millennium. Few ancient works on the subject have been quoted or followed as widely since his day.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-good-of-widowh:
Augustine wrote On the Good of Widowhood for a widow named Juliana. She had decided not to marry again after her husband's death. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the letter-treatise in English.

He honors her choice while insisting that remarriage is no sin. Practical counsel fills the warm and respectful pages that follow. Prayer, almsgiving, and the raising of children each receive attention. Augustine the pastor appears here at his most tender and personal. Deep respect for a woman's devotion runs through every paragraph. The work also gives a lovely glimpse of family life inside the early Christian world.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-grace-of-chris:
Two linked treatises by Augustine travel together in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers volume: On the Grace of Christ and On Original Sin. Both belong to his campaign against Pelagius and the teacher's followers. Together they round out his mature case on how grace works.

In the first treatise, Augustine argues that even Christ's human nature lived by God's gift, not by bare human strength. In the second, he defends the reality of original sin passed down from Adam. His point throughout is that no person stands without help from God. The writing is dense, argued with total conviction, and central to his later fame.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-merits-and-for:
Augustine of Hippo wrote On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins early in his long fight with the Pelagian movement. The treatise, given here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation, also covers the baptism of infants. Its central question is simple to state: why baptize babies who have done nothing wrong?

Augustine answers that every child inherits Adam's sin and so needs grace from the very start of life. Human effort, he argues, cannot earn forgiveness; God must give it freely. That claim became the classic Western teaching on original sin. Few early Christian books have shaped later belief more, or stirred more argument.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-proceedings-of:
In 415, the teacher Pelagius stood trial for heresy in Palestine and walked away acquitted. Augustine, his chief opponent, responded with On the Proceedings of Pelagius, a close review of the whole case. Readers meet it here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Augustine picks apart the trial record with a lawyer's patience, pointing out evasions, soft answers, and half-truths. He argues that the court cleared Pelagius without facing what the man actually taught. The result reads like ancient church politics laid bare. It shows a sharp controversialist at work on the most famous acquittal of his age.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-profit-of-beli:
Augustine wrote On the Profit of Believing for a tempted friend. The friend leaned toward the Manichaeans, the sect Augustine once followed. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the treatise in English.

Believe first and understand later, Augustine urges, and do not call it folly. Trust and authority must come before reason in every field of study. Even natural science rests on believing reports we cannot test ourselves. The defense of faith against doubt stays warm and conversational throughout. It ranks as his most accessible work on the topic. Readers meet a patient guide rather than a scolding judge in these pages.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-soul-and-its-o:
Where does each human soul come from? Augustine admits in On the Soul and Its Origin that he does not know. The treatise, aimed at claims by a young critic named Vincentius Victor, appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Few of his books sound so openly uncertain.

Two views stand before him: God creates each soul fresh, or souls pass from parents to children. Augustine tests both against scripture and finds hard questions on each side. He refuses to pretend a certainty he lacks. The book shows Augustine the honest inquirer rather than the dogmatist, curious and willing to confess ignorance.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-spirit-and-the:
On the Spirit and the Letter takes its title from a line by the apostle Paul: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. Augustine wrote the treatise during his dispute with the Pelagians, and it appears here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. It ranks among his shorter and most loved works.

Augustine argues that God's law, by itself, can only show people their guilt and condemn them. Only the Holy Spirit can change the heart so that a person loves what is right. Rules without inner grace fall short, he says, while grace makes real obedience possible. The book became a charter text for later teaching on grace.
augustine-of-hippo-on-the-trinity-npnf1-:
Fifteen books make up On the Trinity, Augustine's theological masterpiece. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers presents the vast work in English. Its question is the core mystery of the Christian faith itself.

How can God be three persons and yet one single being? Scripture, philosophy, and the human mind all serve the long inquiry. Memory, understanding, and will in us image the Trinity, he argues. The search runs deep and makes real demands on its readers. Many call it the most profound work of Western theology ever written. Sixteen centuries of readers have wrestled with its pages and come back for more.
augustine-of-hippo-our-lord-s-sermon-on-:
Augustine's commentary on the Sermon on the Mount walks through the most famous teaching Jesus ever gave. The Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, and the command to love enemies all receive close attention. His reading appears here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Augustine treats each saying as one step in the soul's climb toward God. Blessings for the meek and the merciful become stages in a ordered path of growth. The result mixes deep theology with a plain guide for daily conduct. For centuries, Christians learned how to read this sermon largely through Augustine's eyes.
augustine-of-hippo-soliloquies-npnf1-188:
Soon after his conversion, Augustine wrote the Soliloquies as a dialogue between himself and his own Reason. What do I want to know, Reason asks, and he answers: God and the soul, nothing else. The early work is presented in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Reason presses him hard, and the new convert argues his way toward trust in the soul's lasting life. Philosophy here becomes a kind of prayer, spoken aloud to oneself. The tone is intimate and searching rather than settled. Readers watch one of history's great minds thinking aloud in the first months of a changed life.
augustine-of-hippo-ten-homilies-on-the-f:
Ten sermons on the First Epistle of John, preached during the Easter season, form Augustine's Ten Homilies. Their text is the letter that says, simply, God is love. The homilies appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition from the Christian Classics Ethereal Library.

Augustine lingers over charity until it becomes the measure of everything else. His best-known saying lives here: love, and do what you will. The sermons are short, warm, and radiant rather than combative. Many readers treat them as the gentlest doorway into the mind of a demanding theologian. They reward slow reading, one sitting at a time.
augustine-of-hippo-the-anti-donatist-wri:
The Donatists held that sacraments from sinful priests were worthless. Augustine spent decades answering that claim in writing and debate. An 1887 Fathers volume collects his anti-Donatist works in English.

Church unity stands at the center of his long defense. Grace, he argues, works by Christ's power, not the minister's holiness. A bad priest cannot spoil a sacrament he does not own. The fight with the Donatists split North African Christianity for generations. Its outcome defined what the word church means in the West. Readers meet Augustine as a tireless controversialist guarding the oneness of his flock.
augustine-of-hippo-the-anti-manichaean-w:
Augustine spent nine years as a Manichaean before his conversion to Christianity. Afterward he spent years writing against his former sect in answer. An 1887 Fathers volume collects those anti-Manichaean writings in English.

The sect taught two warring gods, one of good and one of evil. Free will, the nature of good, and Genesis all come under review. Augustine answers as a man who once believed the system himself. No critic knew its weak points better than its former insider. His case rests on one God, good by nature, who made all things well. The volume shows a convert turning hard-won knowledge into a lifetime of argument.
augustine-of-hippo-the-enchiridion-on-fa:
A friend asked Augustine for a handbook of the faith to keep at hand. The Enchiridion was his compact and careful answer to that request. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers carries the summary in English.
