Faith, hope, and love give the small book its firm frame. Within it, God, Christ, grace, and the last things each receive clear treatment. No wasted words blur the famous clarity of the exposition. New readers of Augustine often start with this short volume. Veterans return to it as the best brief map of his thought. Few handbooks in Christian history have served so many readers so well for so long.
augustine-of-hippo-the-harmony-of-the-go:
Do Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John contradict one another? In The Harmony of the Gospels, Augustine sets out to prove they do not. The work, printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, weaves the four accounts into one ordered story of Jesus's life.

Where the Gospels seem to differ in order or detail, Augustine works to reconcile them with patience and ingenuity. He treats each writer as a truthful witness whose account fits the others. The book founded a long Christian tradition of gospel harmonies. It also shows his deep reverence for the text, verse by verse and scene by scene.
augustine-of-hippo-the-letters-of-st-aug:
More than two hundred seventy letters of Augustine survive in this 1887 volume. The Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series One, carries them in English. Augustine stands as the greatest mind of the early Western Church.

Bishops receive advice, heretics meet debate, and grieving friends find comfort. Hard questions of doctrine mix with the small cares of real people. The saint appears here as a working pastor, not a distant sage. Brilliant and humble by turns, he stays engaged on every page. Few letter collections from the ancient world feel this alive. Readers meet the man whole, in his own words and on his own busy days.
augustine-of-hippo-tractates-on-the-gosp:
One hundred twenty-four sermons on the Gospel of John make up Augustine's Tractates, preached over time to his own congregation at Hippo. The series moves verse by verse through the most mystical of the four Gospels. It is given here in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.

Augustine argues against heresies, unfolds the depths of grace, and always comes back to love. Listeners hear the prologue's high claims about the Word and the quiet talks of the farewell chapters alike. The sermons show Augustine the preacher at full power. Learned, passionate, and pastoral, they remain a landmark of early Christian preaching.
chaucer-canterbury-tales-1387:
Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in the late 1300s, in Middle English. This text gives the Tales and other poems in D. Laing Purves's standard edition. Chaucer stands as the founding figure of English literature as we know it.

Pilgrims ride from London to Canterbury and tell tales to pass the road. A knight, a miller, a wife of Bath, and a pardoner take turns. Their tales range from high romance to rude and hearty farce. Chaucer lets each voice sound true to rank, trade, and temper. The work opens a full world of medieval English life.
cia-0000009787:
An American prisoner of war died at the Viet Cong's K-71B hospital, a March 1974 report states. The heading adds a rear services unit number, cut off before its full designation. Prisoners sick enough for a hospital were often moved through several hands first.

A death in enemy medical care raised questions no battlefield loss did: when he fell ill, and what care he got. The report at least fixed a place and system for the death. Such facts mattered for the man's record and for judging the prison system's toll. The file closes one captive's story in a hospital entry.
cia-0000012287:
A second Helms memo to the Secretary of Defense's assistant followed in August 1961, keeping the Penkovsky correspondence moving at the top of the government. Two memos in two months to the same office show a channel in steady use. The colonel's reporting on Soviet forces demanded constant coordination between the agency that ran him and the department that planned against those forces.

The memo's brisk formality hides the weight of what it carried. Read in sequence, these letters form the case's drumbeat in the summer of 1961. For readers, they show the great spy case administered as routine, which was its own kind of marvel.
cia-0000012387:
Drop sites for Jig, Chalk, and Compass are listed in a CIA report from November 1960. The three code words name operations or channels in the Penkovsky world, and their dead drops formed a clandestine postal system across Moscow. A dead drop let two people who must never meet exchange film, money, or orders through a hollow place and a chalk mark.

The report maps those delivery points with paranoid care. Sites were chosen for cover, escape routes, and the habits of patrols. For readers, the list is the secret war's geography: the parcels' destinations, written down by the men who staked lives on them.
cia-0000013887: A captured American soldier wrote a leaflet by hand, and a CIA note dated October 6, 1967, reports the fact. The leaflet was an NVA or Viet Cong item, made to be spread as propaganda. A prisoner's own hand gave such a leaflet extra force with readers. The note shows how captives could be used in the war of words.
cia-0000014087: Security across five countries of the western Pacific is surveyed in a CIA report dated September 4, 1966. The report takes the region as a whole rather than one state at a time. Safety of bases, staff, and travel all fell under such surveys. A five country sweep let officials compare risks side by side and plan with the whole map in view.
cia-0000015287: A letter to Julius Stratton from H. Marshall Chadwell fills a CIA file dated January 2, 1953. Chadwell was a senior agency science chief. Stratton led a great tech school and advised the government. Their mail sits at the top of the 1953 saucer study, where the panel's shape was being set. The Chadwell letter is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015387: Responsibility for unidentified flying objects is the subject of a CIA file dated January 4, 1956. The stiff title asks whose job the whole topic was. By 1956 the Air Force held the public lead, yet paper still crossed the river. The file records one more round in the long game of passing the saucer desk.
cia-0000024387: Prospects for North and South Vietnam are weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1961. Vietnam had been split since 1954 into a communist north and an American backed south. In 1961 the southern war was growing and drawing in more American advisers. A two state forecast that year faced the hard question of whether the south could stand.
cia-0000042287:
Civilians were to be included in the DIA book of missing and captured personnel, a CIA record dated March 2, 1969 states. The DIA, the Defense Intelligence Agency, kept the official book of the missing. The title names Cocheo in connection with the change.

Inside, the policy point is plain: civilians would be listed beside servicemen. Until then, missing civilians risked falling outside the formal accounting. The file marks a widening of the promise to account for the lost. Reporters, advisers, and aid workers would now stand in the same book as the soldiers they had served beside.
cia-0000042887:
El Salvador's military was lagging on human rights, a CIA record dated April 3, 1990 states. The title ties the judgment to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. Lagging suggests promises made and then kept too slowly.

Inside, the gap between the army's pledges and its practice is the subject. Washington pressed for reform as a condition of its support. Each new aid debate in Congress returned to the same unmet demands on the generals. The generals promised change, and the record kept falling short. The file preserves that standing complaint in the spring of 1990, when the Jesuit case had made the army's rights record impossible for anyone to ignore.
cia-0000049087: Pedro Salazar reappeared in 1984, and a partly blacked-out CIA item records his return, kept with the Truth Commission records. A reappearance mattered when the man had been missing from the files, whether hiding, held, or simply lost to view. The redactions leave his story half told, which is how the series often tells it.
cia-0000049187: Redacted information on the Jesuit murder case fills a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. By then the case had a shape — order, patrol, cover-up — and each new fragment was fitted against it. This item's fragments arrive with their most sensitive names still hidden from the reader.
cia-0000049287:
Rightist violence in El Salvador is catalogued in a CIA paper from 1983, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. By 1983 the violence from the right had a routine: threats, seizures, bodies left where they would be found. It was written while the killing it describes was still rising. The paper sets that routine down as a subject for study.

Inside, the violence is treated as a campaign rather than a spasm, with patterns a reader can follow across cases. Catalogues like this one later served investigators who needed the pattern proven, not just felt. The paper shows the agency counting what the Salvadoran state would not.
cia-0000096487: Destruction of the rice crop in Kwangtung Province by insects is reported in declassified CIA document 0000096487, dated June 1, 1967. The heading names the province, the crop, and the cause. Readers find a short agricultural report from China coverage, a change of subject from politics to food supply in the agency's provincial reporting.
cia-0000097387: A Survey of Possible Soviet Actions with Attached Covering Memo is declassified CIA document 0000097387, dated May 5, 1963. The heading notes the covering memo as part of the package. The brief file is a survey record on possible Soviet moves, preserved with its attachment mentioned in the title, in standard estimate-era packaging.
cia-0000097987: Special National Intelligence Estimate on Prospects for Stability in the Dominican Republic, in shortened heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000097987, dated August 1, 1966. The title names the estimate type and its stability question. Readers get a short formal estimate record, the kind of judged outlook the agency reserved its special label for.
cia-0000098287: A redacted line regarding the Watergate burglary is the whole of declassified CIA document 0000098287, dated January 4, 1974. The heading itself announces that a line was deleted. The brief file is defined by that deletion, a Watergate record whose released form withholds the very line it exists to preserve, as the catalog states plainly.
cia-0000105887:
G-1 Recommendations for Tightening Idonesian Internal Security, Including the S is declassified CIA document 0000105887, dated February 2, 1965 in the catalog. The sample cable, on a February 19, 1965 G-1 meeting, completes the cut-off title. The missing words are the seizure of American oil companies and the expelling of some United States officials.

The summary says the G-1 meeting recommended seizing all Western business interests, including American, British, and Belgian property. It names the Stanvac and Caltex oil companies in particular. It also recommended declaring some United States officials persona non grata, for subversive activities they had engaged in there.
cia-0000107987: National Intelligence Bulletin is the short heading on declassified CIA document 0000107987, dated March 5, 1976. The title names a bulletin, a regular digest form, at national level. No single topic is named in the heading itself. The brief record is one dated issue of that bulletin, filed in the spring of 1976 as released in the files.
cia-0000108487: Dated August 2, 1981, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000108487 concerns an American missionary murdered in Guatemala. Its catalog heading notes the title was deleted, then breaks off at Guatem. The missionary is not named in the surviving heading text itself. The brief record preserves the deletion note, the estimate note, and the broken ending.
cia-0000115487: Dated February 1, 1981, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000115487 links Nicaragua with insurgents in El Salvador. Its heading calls the paper interagency, then breaks off at Interagenc in the title. Support is the link word in the heading itself, between the two countries named there. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000117887: Latin America Brief Deleted for 14 February 1992 - Guatemala: Showing Progess is the heading, with progress misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000117887, dated January 5, 1992. The brief is dated February 14 in its title, weeks after the file's own January date. Part of the brief was deleted, as the heading itself notes. The brief record preserves the misspelling and the date gap as released.
cia-0000118687: Gorbachev's Domestic Gambles and Instability in the USSR Dele is the heading, cut off mid-word, its date an estimate, on CIA document 0000118687 dated August 5, 1989. The title pairs Gorbachev's domestic gambles with instability in the USSR in one line. The ending breaks off at Dele, likely a deletion mark in the heading. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the break.
cia-0000119587:
Dated around August 1966, this CIA document concerns guidance on North Vietnam suggested to Eastern bloc countries. The source of the guidance was deleted before release, and the heading breaks off. During the war, Hanoi pressed its communist allies for aid and public support.

Guidance of this kind shows how the communist world coordinated its line on the war. What bloc capitals were urged to say, and give, shaped the support North Vietnam could count on. The document preserves that message as the agency obtained it, a small window into the diplomacy that ran behind the battlefield during the long fight over Vietnam.
cia-0000126887: A January 1968 CIA report covers Vice President Ky's plan to give up his special powers. The reason in the heading breaks off at a word starting with disco. Ky, South Vietnam's air force general turned politician, was at odds with President Thieu. The paper catches the strain inside Saigon's leadership.
cia-0000132287: Situation Report 596 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 5, 1991, reports a striking mistake: Baghdad believed the ground war had already begun. Iraq's leaders were braced for an invasion that had not yet come. False alarms were part of the fog that surrounded the crisis. The short report captures how the threat of attack looked from inside the Iraqi capital.
cia-0000132587: Growing Soviet attention to Cuba fills a CIA item dated September 2, 1960. Attention, in Cold War terms, meant money, arms, and advisers on their way. The item itself is brief, but the trend it marks was large. Moscow's courtship of Havana was hardening into a commitment that year, and the item records one step in that change.
cia-0000132687: The effects on the United States of a failed revolt in Cuba fill a CIA paper dated March 5, 1961. Early findings are promised in the headline, which breaks off mid-word. The failed revolt it names had already taken place by the time analysts wrote. The short paper weighs what the failure cost and what it taught. It reads as one more warning filed before the larger failure of April.
cia-0000132787:
The Cuban militia is profiled in a CIA paper dated October 3, 1960. The force numbered in the hundreds of thousands by the agency's count. Those men and women were Castro's insurance against the invasion he expected from the north.

The paper sets out the militia's size, arms, and training as analysts knew them. Six months later militiamen would in fact fight at the Bay of Pigs. For readers, the entry gives the order of battle before that test came. It also shows how a part-time citizen force had become a pillar of the regime's hold on the island.
cia-0000135687: A Spanish document dated 1 November 1960 opens the November run of records in the declassified 2506 Brigade files. The exile brigade was then training under CIA supervision for its planned landing in Cuba. The record carries no subject heading for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room. The piece is one dated part of the paperwork the brigade generated in the fall of 1960. That was before the operation had a public name or a known outcome.
cia-0000136087: The CIA cable of 6 March 1954 is about cargo flight schedules, the timetable of the air bridge that moved the operation's supplies, and it survives in declassified form. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136187: The declassified CIA cable dated 6 May 1954 takes up a leaflet drop arranged for BRODFROST, one more paper raid in the war of words. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136287: The CIA cable of 2 May 1954 is about broadcasts in general, one more cable for LANGEVIN in the long radio instruction series, and it survives in declassified form. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136887: A new aircrew man has accepted the offer, this April 1954 cable reports. Salary and a ten-dollar per diem will be set. The man holds a current commercial flight engineer rating. He also holds a pilot rating for single-engine planes. He has copilot time in DC-4s and Beechcraft. Crews should keep quiet around the new chief. No talk of salary. No talk of the true affiliation. LINCOLN should build him a cover story. It should follow the lines used for other crews.
cia-0000136987: References to Czechoslovakia need clarifying, this May 1954 cable advises. Frank Wisner signed it. The main points should be brought out. Czechoslovakia is a principal tool of Russia in Latin America. Czech embassies are used widely for this purpose. The Czech embassy in Mexico is a key coordinating center. The Alfhem arms shipment was arranged by Czechs throughout. The cable turns the arms scandal into a standing propaganda line.
cia-0000139487: Caucasian personnel sighted in North Korea are reported in this January 1954 account. A former prisoner tells the story. His column was marched northward through Manpo in November 1950. At dusk they passed a vehicle by the road. Three or four Caucasians sat in it. A companion had served on a consular staff. He recognized one man as a Soviet consular staff member from Peking. The excerpt also touches on Europeans who refused offers to settle in China. Such sightings evidenced Soviet advisers in Korea.
cia-03177787: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1958/03/29, a CIA publication. The March briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-03187387: January 16, 1959: the bulletin briefed leaders on world affairs. The intelligence community's daily product. The Cold War's new year. The archive guards it with care. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers. Kept for readers.
cia-06171287: BIOGRAPHIC - - JOSE MARIA ANDRES ASENSIO; ANTONIO BUSTOS; CRISTOBAL MARTINEZ B, a CIA document. The biographic file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-06626787: Diplomats got an earful about Jacobo Timerman from Buenos Aires. The 1981 circular painted the jailed editor as a villain. Propaganda dressed as diplomacy. Time has kept the file intact. Scholars of the era will find it useful.
constitution-philippines-1987: Philippines' 1987 Constitution, born of people power, frames its republic. It ousted Marcos. The Tower library holds the full text. It toppled a dictator. Crowds rose. Nuns marched. Democracy bloomed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
dawes-act-1887:
Congress passed the Dawes Act in 1887, in the allotment era's full swing. Tribal lands are broken into single-family plots by its terms. The so-called surplus land is then sold to white settlers.

Reformers promised the act would uplift Native peoples into farming life. Instead it became the greatest land theft in American history. Ninety million acres passed out of Native hands in one generation. Tribes lost land, cohesion, and much of their shared way of life. Assimilation as dispossession stands written plainly in federal law here for all. The act stayed in force for decades before policy finally turned.
dictionnaire-mytho-hermetique-1787: A 1787 mytho-hermetic dictionary decoded alchemical symbols. The hermetic lexicon, another edition. The symbolic dictionary. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the history. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
engels-working-class-1887:
Friedrich Engels was a young German clerk sent to Manchester to work in his family's cotton business in the 1840s. He walked the slums of the factory districts and wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England from what he saw. This English translation by Florence Kelley Wischnewetzky appeared in 1887.

Engels describes crowded courts, open sewers, child labor, and wages that barely kept families alive. He blames the new factory system itself, not the failings of the poor, for the misery around him. The book became a founding text of industrial sociology and of socialist reporting alike.
europmc-pmc10072287:
Osman and a large team review microplastics in a 2023 paper, covering their sources, formation, harms, and cleanup. Microplastics are plastic fragments smaller than a grain of rice. They have been found in oceans, soil, air, food, and drinking water, which has raised concern for human health.

The authors sort sources into ocean-based and land-based kinds. They explain how larger plastic breaks down into tiny pieces over time. They then survey health evidence and methods to remove or reduce the particles. The review is a broad guide to a growing pollution problem.
europmc-pmc10354987:
Uliano-Silva and the Darwin Tree of Life Consortium built a software pipeline in 2023 for a small but key genome. Each cell holds a tiny loop of DNA inside its power units, called the mitochondrial genome. Long, exact DNA reads from PacBio machines capture it well. No set tool had yet pieced it together from such reads.

Their tool, MitoHiFi, takes raw reads or draft pieces and returns the full loop. It labels the genes for proteins and RNA inside the loop. It also sorts out variant copies and DNA bits that leaked into the main genome. The team used it to build 374 such genomes, mostly from animals. Checks on 60 known species showed repeats that past work had missed.
europmc-pmc10504087:
Lee and a large team hunted in 2023 for how myeloma escapes immune drugs that target two marks. The marks are BCMA and GPRC5D, proteins on the cancer cell surface. Drugs that grip them, from lab-grown T cells to linking antibodies, can work well at first. Relapse often follows, and its cause was unclear.

The team read full genomes of cancer cells from 30 treated patients. In two cases, relapse clones had lost both copies of the BCMA gene. Lee found five more cases where small changes in BCMA blocked the drugs, though the protein still showed on cells. Four cases lost both copies of the GPRC5D gene. Choice of drug should match the mark a tumour still holds.
europmc-pmc10651487:
Zhang and a large team split rheumatoid arthritis joint tissue into subtypes in 2023, with the Accelerating Medicines Partnership: RA/SLE Network among the partners. The disease is an immune attack that swells and wrecks joints. Drugs help many patients, yet response varies for reasons still unclear. The team read cells in inflamed joint lining from 79 donors.

In all, they charted more than 314,000 cells with gene and surface data. Tissues fell into six groups, each rich in a distinct cell mix. Zhang shows the range ran from tissue packed with T and B cells to tissue near bare of them. Each group tied to its own risk genes, signals, and blood marks. The groups can shift, and they foretold drug response in the data.
europmc-pmc1079787:
Vanácová and colleagues report a new yeast complex that helps cells spot faulty RNA in this 2005 paper. RNA is the working copy of a gene, and cells must destroy bad copies before they cause harm. Yeast already had known enzymes that add a tail of adenine bases, called a poly(A) tail, to good RNA copies. One yeast protein, Trf4p, had been linked to the break-down of a flawed transfer RNA, a small RNA that helps build proteins.

The team showed Trf4p is the active core of a new complex with helper proteins. In lab tests, the complex tagged flawed RNA far more than healthy RNA. The tag then sped up shredding by the exosome, the cell's RNA disposal machine. The authors compare this tagging system to how bacteria clear out bad RNA.
europmc-pmc1088287:
Ezzati and colleagues test the idea that heart risks rise steadily as countries grow richer in this 2005 study. Heart disease and its diet-linked risks, such as high blood pressure and cholesterol, lead global death counts. Many expected these risks to climb with national income. The team compared body weight, blood pressure, and cholesterol data from over 100 countries against income and city living.

Weight and cholesterol rose fast with early income gains, then flattened and later fell, they found. Weight peaked at a lower income level than cholesterol did. Blood pressure, by contrast, barely tracked income at all. The authors argue the old view of these as diseases of wealth is too simple. They say risk paths bend as countries develop, so policy must fit each stage.
europmc-pmc11039887:
Luo, Zhao, Cheng, Su, and Wang review how immune cells switch modes and drive inflammatory diseases in this 2024 paper. Macrophages are frontline immune cells that can take two broad forms. The M1 form stirs inflammation, while the M2 form calms it. Keeping a steady balance between the two forms is key to body stability, the authors note.

When the balance tips, disease can follow or worsen. The review covers joint, brain, gut, and liver diseases driven by the immune system attacking the body. It also covers allergy diseases, artery clogging, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. For each, the authors explain which form dominates and why. They close by listing compounds and drugs found to shift the balance. Those agents are presented as candidate treatments that work by re-tuning the cells.
europmc-pmc11122687:
GBD 2021 Fertility and Forecasting Collaborators chart global fertility from 1950 to 2021 and forecast it to 2100 in this 2024 study. Birth trends reshape population age structures and bring social, economic, and political challenges. Sound estimates are needed to plan health care, labour supply, schooling, and family support. This study updates those estimates at global, regional, and national levels.

The team synthesised 8,709 country-years of registration data, 1,455 surveys and censuses, and 150 other sources. Statistical models produced birth rates for five-year age groups from age 10 to 54. Summing those rates gave the total fertility rate for each place and year. Forecasts rest on a reference scenario plus policy-dependent alternatives. The authors stress that family planning and gender equality policy hinge on such numbers.
europmc-pmc11224887:
Elendu and colleagues review training with simulated patients and scenarios in medical education in this 2024 paper. Simulation-based training lets students practise care on stand-ins rather than real patients. Modern forms include high-fidelity mannequins, virtual reality settings, trained actors as patients, and hybrids of these. The approach has spread as a transformative force in teaching.

Benefits listed include faster skill gain, fewer errors, and repeat practice with no risk to patients. Immediate feedback and structured debriefing lock in the learning, the authors say. Costs are the main barrier: the method needs heavy investment, specialised equipment, and trained faculty. Doubts persist about realism and whether skills transfer to real wards. Case studies and empirical work are reviewed as counterweight. The authors conclude the method earns its place despite the hurdles.
europmc-pmc11271387:
Ryan and a large team report long-term weight effects of semaglutide in the SELECT trial in this 2024 paper. SELECT enrolled 17,604 adults with prior cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity but no diabetes. Semaglutide had already shown a 20 percent cut in major cardiovascular events there. This prespecified analysis examined weight and body measures by starting body mass index.

Weight loss on semaglutide continued for 65 weeks and held for up to four years, the team reports. At 208 weeks, weight fell 10.2 percent on the drug versus 1.5 percent on placebo. Waist size fell 7.7 centimetres versus 1.3. Meaningful loss appeared in all races, in both sexes, and in every body size and region. Serious adverse events were fewer on semaglutide in every weight category.
europmc-pmc11339187:
GBD 2021 Lower Respiratory Infections and Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators estimate the burden of chest infections other than COVID-19 in this 2024 study. Lower respiratory infections, mainly pneumonia and bronchiolitis, are a major global cause of illness and death. Pandemic-era measures in 2020 and 2021 cut the spread of many other respiratory germs too. Tracking these infections and their causes can guide health system responses.

The analysis covers 1990 to 2021 for 204 countries and territories. It drew on 26,259 site-years of mortality data, fitted with an ensemble model. Incidence and the share blamed on each pathogen were estimated by age and sex. Effects of the pandemic years on select respiratory viruses are built into the estimates. Results are given globally, regionally, and nationally. The authors aim the numbers at funding priorities to cut future burden.
europmc-pmc11445387:
Lu and colleagues review type 2 diabetes in adults, from its causes to prevention and therapy, in this 2024 paper. The disease features a progressive loss of insulin secretion from pancreatic islet beta cells, usually after insulin resistance sets in. Insulin is the hormone that lowers blood sugar. The authors treat the condition as one part of a wider metabolic dysfunction syndrome.

Shared pathways drive both insulin resistance and beta cell failure, they explain. These include inflammation, stress in the protein-folding compartment, oxidative stress, and fat deposited in the wrong organs. There is no cure, but lifestyle intervention and some medications can prevent the disease or push it into remission. If prevention fails, holistic and personalised management should start at once. Companion conditions such as obesity and fatty liver disease must be managed alongside.
europmc-pmc1173087:
Peters and Sette present a software implementation of their stabilized matrix method in this 2005 paper. Many molecular processes recognise short sequences, such as immune peptides binding to MHC molecules, the display platforms that show cell contents to the immune system. From experimental data, a model of that sequence specificity can be built as a motif, a scoring matrix, or a neural network.

Such models summarise results and predict outcomes for untested sequences. Their method, the stabilized matrix method, had already predicted peptide binding to MHC, peptide transport by the TAP transporter, and proteasomal cleavage of proteins. The proteasome is the cell's protein shredder. Here the algorithm is released as publicly available software so other labs can build models the same way. The authors describe the implementation and its intended uses.
europmc-pmc1197287:
Yang and a large team designed broad coronavirus blockers in 2005. Coronaviruses cause common and severe disease in people and animals. No licensed drug then targeted them directly. Fast change and varied entry routes make broad drugs hard.

One viral enzyme, the main protease, looked like a shared weak spot. Crystal views of four forms showed a near identical grip pocket. The team built blockers fitted to that pocket. Tests confirmed the blockers halt the enzyme as designed. Yang offers a route toward drugs that cover many coronaviruses. It appeared in PLoS Biology in 2005.
europmc-pmc1247187:
Kamel and Hoppin reviewed pesticide exposure and nerve harm in 2004. Sudden high-dose poisoning clearly damages nerves. Whether long moderate exposure also harms nerves was disputed. The review weighs studies across pesticide types and outcomes.

Most studies found more neurologic symptoms with moderate exposure. Thinking and movement test scores also tended to drop. Evidence for sensory and nerve conduction harm was thinner. Organophosphate insecticides dominated the record, but fungicides and fumigants showed effects too. Pesticide exposure may also raise Parkinson disease risk. Kamel calls the symptom pattern the most sensitive signal. Gulf War syndrome is named as a like case. Most of the work looked at bug sprays used on farms and in homes.
europmc-pmc1247387:
Eskenazi and colleagues studied pesticide exposure in pregnancy in California farm country in 2004. The cohort held low-income Latina women in the Salinas Valley. Urine tests twice in pregnancy measured organophosphate breakdown products. Blood tests measured enzymes these pesticides suppress.

No adverse link appeared between exposure and fetal growth. Some exposure measures tied to longer bodies and larger heads instead. Gestation length results ran in a different direction in fuller results. Eskenazi reports a mixed picture that defies simple harm claims. The null growth finding itself matters for farm community health debates. Urine was checked two times in each pregnancy.
europmc-pmc1334387:
Benton, Sachse, Michnick, and Vosshall probed fruit fly smell receptors in living flies in 2006. Each smell neuron carries two receptors: a tuned one and OR83b, a shared partner. OR83b is essential for smell and boosts receptor function. Its working mechanism was unknown.

OR83b pairs with conventional receptors early inside the cell. It escorts the pair to the sensory cilia where smelling happens. The pair alone could install odor responses in neurons tuned only to carbon dioxide. Fly receptors also sit in membranes flipped versus known receptors. Their inner loops mediate the pairing with OR83b.
europmc-pmc1551987:
Stress and pollution may team up against mothers and babies. Morello-Frosch and Shenassa argued in 2006 that this double jeopardy helps explain health gaps. Black women in the US bear very low-weight babies at twice the rate of white women. Infant death gaps persist despite overall gains.

The pair propose that chronic stress wears down the body's defenses, captured in a concept called allostatic load. A worn body may suffer harm from pollutants at lower doses. Their framework for the environmental riskscape joins place-based stress with chemical exposure. Morello-Frosch calls for holistic studies of how the two forces interact.
europmc-pmc1637787:
Poisonous algae are blooming more often around the world. Van Dolah reviewed marine algal toxins in 2000, their origins and health effects. The toxins reach people through tainted shellfish and fish, and through water and spray.

Over three decades, toxic incidents grew in frequency and spread. Novel sources have poisoned people for the first time. The rise parallels large-scale ecological disturbance and global warming trends. Van Dolah asks how far human activity drives the increase. Understanding that link matters, since the toxins are potent and the events hard to predict.
europmc-pmc1784087:
Armfield, Stewart and Spencer tested in 2007 the idea of a vicious cycle linking fear of the dentist to poor oral health. In their model, fear leads people to delay visits, delay worsens tooth problems, and problem-driven visits then feed more fear.

The team ran a telephone survey of 6,112 Australian residents aged 16 and over. People with higher dental fear visited less often and expected to wait longer before any future visit. They also reported worse oral health, greater life impact from it, and more need for treatment. Their visits were more often driven by pain or a pressing problem. Among the very fearful, 29.2 percent showed the full pattern of delay, poor health, and symptom-driven care, against 11.6 percent of the fear-free group.
europmc-pmc1874187:
Hayes and colleagues tested whether pesticide mixtures harm frogs at doses that single-chemical tests would call safe. Amphibians are declining worldwide, and most pesticide studies use one chemical at high doses. Real farm runoff holds many chemicals at once, at far lower levels, some of which disrupt hormones.

The team exposed leopard frog larvae to nine cornfield pesticides, singly at 0.1 parts per billion or mixed, plus paired herbicide tests in two frog species. Single chemicals at that dose did little. The nine-pesticide mixture broke the normal pattern where slower developers grow larger: slow larvae ended up smaller instead. The mixture also damaged the thymus, suppressed immunity, and let a bacterial meningitis take hold. A companion study tied the effects to raised levels of the stress hormone corticosterone.
europmc-pmc1896187:
Palmer, Relman, Brown and co-authors followed in 2007 how a baby's gut microbes assemble during the first year of life. A new ecosystem forms in the intestine almost at once after birth, yet its timing, sources, and variation between babies were poorly known. The team built a custom microarray to detect most recognized bacterial groups by their ribosomal RNA genes.

They profiled an average of 26 stool samples from each of 14 healthy full-term infants, including fraternal twins, from the first stool onward. Mothers' vaginal, milk, and stool samples, plus fathers' and siblings' stool, were profiled to trace origins. Community composition shifted over the year in patterned ways, and babies differed from each other. The survey gives a systematic baseline for how the infant gut ecosystem develops.
europmc-pmc1914087:
Vacic, Dunker, Lonardi and colleagues released Composition Profiler in 2007, a web tool that compares the amino acid mix of one protein set against another. Proteins in a functional class often favor or avoid certain building blocks. Spotting those skews by hand across thousands of sequences is impractical.

The user supplies a query sample and a reference sample, such as a standard protein database or a contrasting protein group. The tool reports which single amino acids, or groups sharing traits like charge or water avoidance, are enriched or depleted. Results come back as both text and charts. As an exploratory mining tool, it can steer feature choice for predictors of protein function or shape. For well-separated classes it also works as a quick visual classifier.
europmc-pmc1968187:
Wyllie delivered the 1992 Frank Rose Memorial Lecture, published in 1993, on apoptosis, the orderly self-destruction of cells. Unlike messy accidental death, apoptosis shows characteristic structural features and runs as a gene-regulated program. Cancer genes sit on both sides of its control.

The gene c-myc can act as a two-way switch. With growth factors present it drives cell division. When growth support is withdrawn or the cycle is blocked, it drives apoptosis instead. In living tissue, c-myc activity may mark a high-turnover state where division and death coexist. Other cancer genes, such as ras and bcl-2, rescue cells from apoptosis and tip that balance into rapid growth. The tumor suppressor p53 may trigger apoptosis by halting the cycle in c-myc cells. Sensitivity to chemotherapy, Wyllie argues, partly reflects movement between these states.
europmc-pmc2000887:
Nygard, Jørgensen, Cirera and Fredholm compared reference genes for pig gene studies in 2007. Real-time PCR measures gene activity, but results need a stable internal standard. Such standards are called reference genes. A poor choice can distort every comparison. The team tested nine common candidates in 17 pig tissues.

They used SYBR green PCR and the geNorm tool to rank stability. Stability varied greatly between genes. Beta-actin and ribosomal protein L4 ranked most stable overall. TATA box binding protein and HPRT1 also ranked high. GAPDH ranked least stable. The authors suggest beta-actin and RPL4 for abundant gene messages. They suggest TBP and HPRT1 for low-abundance messages in studies across pig tissues.
europmc-pmc2001387:
Draper, Sanders and Kingston followed 882 patients with retinoblastoma in 1986, an eye cancer of childhood. They asked how often survivors developed a second, separate cancer. The series included 384 patients with the inherited form of the disease. The authors also weighed the treatments used for the first cancer, including radiation and cyclophosphamide.

Thirty patients developed second primary cancers. By 18 years after diagnosis, the rate reached 4.2 percent overall. For the inherited form it reached 8.4 percent, and 6.0 percent for bone cancer alone. Risk was higher inside the radiation field. Evidence suggested inherited cases are especially sensitive to radiation. Rates here were lower than in earlier published series.
europmc-pmc2024987:
Hewitt, Blake and Walder challenged in 1976 the popular idea that the body actively defends itself against cancer. Their evidence came from 27 mouse tumours that arose spontaneously, not from chemicals or viruses. Such tumours were transplanted between genetically matched mice. The authors argue these are the only fair models of human cancer. Chemically induced tumours, they say, create artificial immunity.

Across roughly 20,000 maintenance transplants, not one failed or shrank away. Almost 10,000 tumours from small cell doses were watched, and none regressed on their own. Prior injection of irradiated tumour cells actually made recipients more receptive, not less. Lymphocytes from sensitised mice gave no protection either. The team found no trace of tumour immunogenicity, meaning no immune rejection of these cancers.
europmc-pmc2124787: A medical paper on pleomorphism and pleobiosis of Bacillus bifidus communis. The shape-shifting gut germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2124887: A medical paper with studies in isoagglutination, tonicity in isohemagglutination. The salty clumping. This article preserves that serology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125487: A medical paper on the interrelation of the surviving dog heart and pancreas in sugar metabolism. The organs' teamwork. This article preserves that physiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2126287: A medical paper on the encystment of dysentery amebae in vitro. The encysted amebae. This article preserves that parasitology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2126687: A medical paper on the relation of the pneumococcus to hydrogen ion concentration, acid death-point. The germ's acid limit. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128287: A medical paper with immunological studies on a leptospira strain from a yellow fever case. The jaundice germ. This article preserves that immunology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128587: A medical paper on classification of the hemolytic streptococci by the precipitin reaction. The sorted strep. This article preserves that bacteriology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131087: A medical paper with serological studies on the blood of primates, blood groups. The ape blood. This article preserves that serology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2131287: A medical paper on the etiology of Oroya fever, the response of the skin of macaques. The monkey skin. This article preserves that tropical medicine. It awaits future readers. It holds its historical place. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131487: A medical paper on nitrogen metabolism of normal and sarcomatous fibroblasts in pure cultures. The cells' nitrogen. This article preserves that cell biology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140087:
Rosen and colleagues searched human urine in 2007 for evidence that bladder bacteria live inside cells. Urinary tract infections are mostly caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli. In mice these bacteria invade bladder lining cells and form intracellular bacterial communities, clusters that can seed repeat infections. Whether that cycle happens in women was unknown. The team collected urine from 80 young women with acute cystitis and 20 without symptoms.

Communities shed from bladder cells appeared in 14 of 80 infection samples, which is 18 percent. Thread-like filamentous bacteria appeared in 41 percent. Neither sign appeared in any control sample. All community-positive samples also carried filaments. Among Escherichia coli infections, 22 percent showed communities. No gram-positive infections did. The results suggest an intracellular niche may drive recurrence in some women.
europmc-pmc2235887:
Kitson and co-authors examined the PARiHS framework in 2008, a model for getting research evidence into health practice. PARiHS, short for Promoting Action on Research Implementation (PARiHS) in Health Services, is widely used to frame implementation work. Yet as a concept it remains untested, and its contribution to theory is unquantified. The paper clarifies the difference between a conceptual framework, a theory and a model, borrowing a typology from social policy analysis.

The authors propose using PARiHS in two stages. First, diagnose the evidence and the local context using its elements and sub-elements. Then use those combined scores to choose the most fitting facilitation method. The intervention is thereby shaped by the specific people, place and time. They recommend an international collaborative to collect experiences and test the framework systematically.
europmc-pmc2323687: Living things hum with tiny sparks, and this paper measured the sparks behind life's acts. Tests across live samples set the scale. The life sparks, gauged. The article keeps that life-chemistry study. Kept for study.
europmc-pmc2360687:
Eisen and a large team reported a trial of sorafenib in advanced melanoma in 2006. Sorafenib is a pill that blocks several growth signals in tumors and their blood vessels. Melanoma is a skin cancer that, once spread, had few working treatments at the time.

All 37 patients first took the drug for 12 weeks at 400 milligrams twice daily. Only one tumor shrank by at least a quarter, and 27 grew by that much and stopped treatment. Six patients with stable disease entered a randomised phase, but all on the drug progressed by week 24. Across all patients, 19% had stable disease and 62% progressed, with a median time to progression of 11 weeks. Skin rash affected 51% of patients. A common gene fault, V600E BRAF, did not predict who stayed stable. The authors judged the drug well tolerated but nearly inactive alone.
europmc-pmc2627687:
Altekruse, Stern, Fields, and Swerdlow reviewed Campylobacter jejuni in 1999 as an emerging foodborne pathogen in the United States. The bacterium had become America's most commonly reported bacterial cause of foodborne illness. Human and economic costs were compounded by chronic after-effects in some patients, notably Guillain-Barré syndrome, a paralysing nerve disorder, and reactive arthritis.

Mishandling raw poultry and eating undercooked poultry were the major risk factors for infection. An increasing share of human infections was also proving resistant to antimicrobial therapy, narrowing treatment options. The authors argue that prevention efforts are needed at every link of the food chain. That runs from farm production through processing, retail, and home kitchens. No single intervention point is enough.
europmc-pmc2648987:
Yuan and co-authors showed in 2009 that mouse embryonic stem cells send tiny parcels that can reprogram the cells around them. The parcels, called microvesicles, are bubbles of cell skin shed into the fluid nearby. Blood cells shed them too, and they had already been seen moving proteins and RNA between cells.

The team read what these stem cell parcels carry. They were rich in microRNAs, short RNA pieces that tune how genes are used. The researchers loaded parcels with a glowing marker gene and its protein product. Other stem cells took the parcels in and began to glow themselves. Parcels also passed a share of their microRNAs into mouse support cells in the dish. Stem cells, the authors suggest, may steer their neighbors by mail, not only by direct touch.
europmc-pmc2700087:
Treweek and Zwarenstein argued in 2009 that medical trials are often built to answer narrow questions cleanly, then fail the real world they were meant to guide. A randomized trial is the best tool for judging whether a treatment works. But randomization alone says nothing about whether results apply to other patients, clinics, or countries.

The authors contrast two attitudes. Explanatory trials test a treatment under ideal, tightly controlled conditions. Pragmatic trials test it under the messy conditions of routine care, with ordinary patients and staff. Most trials lean explanatory, so their results travel poorly, and users of research must guess at applicability. The review sets out how to judge that leap honestly. If evidence is to steer practice and policy, they conclude, more trials should be designed pragmatically from the start.
europmc-pmc2701987:
Albert, Robertson, and Miall showed in 2009 that the resting brain is not idle after learning: it replays and processes what was just practiced. Brain networks hum in slow waves even with no task, and what that hum is for was contested, daydreaming or readiness. The team scanned volunteers resting before and after eleven minutes of learning a joystick tracking task.

Only the learners changed. A front-to-back network spanning frontal and parietal areas, plus a cerebellar network never before described at rest, altered their resting pattern after training. Volunteers who merely performed the movements without learning anything new showed no such change. The very networks used during the task were the ones retuned afterward. Rest, the authors conclude, is when the brain files the lesson, which makes resting scans a possible window into memory consolidation.
europmc-pmc2725087:
Petersen and co-authors presented in 2009 a generic method for protein studies. It predicts how exposed each amino acid in a protein is to solvent. It also scores how reliable each prediction is. Knowing whether a building block sits buried or exposed helps infer protein shape and function. Discrete class predictions have natural confidence scores, but a single real-value prediction does not.

An ensemble of neural networks trained on solved protein structures outputs both exposure and a reliability Z-score in one step, rather than bolting reliability on afterward. On a standard test set its accuracy matched the best public method of the time. Among the top fifth of predictions ranked by its score, accuracy beat the rival score at every subset size, which makes its reliability measure more informative.
europmc-pmc2772987:
Half, Bercovich, and Rozen reviewed in 2009 familial adenomatous polyposis. In this inherited condition, tens to thousands of adenomas fill the rectum and colon. The small growths appear from the second decade of life. It strikes about one in eight thousand births, affects both sexes equally, and accounts for under one percent of colorectal cancers. Most patients feel nothing for years, until bleeding, anemia, or cancer appears.

Classic disease follows a dominant pattern and stems from a germline mutation in the APC gene, carried in every cell from birth. A milder attenuated form brings fewer polyps, later onset, and lower cancer risk. A recessive look-alike stems from MUTYH mutations instead. Diagnosis rests on family history, examination, and colonoscopy, confirmed by genetic testing where possible, and relatives should then be tested too.
europmc-pmc2912887:
Gaujoux and Seoighe released in 2010 an R software package that unifies nonnegative matrix factorization, a data-mining method that splits big tables into interpretable parts. The method powers face recognition, text mining, and gene expression analysis, where it can pull tumor subtypes out of thousands of gene measurements. Until then most implementations lived on commercial platforms or demanded programming skill, shutting out many biologists.

The package ports published algorithms into the free R and Bioconductor ecosystem behind one simple interface. Users can swap algorithms and starting methods freely, or bolt in their own variants to test. Built-in benchmark data and plots help judge whether a factorization is stable and meaningful. The goal is reproducibility: one shared testbed where new methods prove themselves against the classics.
europmc-pmc2944787:
Illingworth and colleagues mapped CpG islands, short DNA stretches rich in C and G bases, across human and mouse genomes in a 2010 study. Such islands usually sit at gene start sites and stay free of chemical silencing marks.

Using a capture method plus deep sequencing, they found both species carry very similar island counts, often at matching spots near genes. About half the islands, more than ten thousand, are orphans with no known gene start nearby. Many orphans still sparked gene activity and changed during development, often gaining silencing marks as their active features faded.
europmc-pmc2945087:
Taccone and colleagues ran a 2010 study across four Belgian intensive care units. They checked whether standard first doses of common antibiotics reach strong enough blood levels in the sickest sepsis patients. Severe illness reshapes how drugs spread and clear from the body.

Eighty patients received one of four beta-lactam antibiotics, with blood sampled over the hours after the first dose. For each drug, levels stayed above a demanding target for only part of the dosing gap, ranging from about a third to just over half the interval. The results argue that first doses in severe sepsis often fall short.
europmc-pmc2946687:
Manchanda, Sanchaita, and Singh reviewed multidrug resistant Acinetobacter, a hospital germ increasingly hard to treat, in a 2010 article based on database searches. The bacteria survive well in hospital surroundings and cause many care-linked infections.

The review sorts out confusing labels for levels of resistance. It then walks through how the germ defeats drug after drug. Enzyme families that break key antibiotics get full treatment. Current options get full coverage for adults and children alike. They range from older last-resort drugs such as colistin to newer agents and paired drug mixes. Strong infection control and careful antibiotic use are urged to slow further spread.
europmc-pmc3026687:
Alonso and a large expert group introduced in 2011 a shared research agenda aimed at wiping out malaria for good. Policy had recently shifted from only controlling the disease toward stopping its spread entirely and eradicating it. The group, called malERA in short, spent two years of meetings sorting out what science still had to deliver for that goal.

Their agenda lists the knowledge, tools, and strategies still missing, from better drugs and vaccines to ways of tracking silent infections. The paper opens a supplement that works through each theme in depth. Acting on the plan could make elimination possible even in the hardest hit regions, the authors argue. They warn that commitment has to start right away, not after control programs stall.
europmc-pmc3068987:
Carroll, Booth, and Cooper presented in 2011 a worked example of a shortcut method for combining interview based research, which they call best fit framework synthesis. Systematic reviews increasingly include people's views, not just trial numbers, but the classic methods for merging such studies are slow. Their test case asked how adults feel about taking pills or supplements that might prevent bowel cancer.

Starting from an existing model in the literature, they coded twenty papers from four regions against its themes, then added new themes the model missed. The result was a richer model of how people weigh uncertain benefits against daily burden and side effect worries. The method finished within a tight assessment timetable. The authors judge it fit for purpose and recommend wider trials of the approach. It offers review teams a structured yet flexible middle path.
europmc-pmc3078587:
Chua, Charles, Baracos, and Clarke showed in 2011 that a ratio from a routine blood count can forecast how advanced bowel cancer patients will do on chemotherapy. The ratio compares neutrophils, front line infection fighters, with lymphocytes, and it rises with body wide inflammation. The team checked it in two separate patient groups receiving first line treatment for cancer that could not be removed.

A high starting ratio meant less benefit from treatment, faster progression, and shorter survival in both groups, even after other factors were counted. How a patient generally functioned also mattered, but the ratio added independent warning. In patients whose ratio settled back to normal after one treatment cycle, the disease stayed controlled longer. Because the test is cheap and already in the chart, the authors propose it for everyday risk sorting, including in clinics with few resources.
europmc-pmc3113287:
The Endogenous Hormones and Breast Cancer Collaborative Group pooled data from seventeen long-term studies for a 2010 report in The Lancet Oncology. They studied a growth factor in blood that drives cell division and blocks cell death, asking whether higher levels predict breast cancer. Records covered thousands of women who later developed the disease and matched controls in twelve countries.

Women in the highest fifth for the growth factor had a notably higher risk of breast cancer than women in the lowest fifth. Adjusting for its main binding protein did not change the result, and the link held before and after menopause. The raised risk appeared only for tumours that respond to the hormone oestrogen. The study gives one of the firmest estimates of this hormone-related risk.
europmc-pmc3168787:
Ramesh Kuhad, Rishi Gupta, and Ajay Singh reviewed microbe-made enzymes that digest plant fibre in a 2011 paper in Enzyme Research. These cellulases, built from mixing-and-matching modules, are produced by a wide range of fungi and bacteria growing on plant material. Their industrial reach keeps expanding.

Uses span paper and pulp, textiles, laundry detergents, biofuel making, food and animal feed, brewing, and farming. The review explains the three-part enzyme team that together snips fibre chains down to sugar. It contrasts the simple free enzymes of fungi with the scaffolded enzyme complexes of some bacteria. Attention now centres on cutting production costs so fibre-based processes can compete. The authors survey production advances and the economic hurdles still blocking wider use.
europmc-pmc3182887:
Wing To and Kim Midwood reviewed the two lives of a versatile repair protein in a 2011 paper in Fibrogenesis and Tissue Repair. Fibronectin circulates dissolved in blood and is also built locally by cells into a fibrous mesh. During healing, the blood form joins the early clot, helping platelets seal the wound.

Cell-made fibronectin then takes over as cells migrate in, assembling a three-dimensional scaffold that is far more than packing material: it directs cell behaviour throughout repair. Assembly follows a strict stepwise process with many regulators. When assembly runs wild, the same mesh drives fibrosis, the stiff scarring that ruins organs. Understanding its controls, the authors argue, may yield therapies that keep repair on the healthy side of that switch.
europmc-pmc3231187:
Che-Chang Yang and Yeh-Liang Hsu reviewed wearable motion detectors built on accelerometers in this 2010 paper in Sensors. How a person moves reveals much about mobility, chronic disease, and aging, and small worn accelerometers offer a practical way to measure it. The authors survey how the technology developed and where it is used.

They explain how accelerometry works, the properties of the sensors, and where on the body they are placed. Studies they review classify posture and movement, estimate energy expenditure, detect falls, and evaluate balance. The paper then compares commercial products, giving a snapshot of the market at the time. It closes with an outlook on emerging technologies for activity monitoring.
europmc-pmc3257687:
Margaret Clagett-Dame and Danielle Knutson reviewed vitamin A in reproduction and development in this 2011 article in Nutrients. The vitamin's importance for reproduction was recognized in the early nineteen hundreds, and its role in the developing eye soon after. The active form is retinoic acid, and the review explains how that conclusion was reached from feeding studies in rats and genetic studies in mice.

Retinoic acid reverses most blocks caused by vitamin A deficiency, and mice lacking its receptors reproduce most of the same defects. Enzymes that destroy the acid control which tissues get access to it, a key regulatory trick. In females, reproduction fails before implantation without the vitamin; in supported but deficient pregnancies, embryos form with a characteristic set of defects. The vitamin also maintains the male reproductive tract, drives sperm production, and triggers meiosis in the developing gonads of both sexes.
europmc-pmc3266187:
Yoshio Sumida and colleagues validated a simple blood-based fibrosis score in Japanese patients with fatty liver disease, in this 2012 paper in BMC Gastroenterology. Doctors need a cheap, noninvasive way to tell which patients have advanced liver scarring without a biopsy. The FIB4 index combines age, two liver enzymes, and platelet count, and the team tested it against biopsy results in nearly six hundred patients.

The index outperformed six rival scoring systems at separating advanced from mild fibrosis. Below its proposed low cut-off it missed very few advanced cases, correctly clearing ninety-eight percent of patients it flagged as low risk. Above the high cut-off it overcalled more often, so a high score still needs confirmation. Using both cut-offs, most patients were classified correctly, and adopting the index would spare well over half of them a liver biopsy.
europmc-pmc3274487:
Peter Gething and colleagues produced a new world map of falciparum malaria for 2010, in this 2011 paper in the Malaria Journal. How intensely malaria transmits shapes nearly every decision about controlling it, and maps must stay current to guide those decisions. The team updated the first global endemicity map, made for 2007, and added two new layers.

They combined incidence records from more than thirteen thousand administrative units with over twenty-two thousand parasite surveys in a geostatistical model to draw a continuous surface of transmission. Further models converted that surface into the rate at which mosquitoes deliver infectious bites and the parasite's basic reproduction number, each map carrying its own uncertainty estimates. Over a billion people lived at risk of unstable transmission and nearly one and a half billion at risk of stable transmission; extreme values clustered in Africa.
europmc-pmc3314787:
Weller led a consensus group that set shared standards for research on diagnosing cancer early, published in 2012. Catching cancer sooner improves survival, but studies of the path from first symptom to diagnosis used clashing terms and methods. That made results hard to compare or trust, so experts met in Aarhus, Denmark, to agree on common ground.

The statement offers shared definitions for the time points and intervals along the path to diagnosis, plus advice on study design. A companion checklist, named after the host city, lets researchers show they measured and reported those intervals clearly. The group hopes the standards will make future studies more precise and open, and plans to update the guidance as researchers report back on using it.
europmc-pmc3344687:
Lin and colleagues traced how blood pigment released by a brain bleed drives inflammation and worsens injury, in a 2012 study. Bleeding inside the brain, called intracerebral hemorrhage, kills or disables many patients, and inflammation around the bleed adds heavily to the damage. The team focused on a sensor protein, TLR4, that switches on immune defenses in brain support cells called microglia.

After a bleed in mice, TLR4 levels climbed sharply in activated microglia around the clot. Mice lacking TLR4 suffered less swelling and milder movement problems, and two partner pathways beneath it were both involved. Adding hemin, the iron bearing part of blood pigment, raised TLR4 further and worsened injury in normal mice but not in those missing the sensor. Blocking TLR4 with an antibody calmed the microglia. The authors propose the pathway as a drug target for brain bleeds.
europmc-pmc3346787:
Johnston and colleagues estimated how many deaths worldwide are caused each year by smoke from landscape fires, in a 2012 study. Fires in forests, grasslands, and peat release enormous amounts of carbon and blanket whole regions in haze, often in poor tropical areas. The team combined a global air chemistry model with satellite readings to map daily and yearly exposure to fine smoke particles from 1997 to 2006.

Their central estimate lands near three hundred forty thousand deaths a year attributable to fire smoke, with a wide uncertainty band. Sub Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia carried the heaviest burdens. Deaths roughly doubled in El Niño years compared with La Niña years, showing how climate swings drive the toll. The authors argue that curbing the burning of tropical rainforest, which rarely burns naturally, could save many lives.
europmc-pmc3388687:
Heyland, Dhaliwal, Jiang, and Day built a nutrition risk score in 2011 for intensive care patients, the group feeding helps most. Their prospective study enrolled nearly six hundred patients expected to stay over a day. Candidate ingredients ranged from age and illness severity scores to recent weight loss and blood markers of inflammation.

Points were assigned by how strongly each factor tracked with death within twenty-eight days. As the score rose, so did death rates and time on breathing machines. Some ingredients, including body mass index and two inflammation markers, were dropped from the final score. Crucially, good feeding changed the score's link with survival, which is what a useful triage tool should show.
europmc-pmc3391987:
Maes and colleagues argued in 2012 that depression and the sluggish misery of being sick may be two faces of one immune process. Sickness behavior, the tired, withdrawn state that comes with infection, helps the body save energy for fighting inflammation. Its features, from lost appetite to aching and low mood, overlap heavily with depression.

In true clinical depression, though, the shared pathways harden into something damaging. The authors describe growing sensitivity of immune pathways, chemical stress injuring fats, proteins, and DNA, and immune attacks on the body's own tissues. europmc-pmc3398887:
Dakos and colleagues compared methods in 2012 for spotting early warnings that a system is near a tipping point. Lakes, oceans, bodies, and markets can all flip suddenly into a different state, with little chance to reverse. Theory says telltale signals in data streams can betray an approaching flip.

Many warning methods exist, but opinions on their practical worth split widely, and no head-to-head test had been done. The authors lay out the available signals and try them on two simulated time series typical of systems near transition. Beyond the comparison, the paper provides a working toolbox. Fields from ecology to finance can use it to watch for trouble.
europmc-pmc3484687:
Stringaris and colleagues introduced a short scale for measuring irritability in children, in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry in 2012. Irritable mood draws growing scientific interest, yet researchers lacked a brief, sound way to measure it. Their Affective Reactivity Index asks parents or children themselves about easy annoyance, anger, and temper outbursts over the past six months, in just seven items.

The team tested the scale in clinic and school samples in the United States and Britain. Scores hung together well and formed a single dimension in both places. Irritability rose in a clear ladder from healthy volunteers to children with severe mood problems. Stringaris's group argues the short scale suits both busy clinics and large studies of mood.

frus-1861-d187:
A letter dated 11 November 1861 went from William H. Seward to Carl Schurz in Madrid. The letter is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By 11 November the Trent affair was about to burst upon the capitals. Seward's note to Schurz still speaks in the even tone of routine. Spain's reaction to the crisis would matter, and this letter kept the Madrid post primed for it. Spain's voice in the Trent talks would count, since its island lay beside the sea road. Its island beside the sea road made Spain's voice count beyond its strength.
frus-1861-d287:
On 7 September 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Mr. Haldeman. It stands as Document 287 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d87:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 September 1861. The dispatch is document 87 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams closed September with a report on the state of the London game. No crisis had broken, and that itself was the news. His steady word from across the sea let Lincoln's cabinet turn its mind to the armies, at least for a while. A quiet month in London was the best news the cabinet could get that fall. News by silence is still news, and Adams knew how to report it plainly.
frus-1862-d187:
Document 187 is the third of four Seward dispatches to London dated 10 November 1862 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All four went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

By mid-November, word had reached Washington that Britain would not join the French truce scheme. The danger of foreign action was fading, though slowly. Seward still wrote often, because warships for the South were fitting out in British yards. This letter belongs to the watchful weeks after the worst of the crisis passed. London's answer, when it came, would turn on battlefield news ten days old or more.
frus-1862-d287:
A second Dayton report followed on 13 June 1862, printed as Document 287 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two reports in two days often split a formal account from enclosures or private impressions. For Paris in 1862, the private side mattered, because the emperor's real views surfaced in hints. This report, read with its mate of the day before. Gives the legation's full picture for the week before the Seven Days battles changed every calculation. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d387:
Filed as Document 387 but dated 1 August 1862, this report from Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The printers placed it after a later Cameron report in the 1862 volume.

Cameron wrote at the start of August, in the weeks when the Alabama raider's escape from Britain was angering Washington. Russia's ports and courts offered no such grievances. The report's date places it beside Document 386 in substance, though the file separates them; together they give the legation's August account. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d487:
Two days later, on 10 March 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a further instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. The note is Document 487 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The follow-up came just after the ironclad fight at Hampton Roads, an event that made every maritime nation rethink its navy. The Dutch, with a fleet and colonies to protect, studied such news closely, and Pike needed Washington's version of it. Short supplementary orders were Seward's way of keeping his men current between the long formal instructions. Together with the order of 8 March, this note shows the tempo of wartime correspondence at its quickest.
frus-1862-d587:
Thomas Corwin in Mexico City received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 May 1862. It is Document 587 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Seward wrote five days after the Mexican victory at Puebla, though the news traveled slowly. His instructions to Corwin had a hard balance to strike. They had to show warm sympathy for Juárez's republic. They also had to make no commitment the Union could not honor while fighting the Confederacy. Corwin also had to be kept from promising more than Washington meant. The letter is a study in restrained diplomacy, from a government that believed in the Mexican cause and could spare it almost nothing but words.
frus-1862-d687: On 20 February 1862, a Mr. De Long wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 687 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed just after the Egypt papers. The evidence names the writer and the date. It does not state the post he held or the place he wrote from.
frus-1862-d87:
On 26 June 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 87 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d187:
Washington's orders to London on 5 May 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d287: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 September 1863. It is document 287 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d387:
Britain's side of the Washington exchange speaks in this note, sent by Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 February 1863. It is document 387 of the 1863 papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Seward kept every note, and the State Department printed the exchange for Congress. Reading Lyons's side shows how the crisis looked from the other desk. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d487:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 1 May 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d587:
Document 587 in the volume is a letter of 15 July 1863 from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d687:
