Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 November 1863. His letter is document 687 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume. Here the voice runs the other way, from the British side of the exchange.

Lyons had to guard British trade and ships while the Union navy stopped vessels at sea. He also had to judge how far the North would go. His notes to Seward put British concerns in plain, formal terms. For a reader, the gain is balance. Set beside Seward's replies, this letter shows both sides of a tense tie at work on the same day.
frus-1863p1-d87:
On 19 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 87 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The middle sheet of a three-letter day often held the meat: a talk set down in full, or a claim worked through point by point. Adams wrote in that pattern through the winter. This letter is the second of his 19 February set. With its mates, it let Seward see London whole for one day, through the eyes of the man he trusted most abroad.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d187:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff put a proposal to Washington on 3 November 1943 about who should run the war in the Mediterranean. At the time, General Eisenhower ran the central part, while a separate commander in Cairo ran the east and the Balkans.

The paper argues that split command caused delays, since moving even small forces needed approval from the Combined Chiefs of Staff, and chances in the Aegean had been lost that way. It proposes one commander for the whole sea, adding Greece, the Balkans, Crete, the Aegean islands, and Turkey to his charge. It also suggests renaming the air command the Mediterranean Allied Air Forces, and asks for the American chiefs' views.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d287:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a long secret telegram from Washington on 22 November 1943. Its lead item is Turkey's official reply, reported by Ambassador Steinhardt, to Anthony Eden's recent proposals that Turkey grant air bases and move toward war.

Ankara refuses the bases, holding that granting them means war with Germany whatever Britain thinks, and that the minimum arms promised at Adana were never supplied. Coastal cities and industries would be destroyed, Turkey warns, leaving her a liability, not an asset. Hull adds von Papen's threat of a German and Bulgarian attack within days. He adds Finland's tighter turn toward Germany and Portuguese coolness over the Azores. He ends with a French committee vote to recall Helleu from Lebanon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d387:
President Roosevelt handed Marshal Stalin a secret written proposal at Tehran on 29 November 1943. It restated what the American delegation had proposed at the Moscow Conference about air bases in the Soviet Union. It is one of three such papers Roosevelt gave Stalin that day.

The proposal asks that American aircraft on shuttle-bombing runs from the United Kingdom be allowed to refuel, make emergency repairs, and rearm at Soviet bases. It also seeks a better mutual exchange of weather information and improved signal and air communication between the two countries. Roosevelt records his understanding on two points. Moscow agreed to these ideas in principle at the Moscow Conference. And Soviet authorities would be told to meet his military mission to work out the concrete measures. He hopes the arrangements can be made promptly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d487:
Prime Minister Winston Churchill wrote directly to Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant, on December 5, 1943, in the middle of the Second Cairo Conference. Churchill often used Hopkins as his fastest route to Roosevelt. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Hopkins lived in the White House and carried messages no formal channel could match for speed or candor. A Churchill note to him is summit diplomacy at its most personal: one leader reaching the other through a trusted friend. Readers get a glimpse of how much of the alliance ran on this single relationship, bypassing embassies and foreign offices entirely.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d87: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on November 2, 1943, and the letter stands as Document 87 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two men would meet in Cairo in three weeks, but the letters never paused for the coming journey. The record gives the date and the names and no topic. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the volume's November sequence.
frus-1944-quebec-d187:
Cherwell also recorded the lend-lease conversation of September 14, 1944, between Roosevelt and Churchill. With Germany beaten, Britain hoped food, shipping, and munitions would keep coming during the war against Japan to cover reasonable needs. Roosevelt indicated assent, but Morgenthau pressed for definite figures rather than proportional aid.

The figures discussed were about 3.5 billion dollars of munitions aid in the first year and 3 billion in other supplies, offset by reverse lend-lease. All supplies would be on lend-lease terms. There would be no conditions jeopardizing Britain's export recovery, and no lend-lease articles could be exported. Roosevelt himself added the words "or sold for profit." A joint committee, informal at first and headed by Morgenthau, would work out the details.
frus-1944-quebec-d287:
The final report of the Combined Chiefs, C.C.S. 680/2, was submitted to Roosevelt and Churchill on September 16, 1944. It is the approved version of the draft the leaders had amended in plenary the day before. The over-all objective now reads as the unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan, sharpened from the draft's broader phrase about the Axis Powers.

The strategic concept and undertakings follow the draft, with small telling changes. French and Italian forces are to be assisted against Germany and/or Japan. Other co-belligerents are helped against "the enemy Powers." The redeployment sentence carries the compromise wording settled during the week: highest priority, having regard to other agreed and/or inescapable commitments. The report closed the conference's military business.
frus-1944-quebec-d87: Document 87 is where the editors, not the wartime officials, speak. The entry is an editorial note in the Quebec 1944 volume. State Department historians inserted notes to explain, connect, and cross-reference the papers. That help matters among the many staff memos written before the conference. Quebec hosted Roosevelt and Churchill in September 1944. Their agenda covered Germany, aid, and the Pacific war. The note offers orientation inside that record.
frus-1945-50-intel-d187: A short note records a talk held on 19 February 1947. It is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume on United States intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Such notes were made right after a talk, while the words were still fresh. They name the men in the room and the points each one made. That year the postwar spy service was still young, and its shape was still being set.
frus-1945-50-intel-d287:
A letter from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Assistant Executive Secretary of the National Security Council(Lay) on 9 June 1948. The State Department prints it as document 287 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

A letter fixed a position in a way a phone call never could: dated, signed, and filed for both sides to cite later. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d387:
The Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) addressed a letter to Attorney General Clark on 7 July 1949. It stands as document 387 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d87:
Panuch, a deputy assistant secretary for administration, wrote to Russell on 16 April 1946. The paper moved inside the State Department's administration wing in the spring. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Spring 1946 was the season of transfer and shrinkage for the State intelligence office. As the central group took shape and the department shed wartime growth. A deputy's memorandum to his chief belongs to that grinding work of moving people and files. Readers who stay with these housekeeping papers earn a truer picture of institutional change than the famous directives give. Empires do not fall in a day; they are inventoried, reassigned, and filed away.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d187:
Washington set out its Rome instructions for London in an aide-mémoire of 8 December 1944. Sent to the British Embassy, the paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It tells what Ambassador Kirk has been ordered to say to Premier Bonomi.

Kirk is to voice this government's concern over the long-drawn crisis in the Italian government. He is to stress its deplorable effect on American public opinion, just as Congress weighs the renewal of formal relations with Italy. Washington earnestly hopes the broad character of the last Italian government will be kept in any settlement. The cabinet's make-up remains an Italian question. But American interest runs to the friendship a new government shows the United Nations, and to its taking up all of Italy's past pledges.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d287:
Secretary of War Stimson sent the President a Moscow letter on 3 January 1945 and vouched for it. His covering memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, attaches General Deane's letter to General Marshall of 2 December 1944. The chief of staff joins him in the endorsement.

Deane's letter, Stimson writes, is an apt presentation with sound recommendations. Deane reports that Ambassador Harriman has seen it and concurs fully. Harriman believes its thoughts apply with equal force to political matters as to military ones. He adds one caution. A short letter cannot give an accurate picture of Russia. He would welcome the chance to speak at length, if a change in policy toward the Soviet government is weighed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d387:
Care and repatriation of freed prisoners form the heart of a draft agreement approved by the Combined Chiefs on February 8, 1945. The preamble states the aim plainly. Moscow and Washington, with London in the same frame, wished to arrange care for Soviet citizens freed by Allied troops. American and British citizens freed by the Red Army would get the same treatment.

Article 1 begins the bargain: all Soviet citizens liberated by forces under American or British command fall under the agreement. The same holds in reverse for the other side's people. The draft became the text taken to the Russians that day. It later governed the return of millions, willing or not.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d487:
Washington answered the Irish aviation complaint in Grew's cable of February 8, 1945. During the Chicago conference, Grew explained, full multilateral agreement had grown doubtful. The Department had then held early talks toward bilateral air agreements with a number of countries. When the Spanish agreement was signed, Berle had stated publicly that similar agreements would follow.

Ireland was a natural case, given its obvious geographic importance to American air routes. The Department saw no reason to consult the United Kingdom. The agreement followed the standard form drawn up with British participation. Grew's defense is brisk: London had helped design the template it now protested.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d87:
Soviet Ambassador Andrei Gromyko talked at length with Leo Pasvolsky in Washington on 11 January 1945. Pasvolsky's record of the conversation is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The two men went over the Dumbarton Oaks document, and voting procedure in the Council dominated.

Gromyko said Roosevelt's proposal to Stalin changed nothing from the American position at Dumbarton Oaks, and Moscow's position was unchanged too. Above all, he explained, the Soviets want to avoid even the appearance of disagreement among the great powers. Peace, in their view, rests on unbroken great-power unity. Barring a great power from full part in settling a dispute touching it could open exactly the rift they fear.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d187:
The State Department backed a plan for supervised Greek elections in an aide-mémoire extract dated July 5, 1945. The extract is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full text appears later in the volume, attached to another document.

The surviving passage says the Department thinks it desirable for the British and American ambassadors to approach the Greek government. This should happen within the next few days. That way, the matter can be discussed at the Big Three meeting. The approach, a note explains, would tell Athens that in the view of the United States and Britain the Greek elections should take place under Allied supervision. Greece, sliding toward civil war, was one of the places where the Yalta pledges on free elections would be tested.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d287:
A background paper surveyed Hungary's armistice and politics, dated July 5, 1945. The paper is document 287 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is the briefing book's country study of the former Axis satellite.

Hungary signed its armistice on January 20, 1945, and has complied more or less satisfactorily, the summary says. But the Allied Control Commission's work sits in Soviet hands, its decisions made without reference to the American and British members. Soviet requisitioning and heavy reparations demands have deepened the damage of war and Nazi looting; Hungary will produce only a fraction of its normal output this year. Politically, the provisional government is a coalition of all important anti-Nazi parties, with the Communists the strongest party machine though perhaps not the most popular. The paper urges a three-power agreement that Hungary's coming elections be truly free.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d387:
German shipping and shipbuilding are treated together in a briefing book summary. The questions, it says, must be viewed from two sides at once. One is the immediate use of German resources for the United Nations' war and rebuilding program. The other is the long-range future of German shipping and shipbuilding as industries.

Each side, the paper warns, can prejudice the other if decisions are taken in haste. A major step toward order would be Soviet membership in the United Maritime Authority, or at least a friendly Soviet attitude toward it. The summary shows Potsdam's planners thinking past the surrender, to the sea trade of a beaten Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d487:
Presidential approval arrives in Grew's cable to Harriman of June 23, 1945. The President has approved in principle the recommendation that the United States recognize the new Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. As soon as it is announced that the new government is functioning in Poland, the Secretary will telegraph the Polish foreign minister in Warsaw with the decision.

It is then planned that the President himself announce the recognition. In making that announcement, the Department proposes, he should restate the Yalta provisions. The new government, under that agreement, stands pledged to hold free and unfettered elections. Grew adds that Harriman will meanwhile have had his chance to win the assurances Washington listed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d587:
Moscow ambassador Sato sent a second, anxious cable to Tokyo on July 13, 1945. It is document 587 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference, printed in translation. Sato fears the Konoye mission will fail if it carries no real peace terms.

Sato presumes Moscow may agree to receive a special envoy. But if the envoy brings only vague talk, the Soviets will simply not weigh it. Worse, he warns, empty phrases would leave Soviet leaders feeling mocked. That could bring trouble on the Imperial Household itself. In Sato's view, the mission's aim must be nothing less than a proposal for peace. He asks Tokyo to state the envoy's task plainly, in case Moscow asks what the mission is for.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d687:
Loy Henderson sent the Acting Secretary a one-page office memo on the Turkey dispute, June 22, 1945. It is document 687 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It concerns the wording of a U.S. reply to the British Embassy, printed next as document 688.

Henderson suggests a verbal point be made as the reply is handed over. Department officers who were present at the Yalta talk in question, he notes, do not recall Stalin's stand that way. Britain's aide-memoire had Stalin firmly backing Turkey's independence and integrity. The U.S. officers recall no such definite position from him at Yalta. A handwritten note on the memo by H. Freeman Matthews sharpens the point. There was no mention of Turkey's integrity at Yalta at all.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d87:
Admiral Leahy sent Ambassador Harriman the first headcount of the President's party on June 23, 1945. The telegram is document 87 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering Moscow's urgent request for numbers so the Soviets could plan housing at Babelsberg.

The President's own party totals 37, Leahy reports, including himself, James Byrnes, Harry Hopkins, and Fred Vinson, plus aides, Secret Service men, and twelve servants. The Secretary of State's party adds 26, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff party another 75, with ten admirals or generals among them. Leahy also clarifies his earlier question: it was whether Stalin would rather no formal staff meetings be held in Berlin, given how that might look abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1087:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the conference secretariat, summed up the Berlin Conference's handling of Yugoslavia in this extract dated August 8, 1945. Greek-Yugoslav differences came up again and again during the talks. The Soviets accused the Greeks of aggressive designs against Yugoslavia.

The British answered that Belgrade and Moscow radios were spreading fantastic, unfounded stories. Britain proposed a joint call on both governments to avoid hostile action pending an impartial inquiry. The Soviets countered with two proposals aimed at Greece. In the end, all three papers were withdrawn, and no action was taken.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1187:
Winant sent his first dispatch of the summit from London on 17 July 1945, as Potsdam opened. In it he set the baseline: British hopes, press mood, and official thinking on day one. Later cables from his post would be read against this opening report.

An embassy's first word in a crisis frames all that follows. Winant knew the British scene as few Americans did, after years at the post. This dispatch opens the London end of the conference record. Everything Washington later received from the embassy built on the picture drawn here, in the summit's first hours.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1287:
Shipping chief Land joined Bissell, his ship requirements director, in this message to Acting Administrator Conway on 23 July 1945. The note ran inside the War Shipping Administration, from its head and its hull-counting chief to the man holding the acting post.

The agency's business was the fleet: which ships sailed where, and what the war still needed of them. With one war ended, that business was being rewritten weekly. A joint note from the top shows the rewrite being directed. It is wartime logistics in its own words, filed among the summit's grander papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1387:
A third memorandum by Stanisław Mikołajczyk, dated 26 July 1945, continues the Polish deputy prime minister's papers in the volume. He wrote on the day the Potsdam Declaration went out to Japan. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

While the world's eyes turned to the Pacific, Mikołajczyk kept writing about Poland. That contrast is the point of his file: great events crowded together in July 1945, and small nations fought not to be forgotten inside them. His third paper in three days shows a man using the only tools he had. They were words on paper, aimed at governments that held his country's fate. The run rewards slow reading.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-87:
A rapporteur's report dated July 24, 1945, forms part of the Potsdam Conference record in the second volume. At big talks, a rapporteur is the officer charged with summing up a group's work. The report then goes to a senior body that must act on it. Potsdam ran much of its work through subcommittees, so such reports moved business upward.

Inside, readers find the distilled state of play on the group's assigned topic. Agreements reached sit beside points still in dispute. The form matters: leaders who lacked time for long files could act on a short, clear report. It shows conference work at the level where texts were shaped.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d787:
Erhardt sent a further report on Austrian affairs on July 28, 1945, in document 787. The political adviser wrote to the Acting Secretary as Potsdam entered its last days. Austria's treatment in the final texts was still being weighed. His report joined the second Potsdam volume.

Late reports from the field could still move a summit. Erhardt's facts arrived while lines were being fixed. Readers see the last chance for ground truth to shape a decision. The document shows an adviser pressing his knowledge into the closing hours. It gives Austria's file a voice at the very end of the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d887: American delegates revised the Soviet proposal on a central German administration on July 30, 1945. Their version keeps the core idea. Help would be given to set up central offices for foreign trade, industry, finance, transport, and communications. These offices would act under the Control Council. The revision drops the Soviet sentence about coordinating provincial governments. That cut matches the change Secretary Byrnes had suggested on the Soviet text.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d987:
American staff prepared this undated memorandum on German external assets during the Potsdam talks. It urges prompt action to gain control and power of disposal over such assets. Assets in neutral countries matter most. Two reasons are given for speed.

Control serves Allied security. It also keeps the assets intact for Allied purposes before they can vanish. The paper asks that the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union issue a declaration claiming authority over the assets. France should join if possible. The paper also asks that the matter go to the Economic Subcommittee at once.
frus-1961-63v10-d187: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the Cuba volume. The island's revolution preoccupied Washington. This document holds that memo. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-295587: Kenneth Ashe took a March 2005 beef to GAO, and this ruling is the decision. One man's claim met the referee head-on. The docket got its full hearing, small name and all. The hearing was granted in full. The referee was fair.
gao-gaoreports-b-295987: General Dynamics-Ordnance doubled its May 2005 protest — two case numbers, one munitions fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-287: VA's trauma care delays needed ending in 2005, and GAO's report says the department had to move faster on the fixes. The review pushes for the action now. The haunted veterans deserved the faster help. The help had to come fast.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-687: Small and medium ammo needs were being met in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon covered the calibers, though more actions were necessary. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the bullets deserved steady supply. The actions had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-787: D.C. foster care improvements were underway in 2005, and GAO's report says federal funds launched new programs, though challenges remained. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the foster kids deserved better care. The challenges had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-387: Bank preemption rules needed clarifying in 2006, and GAO's report says the OCC should further clarify which state consumer laws applied. The findings demand the clarity. The report warns that the borrowers deserved to know their protections. The rules had to be clarified.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-887: Some workplace-giving charities owed back taxes in 2006, and GAO's report says certain Combined Federal Campaign charities owed payroll and other federal taxes. The findings name the debt. The report warns that the do-gooders should pay their dues. The taxes had to be paid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1087: Gold-star lenders were cashing in on student loans in 2007 — GAO's report says killing the ‘exceptional performer' perk would save serious money. The findings show the bonus label paid lenders extra for doing their jobs. The report's math: end the gold stars, keep the billions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-387: Missile defense bought speed at a steep price in 2007, and GAO's report says the acquisition strategy delivered hardware but less capability for more money. The findings grade the trade-off in detail. The report's verdict is wry: results, yes — at a cost that would make a banker blush.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-87: Abstinence education needed proof in 2007, and GAO's report says efforts to assess the accuracy and effectiveness of the funded programs were required. The findings demand the evidence. The report warns that the classroom claims needed checking. The programs had to prove it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-987: The nation's attic filed its spending plan in 2007 — GAO's report reviews the Archives' budget for guarding America's paper memory. The findings check the dollars behind the documents, from vaults to reading rooms. History's keeper, the report implies, deserves books as orderly as its shelves.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-187: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at supply Chain Security: Examinations of High-Risk Cargo at Foreign Seaports Have Increased, but Improved Data Collection and Performance Measures Are Needed. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-287: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on freight Transportation: National Policy and Strategies Can Help Improve Freight Mobility. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-87: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on medicaid Demonstration Waivers: Recent HHS Approvals Continue to Raise Cost and Oversight Concerns. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gebelin-monde-primitif-vol8-1787:
Tarot history starts in print in 1787, inside the eighth volume of Antoine Court de Gébelin's Monde primitif. His dissertation Du Jeu des Tarots, printed among mixed essays with six plates, first claimed the cards came from ancient Egypt. Court de Gébelin compared the modern world with the primitive one across his huge, unfinished work.

The claim had no proof, yet it launched two centuries of tarot lore at a stroke. Every later writer on the cards' hidden meaning answers Gébelin, knowingly or not. The French text of Tome VIII thus stands as the founding document of tarot history, the spring of the whole occult tradition of the pack.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib5-1587:
Gesner died in 1565, but his Historiae animalium still lacked its serpents. Other hands completed this fifth volume on the nature of serpents, and it appeared in 1587. Snakes, lizards, and dragons of report close the great Renaissance survey of animals, faithful to its founder's vast plan.

The entries follow Gesner's own method of names, pictures, habits, and authorities. Real vipers share the pages with winged serpents drawn from travelers' tales. The editors gathered what Gesner left and added what they could find. With this volume the most ambitious animal book of its age stands complete. Its mix of care and credulity captures its century perfectly.
gibson-monsters-of-the-sea-1887:
John Gibson ranged the whole sea monster shelf in Monsters of the Sea, printed in 1887. His survey runs from the kraken and the sea serpent to the giant squid. Gibson writes for the broad Victorian reader who loved a wonder with a fact in it.

He marks each tale as legend or as truth, and tells why he judges it so. The book hops from Norse myth to fresh reports from steamship decks. Its charm is its range: the deep as one great cabinet of beasts. The volume is the era's popular guide to the monsters of the sea.
gurney-tertium-quid-1887:
Edmund Gurney seeks a third path in Tertium Quid, his book of tales of thought from 1887. The name means a third thing. Gurney, a chief of the new study of ghosts, balks at two camps: fraud or ghosts. His tracts on trance, dreams that wound, and thought leaps hunt a mid law that could make sense of the scraps that stand firm.

His prose is keen, fair, and hard to fault. Death cut his work short a year past this book. The field lost its best mind young. These tracts are its base in thought.
hardy-woodlanders-1887:
Thomas Hardy published The Woodlanders in 1887, setting it in the deep woods of Little Hintock in Wessex. Hardy called it one of his favorite novels. The story grows out of the timber trade, apple orchards, and cider making of a small woodland village.

Grace Melbury, educated beyond her village, returns home torn between two men. Giles Winterborne, the faithful woodsman who loves her, has lost his houses and standing. The charming doctor Fitzpiers wins her hand instead, then proves feckless and unfaithful. Hardy tracks the damage through the seasons. The novel is a tender, sorrowful study of class, love, and loyalty among trees.
hartmann-life-of-paracelsus-1887:
Franz Hartmann brought a famed healer back to life in The Life of Paracelsus, his life tale of 1887. Paracelsus was a bold Swiss healer of the age past Luther. He scorned old books, healed with new drugs, and roamed from town to town in search of truth.

Hartmann reads him as a mage as well as a healer. He draws on the healer's own books and old tales of his cures. Fans of the occult in England had scant on him in their tongue. Hartmann's tale filled that gap and made him a hero. The healer's cures were famed and fought in his own day. Hartmann sides with the famed tales, yet keeps the man's grit in view.
heine-prose-writings-1887:
Havelock Ellis edited this selection of Heine's prose in 1887, drawn from across his career. The Travel Pictures, or Reisebilder, mix journeys in Germany and Italy with jokes, dreams, and sudden deep feeling. The Romantic School judges Germany's recent writers with wit that spared no reputation, including Heine's own friends.

Florentine Nights tells eerie tales in a sickroom frame, full of art and ghosts. The Gods in Exile imagines the old pagan gods hiding in a Christian world. Ellis chose the pieces that show Heine the prose ironist at full stretch. The result is a sharp, funny, melancholy tour of his mind. English readers met modern German prose largely through volumes like this one.
hitopadesa-wilkins-1787:
Charles Wilkins gave England the Hitopadesa in 1787, the first English version of the Sanskrit fable set. The Sanskrit title page names the sage Vishnu Sharma as its source. Wilkins had learned Sanskrit in India and printed the book at Bath.

A king hires the sage to teach his dull sons the art of wise rule. The sage uses beast tales, each with a moral in verse. Foxes, lions, and birds show how trust, greed, and haste play out. These shrewd tales taught princes and pleased plain readers alike. Wilkins also made the first Sanskrit grammar in English.
hugo-les-miserables-hapgood-1887:
Victor Hugo wrote Les Misérables in French, and Isabel Florence Hapgood made it English in 1887. Hapgood's full version became the standard public-domain English text of the vast novel. Hugo built the book over decades and published it to worldwide fame in 1862.

Jean Valjean, jailed nineteen years for stealing bread, starts life anew in France. Inspector Javert hunts him for years, bound to law more than to mercy or grace. Valjean raises Cosette, joins the Paris rising of 1832, and spares his hunter's life. Hugo pauses for long essays on Paris sewers, Waterloo, convents, and the poor of France. The novel pleads for mercy toward the poor with unmatched scope and heart.
io-francisci-pici-mirandvlae-et-concordi: Io. Francisci Pici De auro, 1587. The three books on gold. This book preserves that work. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
jacobi-tollii-fortuita-in-quibus-praeter: Jacobi Tollii Fortuita, 1687. The fortuitous Tollius. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lunel-hebr-1018:
Lunel, a town in the Hérault department of France, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn. Its Jewish community was ancient and grew famous in the twelfth century. Benjamin of Tudela counted 300 members in 1166, many learned and wealthy, and praised its academy.

The article calls that academy a dwelling-place of the Torah and names the sages of Lunel: Judah and Samuel ibn Tibbon, translators of Maimonides; Zerahiah Gerundi; and Abba Mari. Mari preserved letters from the fight over science and philosophy. It also records kind treatment by local lords, an arrest of Jews in 1319, and the community’s end. By the time of writing, no Jewish family remained, and only traces of the synagogue survived. The entry mourns a lost center of learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-ben-sha:
Michael ben Shabbethai, known in Latin as Magister Zematus, was a rabbi of Rome in the sixteenth century and a leading cabalist. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. His odd Latin name came from his own signature, where a word for an African place of family origin was Latinized as Zematus.

A legal decision of 1539 carries that signature, the article notes. Michael taught Cabala to Christian scholars, among them Ægidius of Viterbo and Widmanstadt, a sign of his standing beyond the Jewish community. Elijah di Nola, writing in 1555, also praised his excellent collection of cabalistic works, which the entry cites from Perles's studies of Roman Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mitzkun-david-m:
David Moses Mitzkun, a Russian Hebraist born in May 1836, made his living teaching Hebrew and his name writing it, as Herman Rosenthal and J. S. Raisin record in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote both Hebrew prose and poetry. He died at Wilna on July 23, 1887, at fifty-one.

His one named book is Kinnor Dawid, a collection of his Hebrew poems published at Wilna in 1863, when he was twenty-seven. The entry is brief and its bibliography points to the Hebrew periodicals of the day — Kohner's study of 1865, Fuenn in Ha-Karmel, and an obituary notice in Ha-Asif for 1887. A small life, preserved because the Hebrew revival counted its teachers among its writers.
john-chrysostom-an-exhortation-to-theodo:
When Theodore, a friend of the young John Chrysostom, left the monastic life for marriage and the world, Chrysostom wrote to win him back. An Exhortation to Theodore After His Fall is that letter, in two parts. It survives in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Chrysostom writes in tears rather than anger. No fall, he argues, is final while a person can still repent and return. He mixes grief for his friend with strong hope for his recovery. The letter shows pastoral care at its most tender. It also hints at the heart behind the famous golden mouth of later years.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-1-thessaloni:
Young converts in Thessalonica were grieving their dead when Paul wrote them his earliest letter. Chrysostom's eleven Homilies on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians take up their sorrow directly. The sermons appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Comfort rests on the promise that the dead in Christ will rise. Around that hope, Chrysostom urges clean and watchful living while the church waits for Christ's return. He never lets doctrine float free of the mourners in front of him. The result is tender pastoral care from a preacher who believed theology must console.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-1-timothy-np:
Church order, the marks of good leaders, and the danger of false teaching fill Paul's First Letter to Timothy. Chrysostom, himself a bishop, preached eighteen homilies on the letter. They stand in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A bishop preaching to future bishops gives these sermons unusual weight. Chrysostom spells out how overseers and deacons should live, handle money, and guard the teaching they received. He also warns young leaders against greed and quarrels. Anyone studying how the early Church governed itself will find this series essential reading. Its counsel on prayer and widows' care shows the same care for detail at ground level.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-2-thessaloni:
Persecution, a mysterious man of lawlessness, and idle members fill Paul's second letter to Thessalonica. Chrysostom answers with five compact homilies, printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The letter tries to steady a frightened church, and so do the sermons.

He calms fears about the end times without letting urgency fade. Then he turns practical: those who refuse to work should not expect the church to feed their idleness. Prophecy and plain duty sit side by side without strain. Brief as the set is, it packs in a great deal of pastoral sense.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-2-timothy-np:
Paul wrote Second Timothy from prison, near death, with the famous words: I have fought the good fight. Chrysostom preached ten homilies on that farewell letter. The series appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A dying apostle charges the next generation to guard the faith and endure hardship. Chrysostom, who would himself die in exile, handles those charges with special feeling. He keeps returning to courage, patience, and loyalty to the message. Reading the sermons feels like hearing one tested pastor honor another across three centuries of the same hard calling. Few sermon sets carry quite this much earned feeling in every paragraph.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-colossians-n:
Twelve sermons take up Paul's letter to the Colossians in Chrysostom's Homilies on Colossians. The letter defends Christ's place above every rival power and philosophy of its age. The homilies are given in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Chrysostom unpacks the letter's wide vision with his usual clarity: Christ as head of all creation and of the Church. He warns against empty wisdom that shrinks that claim. The set is short enough to read in a few sittings. It is also deep enough to reward return visits for years, as readers have found.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-galatians-an:
Two very different letters of Paul share one volume in Chrysostom's Homilies on Galatians and Ephesians. Galatians blazes with a defense of grace against legal rules, while Ephesians lifts a soaring vision of the Church. The sermons appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The Galatians sermons crackle with the preacher's own passion for free grace. Moving into Ephesians, he slows down to admire the picture of Christ's body joined in love. Polemic and poetry pair naturally in this set. Readers get both Chrysostom the fighter and Chrysostom the contemplative in one binding.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-philemon-npn:
Paul's shortest letter pleads for Onesimus, a runaway slave, asking his master to take him back as a brother. Chrysostom needed only three homilies to preach on Philemon, and they appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Small text, large consequences.

The preacher marvels at Paul's tact: no command barked, just love applied with perfect pressure. Master and slave stand as brothers in Christ, a quiet revolution inside a household letter. Chrysostom draws the lesson out gently rather than shouting it. His three sermons remain a lovely guide to the letter's understated power.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-philippians-:
Joy written from a prison cell fills Paul's letter to the Philippians, and Chrysostom preached fifteen homilies on it. The series survives in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Its themes suited a preacher who would suffer for his own preaching in time.

He lingers over the hymn of Christ emptying himself, in Philippians chapter two, and over the call to rejoice always. Contentment, humility, and courage under loss fill the applications. The sermons feel warm rather than combative, aimed at steadying ordinary believers. They remain a friendly way into both Paul's letter and Chrysostom's gentler side.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-st-ignatius-:
Two festal sermons by John Chrysostom honor martyr-bishops of Antioch: Ignatius, thrown to the beasts at Rome, and Babylas, who defied an emperor. The Homilies on Saint Ignatius and Saint Babylas come from the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Both were preached to crowds gathered at the martyrs' shrines.

Chrysostom tells their stories in vivid, dramatic strokes meant to stir courage in his listeners. He also reflects shrewdly on how martyr tales shape the soul of a whole city. The sermons belong to ancient preaching at full stretch. They make the honored dead feel present to the people standing before their tombs.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-acts-of-:
Bold, generous, and united: that picture of the first Church drives Chrysostom's Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles. He preached through Acts to show his own congregation what the Church was meant to be. The sermons stand in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Again and again he sets the apostles' fiery common life beside the lukewarm habits of his own day. Sharing goods, facing danger, and praying together all become quiet rebukes. Yet the tone stays hopeful, since the same Spirit still works. The homilies inspire and convict in equal measure, which was exactly his aim.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-epistle-:
Thirty-four homilies take up the Epistle to the Hebrews, with its claim that Christ surpasses angels, Moses, and the old covenant. Chrysostom's series is printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The golden-mouthed preacher faced a text as lofty as his own gift for speech.

His preaching rises to match the epistle's heights, moving from high priesthood to the heroes of faith. Moral applications cut close to the heart, warning hearers not to drift away. Ancient eloquence here serves a single aim: holding a tired church to its confession. The homilies count among the most powerful of his surviving works.

Thirty-two sermons unpack Paul's letter to the Romans, the weightiest letter the apostle ever wrote. Chrysostom's Homilies on the Epistle to the Romans appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Romans shaped Western theology, and Chrysostom preached it in the East a thousand years earlier.

He unfolds the letter's great themes in order: sin, grace, faith, and the mystery of Israel. A preacher's clarity carries hard doctrine, while a pastor's heart keeps it close to life. His moral applications are famous for leaving no hearer comfortable for long. Generations have ranked these sermons as the classic Eastern reading of Paul's masterwork.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-first-ep:
A divided church, troubled by scandal, received Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians, and Chrysostom preached on it in forty-four homilies. His series includes the well-loved reading of the hymn to love in chapter thirteen. The text comes through the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Factions, lawsuits, and loose morals in Corinth sounded much like problems in Chrysostom's own city. He answers with equal parts rebuke and encouragement, never letting the congregation off easily. His treatment of the resurrection chapter stands out for its hope and force. Few books show practical Christianity preached at so high a level.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-gospel-o:
Ninety sermons work through the Gospel of Matthew verse by verse in Chrysostom's Homilies on the Gospel of Saint Matthew. The set counts as the largest surviving commentary on a Gospel from the early Church. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition presents the full series.

Chrysostom first explains the text with unmatched clarity, then turns it on daily life without mercy. Wealth, pride, and hypocrisy all come under fire from the pulpit. Ordinary hearers were expected to follow long arguments and apply them at home. For fifteen centuries, preachers and readers treated these homilies as the standard guide to the first Gospel.

Eighty-eight homilies guide hearers through the Fourth Gospel, from its soaring prologue to the resurrection scenes. Chrysostom's Homilies on the Gospel of Saint John appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The series was preached to ordinary congregations, not scholars alone.

Signs, long talks, and the farewell words of Jesus all receive patient attention. Against heretics the preacher stands firm; toward seekers he stays gentle and clear. Daily life is never far away, since each doctrine lands in some duty or comfort. This set long held the place of a gold standard for preaching on John.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-second-e:
Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians is his most personal letter, and Chrysostom answers it with thirty warm homilies. The series is printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Suffering and comfort run through both the letter and the preaching on it.

Chrysostom draws out the apostle's heart: his hardships, his tears, and his tender appeals to a church that doubted him. Weakness made strong becomes the thread that ties the sermons together. A preacher who knew exile himself handles Paul's pain with special sympathy. These homilies console readers who have known hardship in any century.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-statues-:
Riots in Antioch in 387 smashed the emperor's statues, and the city waited in terror for punishment to fall. Week after week, John Chrysostom preached to the frightened crowds, producing the twenty-one Homilies on the Statues. They appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A political crisis becomes, in his hands, a long lesson on repentance, anger, and God's mercy. He rebukes the rioters, steadies the fearful, and begs the city to change before judgment comes. Preaching rarely gets more urgent than a sermon series delivered under threat of an army. The homilies made his name across the empire.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-titus-npnf1-:
Crete needed elders appointed, false teachers silenced, and households taught how grace trains people to live well. Paul's short letter to Titus covers all of it, and Chrysostom preached six homilies on the text. They appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

From a compact epistle, the preacher draws practical lessons for church life at every level. Sound teaching, self-control, and good works done quietly fill his applications. The sermons move fast and waste few words. They carry the trademark moral energy that made Chrysostom's preaching famous, applied to the ordinary duties of a small island church.
john-chrysostom-homily-concerning-lowlin:
One sermon carries Chrysostom's whole moral medicine in a single dose: the Homily Concerning Lowliness of Mind. Its subject is humility, preached with his trademark directness. The text appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Pride, he argues, sits at the root of nearly every sin. The humble tax collector of Jesus's parable goes home right with God, while the boasting Pharisee does not. Chrysostom aims the lesson at respectable churchgoers who need it most. Short as it is, the homily leaves readers with a clear test for their own hearts. It also shows how much weight one short sermon can carry when the preacher wastes no words at all.
john-chrysostom-instructions-to-catechum:
In the weeks before Easter baptism, John Chrysostom preached a course of sermons to new converts. The Instructions to Catechumens preserve that teaching for those about to enter the Church. They are printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

He tells the candidates plainly what they are leaving behind and what life they are entering. Old habits, public shows, and loose speech all come under his warning. A sense of urgency runs through every address, since the hearers stand at the edge of a new life. Few sources show so clearly how the ancient Church formed its members.
john-chrysostom-letter-to-a-young-widow-:
A young woman lost her husband, and John Chrysostom wrote her a letter of comfort. His Letter to a Young Widow, preserved in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, tries to turn raw grief toward hope. It is one of his most personal short pieces.

He grants that grief is natural and does not scold her for tears. Death, he urges, is a kind of sleep, and her loss can become a path to spiritual gain. Alongside deep comfort he gives practical counsel about money and household affairs. The letter shows the great preacher working as a counselor, plain about earth and firm about heaven.
john-chrysostom-letters-of-st-chrysostom:
From lonely exile, John Chrysostom kept writing to Olympias, the deaconess who had stood by him in Constantinople. Their correspondence fills the Letters of Saint Chrysostom to Olympias in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. She had been his closest friend and steadiest supporter in the capital.

The letters mix practical advice, spiritual counsel, and plain news of his sufferings on the road. He thanks her, worries over her health, and urges her not to lose heart. Readers meet the private Chrysostom here: grateful, lonely, unbroken, and tender. Few ancient letter sets show a friendship between a bishop and a deaconess so fully.
john-chrysostom-on-the-priesthood-npnf1-:
John Chrysostom earned lasting fame as a preacher, but On the Priesthood may be his most searched-for book. Written as a dialogue in six books, it asks what it really means to serve as a priest. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition carries the text here.

Chrysostom had dodged ordination himself, and he writes honestly about the calling's terrors and dignity. A priest, he says, must answer for the souls of others, a burden few can carry well. Praise and warning stand side by side on every page. Pastors have read the book for sixteen centuries, and it still makes them tremble.
john-chrysostom-select-homilies-npnf1-18:
No short volume can hold all of John Chrysostom's preaching, so the Select Homilies offer a chosen sampler. Festal sermons, moral warnings, and doctrinal talks sit side by side in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The choices aim to show his range rather than one theme.

Readers meet the golden mouth in many moods across these pages. He thunders against vice, speaks gently to sinners, and opens scripture with bright clarity. Newcomers to Chrysostom often start here before tackling his long sermon series on whole Bible books. The selection gives a fair first taste of why the ancient world prized his voice.
john-chrysostom-that-no-one-can-harm-the:
Banished from his city and his pulpit, John Chrysostom wrote That No One Can Harm the Man Who Does Not Injure Himself. The treatise, kept in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, argues that real harm can only come from within. Exile gave its author every reason to test that claim.

No emperor, slanderer, or prison can truly injure a person, Chrysostom insists, because outer losses cannot touch the soul. Only our own sin does lasting damage. He writes with the calm of a man refusing to be crushed by disgrace. The book's inner freedom sustained him in banishment, and readers under pressure have leaned on it ever since.
john-chrysostom-two-homilies-on-eutropiu:
In 399 the fallen court minister Eutropius fled to the altar of Chrysostom's church and clung there for safety. His enemy the archbishop then preached over him, in public, on the emptiness of power. The Two Homilies on Eutropius survive in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

All Constantinople watched as Chrysostom urged mercy for the man who had persecuted others. Yesterday's ruler, he told the crowd, now trembles before the altar he once ignored. The sermons count among the most dramatic ever preached. They join a plea for compassion to a sharp warning about how fast fortune turns.
kabbalah-unveiled-mathers-1887:
S. L. MacGregor Mathers, a founder of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, published The Kabbalah Unveiled in 1887. The book translates three key parts of the Zohar, the central work of Jewish mysticism, from Latin into English. It was the first English version of any part of the Zohar.

The three books are the Book of Concealed Mystery and the Greater and Lesser Holy Assemblies. They picture the divine nature through the ten sephiroth and vast symbolic faces of God. Mathers adds a long introduction mapping the Kabbalistic system for beginners. The translation fed the whole modern occult revival in the English-speaking world.
king-gnostics-and-their-remains-1887:
Strange engraved gems, stamped with secret names, angels, and symbols, led C. W. King into the world of the ancient Gnostics. The Gnostics and Their Remains, published in 1887, catalogs those magical seals and uses them to explain Gnostic religion. It was the founding English survey of its subject.

King treats the gems as documents, reading whole systems of belief off tiny stones. Basilideans, Ophites, and other sects take shape through their amulets and invocations. Part archaeology and part religious history, the book defined its field for decades. Its plates still fascinate, and its Victorian enthusiasm is catching. Later scholars corrected much, but they all started where King began.
kirwan-essay-on-phlogiston-1787:
Richard Kirwan, an Irish chemist, gave the phlogiston scheme its last great defense in this book of 1787. By then the new French school had strong proof on its side. Kirwan knew that proof well and set out to answer it all. He was no crank, but a sound chemist with a strong name in his field.

He held that phlogiston was a real stuff, bound up with the gas called inflammable air. He dealt with acids too, and how they form and change in his scheme. The book was so strong that the French school felt bound to answer each point in print.
la-vera-dichiaratione-di-tutte-le-metafo: La vera dichiaratione, 1587. The true declaration. The archive keeps it. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-1-1887:
Henry Charles Lea was a Philadelphia publisher who became America's great historian of the church's dark side. His History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages appeared in 1887. This first volume lays the ground: the rise of heresy, the church's turn to force, and the building of the tribunal. It is the foundation of modern Inquisition studies.

Lea traces the Albigensian Crusade, the papal inquisitors, and the rules of procedure: secret charges, no counsel, torture by law. He works from the records themselves, in a cool and damning style. France and Italy are his chief ground in this volume. The book made his name on both sides of the Atlantic.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-2-1887:
The second volume of Henry Charles Lea's History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, from 1887, follows the tribunal across Europe. Lea wrote from printed records and archives with a lawyer's care for proof. His subject here is the Inquisition at work in Spain's neighbor lands, Italy, and Germany, among other fields.

He treats the Spanish peninsula before its own great tribunal rose, the Italian cities, and the German lands where the inquisitor Conrad of Marburg spread terror. Sorcery and witchcraft enter, as the church begins to hunt them with the heretics. Lea's calm tone makes the burnings and confiscations hit harder. The volume widens his map of fear.
leopardi-poems-townsend-1887:
Frederick Townsend translated the poems of Giacomo Leopardi into English in 1887. Leopardi, who died young in 1837, wrote the lyrics known in Italy as the Canti. Townsend's volume holds that lyric work complete; Leopardi's prose dialogues are staged apart from it in the library.

The poems speak to the moon, to Silvia, to his native village, and to his own heart. Love, boredom, lost youth, and nature's indifference are his great themes. His pessimism is famous, yet the verse itself is full of sweetness and light. Italians rank Leopardi as their greatest lyric poet after Dante. Townsend gave English readers the whole arc of that brief, intense career in one volume.
lotze-outlines-logic-1887:
Ladd translated Lotze's Outlines of Logic, with his encyclopaedia of philosophy, into English in 1887. Hermann Lotze had taught at Göttingen for decades, and his lecture outlines distilled his system for students. Logic comes first in that system, since every other branch of philosophy depends on how we think.

The Outlines present logic not as a bare game of forms but as the study of thought aiming at truth. Lotze adds a survey of the whole circle of philosophy, placing logic, metaphysics, ethics, and aesthetics in their proper order. Ladd's version made the German master's classroom available to English readers. The volume helped form a bridge from German idealism to the new logic being built in Britain and America, and it was widely used as a textbook.
loudun-devils-1887:
Des Niau saw the strange events at Loudun and wrote them down, and his tale reached English readers in 1887. Goldsmid turned the French text into English for this book. The case centers on a group of Ursuline nuns in a small French town.

The nuns said demons had seized them, and crowds came to watch the rites used to drive the spirits out. At the heart of it stands Urbain Grandier, a priest put on trial in 1634 and put to death. Few tales show so well how fear, faith, and law can mix.
mallarme-poesies-french-1887:
Stéphane Mallarmé published his Poésies in 1887, gathering the poems of his career to that date. The text here is the French original. Mallarmé led the Symbolist movement in France, and his poems favor suggestion over plain statement, music over argument.

Among the best-known pieces are 'L'Après-midi d'un faune,' about a faun's drowsy afternoon dream, and the swan sonnet of a bird trapped in ice. His verse is dense, polished, and hard to unlock on a first reading. Patient readers find exact, haunting images of absence, purity, and art itself. The Poésies mark the high point of Symbolist poetry in French.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette: This volume of Madame Campan's memoirs follows the queen through her glittering prime. Trianon's elegant pleasures and strict court ceremony fill the happy years together. The fond memoirist recalls fashions, fetes, and lasting friendships. Versailles appears here at its most enchanting and most doomed.
michaelis-majeri-secretioris-naturae-sec: Michaelis Majeri Secretioris naturae secretorum scrutinium chymicum, 1687. The Maier scrutiny. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
michelson-morley-relative-motion-ether-1:
Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley ran the famed ether test at Cleveland in 1887. Their tool was far finer than the one Michelson used at Potsdam in 1881. They floated the stone base on mercury so it could turn with no jar or shake.

As the base turned, the light bands should have crept if the Earth moved through the ether. They did not creep at all, in test after test, at all times of year. The blank result is the most famed failed trial in physics, and relativity grew from it.
nachtrag-originalschriften-1787:
The Nachtrag of 1787 is the Bavarian government's supplement to its first publication of Illuminati papers. Its long title promises further original writings concerning the Illuminati sect in general. More seized material followed the first volume within the same year, completing the documentary record of the order's suppression.

The supplement prints papers of Zwackh, the order's second figure, and others of its archive. Internal quarrels, membership plans, and the machinery of the grades appear in the members' own words. Published by the men who destroyed the order, the volume is hostile in intent and priceless in content. Together the two 1787 publications give the archive of a secret society, opened by its enemies for all to read.
northwest-ordinance-1787:
The Congress of the Confederation passed the Northwest Ordinance in July 1787, the old Congress's noblest achievement. The law governed the lands northwest of the Ohio River, the young republic's first great western territory. It had to answer hard questions: would new lands be colonies, or equals? Would slavery follow the flag west?

The ordinance bars slavery forever from the territory, a clause that shaped the map of free and slave states for decades. It sets aside land in each township for public schools and promises fair dealing, often broken, with Native nations. Above all, it lays down the path by which territories become states on full equality with the original thirteen. The charter under which the American West was born governed the making of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin.
openalex-w1557481987: Colombian folk medicine uses plants against infection — do they work? Rojas and colleagues' 2006 study screened ten medicinal plants from Colombian folkloric medicine for antimicrobial activity. The screening measured which plant extracts killed microbes and at what doses.
openalex-w1997664087: Standard microscopes miss malaria — sharper tests tell a different story. A 2009 study used sensitive detection of Plasmodium species to reveal links between species infections and shifts in age distribution. The sharper tests rewrote local malaria maps.
openalex-w2120530887: Thick foods help swallowing — but terms are a mess. A 2014 paper examined how food and liquid thickness affect swallowing. The work called for one shared terminology for dysphagia care — clarity saves lives daily.
openalex-w2128360087: A rare amino acid gets used sparingly — evolution explains why. A 2006 study traced how bacteria use it over deep time. The work balanced its catalytic edge against selective, costly use — the trade-off, mapped in full detail for all.
openalex-w2254226187: The first gravitational-wave signal was just the beginning — this companion 2016 paper works out what made it. Analyzing GW150914 coherently across both LIGO detectors, the authors characterize the source: two black holes that spiraled inward and merged, and the masses, spins, and distance the data imply. It is the first portrait of a black-hole collision ever drawn from direct observation.
openalex-w2473397587: In ALS, aberrant glial cells proliferate in the degenerating spinal cord as paralysis races ahead. This 2016 study tests masitinib — a tyrosine kinase inhibitor — in the SOD1G93A rat model of inherited ALS, given after paralysis onset. The drug calms neuroinflammation and slows disease progression, suggesting that taming rogue glia could buy time even once symptoms have begun.
openalex-w2562375087: Plant breeders juggle messy field trials across mating systems and propagation types. This 2016 paper presents Selegen-REML/BLUP, software that uses mixed models to optimize breeding programs — handling allogamous, autogamous, mixed-mating, and clonal crops, plus varied experimental designs. It's a practical tool for turning trial data into better varieties.
openalex-w2610193187: The Wnt/β-catenin pathway is one of evolution's favorite control circuits — governing growth, differentiation, and stem cells. This 2017 review examines how it also modulates the immune system's attack on cancer. Understanding the pathway's role in anticancer immunity could reveal how tumors evade destruction — and how to stop them.
openalex-w2767050687: Schizophrenia's fingerprint on the brain's wiring has been blurry — small studies disagreed. This 2017 Molecular Psychiatry paper pools 4,322 individuals through the ENIGMA consortium, finding widespread white matter microstructural differences. The mega-analysis pins down what varied single studies could not.
openalex-w2799873087: Leptospira bacteria lurk in water and soil worldwide — some cause leptospirosis, most don't. This 2018 Frontiers in Microbiology research article surveys the biodiversity of environmental Leptospira, improving identification methods and revisiting how the disease is diagnosed. Better taxonomy means fewer missed cases and fewer false alarms.
openalex-w3000355687: Climate projections come coarse (70–400 km) — but crops and species need fine detail. This 2020 Scientific Data paper presents a global database of future climates at high resolution, bias-corrected via the delta method. The downscaled projections let impact models see the local future.
openalex-w7204480187: A swollen gallbladder can rot, and surgeons now often take it out through small cuts even in bad cases. This paper sums up what studies say about keyhole gallbladder removal for severe sudden inflammation. The authors weigh safety and results. A surgery review tracking how far the small-cut method has come.
openalex-w7204598387: Online learning is here to stay, but what makes a good virtual classroom? This study reflects on e-learning environments today, using published research to analyze what helps students learn at a distance. The authors take a qualitative look at the digital spaces where modern education happens. A thoughtful overview for teachers building courses for screens.
originalschriften-illuminatenordens-1787:
In 1787 the Bavarian government published Einige Originalschriften des Illuminatenordens, a selection of the Illuminati's own papers. Police had seized the order's archives from its leading members. Printing them was the state's way of exposing the secret society to public judgment, and the volume remains the foundational documentary source for the order's real history.

Letters, statutes, and plans of Adam Weishaupt's order stand here in the original German. The grades, the code names, and the reforming aims all appear without legend's varnish. Conspiracy theory meets the archive in these pages, and comes away changed. Historians build the true story of the Illuminatenorden on this publication and its supplement.
plos-pone-0000087:
Sarah T. A. Roord, Evelien Zonneveld-Huijssoon, and their team tested a combined therapy for autoimmune disease in PLOS ONE in 2006. In such diseases, T cells attack the body's own tissues. Their approach paired a dose aimed at the specific target of the attack with a low dose of drugs that calm cytokine signals.

Each part alone can be weak or harsh. Together, the targeted part steers the calming part where it is needed, so doses can stay low. The authors report control of the autoimmune response in their test system. The design idea, precise aim plus gentle damping, is a template that immune therapy still pursues for diseases like type 1 diabetes.
plos-pone-0000187:
Yesser Hadj Belgacem and Jean-René Martin published this fruit fly genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. A small gland in the fly, the corpus allatum, makes juvenile hormone. The authors show that the gene Hmgcr in that gland controls sex differences in locomotor activity and body size, acting through the insulin pathway.

How males and females grow to different sizes and move differently is a basic question in biology. The paper ties a hormone gland, a metabolic gene, and insulin signaling into one chain. Because insulin pathways are shared across animals, the fly work offers a model for studying sex differences in growth.
plos-pone-0000287:
Scott Smemo and Justin O. Borevitz published this genomics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, on redundancy in genotyping arrays. Genotyping arrays read DNA variants at set positions, and some probes on them overlap or duplicate each other's information. The authors assess that redundancy and what it means for studies using the arrays.

Redundant probes waste money but can also serve as built-in checks. Knowing how much of an array is redundant helps designers trim waste and helps analysts judge data quality. The paper is a practical audit of tools that powered thousands of genetics studies.
plos-pone-0000387:
Jessica Strid and colleagues tested an unusual route to calm arthritis, publishing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Instead of injecting a treatment, they applied type II collagen through the skin, a method called epicutaneous immunization. Collagen is a target of the immune attack in the arthritis model they used, where the body turns on its own joints.

The authors report that skin-based treatment with collagen held back both the start and the advance of chronic collagen-induced arthritis. Teaching the immune system to tolerate its own tissue, through the skin, could point toward gentler therapies for autoimmune disease. The study adds to work on needle-free ways to retrain immune responses.
plos-pone-0000487:
Kevin A. Edwards and colleagues built a reference collection of fly wing diversity, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hawaiian Drosophila are a famous radiation of species, hundreds of fruit flies that evolved on the islands. The team created a database of wing diversity across these species.

Wings record evolution clearly: their veins and shapes vary between species in ways that can be measured and compared. A shared database lets researchers test how wing form evolves and how it relates to each species' way of life. Hawaiian flies are a natural experiment in diversification, and reference collections turn scattered specimens into usable evidence.
plos-pone-0000587:
Eva H. Shang and Irina V. Zhdanova studied how a mother's cocaine exposure affects the unborn child's body clock, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The circadian system runs daily rhythms of sleep, hormones, and activity. Their work shows the circadian system is both a target and a modulator of prenatal cocaine effects. The drug disturbs the system. The system, in turn, shapes the drug's impact.

A two-way relationship is easy to miss if researchers look only at immediate toxicity. Circadian disruption could explain some lasting sleep and behavior problems after prenatal exposure. The study argues for rhythm as an outcome to measure in developmental toxicology.
plos-pone-0000687:
Katsuya Miyake, Toru Tanaka and Paul L. McNeil proposed a new mechanism for a familiar food poisoning, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lectins are proteins found in certain vegetables. Eaten in improperly cooked vegetables, they can cause acute distress in the gut. Exactly how they poison people was unknown, and that gap is what the authors set out to fill.

Gut lining cells live under constant mechanical and other stresses, and individual cells are often wounded and repaired. The team's mechanism ties lectin toxicity to that wound-and-repair life of the gut surface. A clear mechanism matters beyond the kitchen: it could explain other protein toxins and suggest how the gut normally defends itself.
plos-pone-0000787:
Daniel Meulemans and Marianne Bronner-Fraser looked to a humble sea animal for the origin of the vertebrate head, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The origin of the head is central to vertebrate evolution, but paleontology and comparative anatomy struggle with it, lacking unambiguous intermediate forms. Much of the head is built during embryonic development from two ectodermal cell populations.

Amphioxus, a small fish-like creature without a true head, is their window. Studying its development can reveal what came before cartilage, the tissue that scaffolds the vertebrate skull. Insights from amphioxus suggest the head's parts were assembled stepwise, from simpler chordate beginnings.
plos-pone-0000887:
Tero Harkonen, Karin Harding, Thomas Rasmussen and co-authors studied who died in a seal distemper outbreak, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Phocine distemper virus swept through European harbour seals as a new wildlife epidemic. Studies of disease in wild animals often treat every animal as the same, yet age and sex can change the outcome a great deal.

The team broke mortality down by age and sex across the outbreak. Those patterns shape what an epidemic does to a population over years, not just in one season. Their work is a warning against simple averages in wildlife health. It also gives seal managers a clearer sense of which groups need watching.
plos-pone-0000987:
Eric Griez, Alessandro Colasanti, Rob van Diest and colleagues measured how breathing carbon dioxide stirs negative feelings, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inhaling carbon dioxide can trigger a panic like state in people with panic disorder. What it does to healthy people was less clearly charted.

Sixty-four healthy volunteers inhaled four gas mixtures in a double dose setup. The team report the negative affect grew with dose and shifted with age. A safe lab trigger for unease is valuable: it lets researchers test calming treatments under controlled conditions. Age effects also warn against treating all volunteers as one group.
plos-pone-0001087:
Xiaohong Zhang and Hung Tseng studied what happens to the cornea's surface when basonuclin is missing, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The corneal epithelium, the eye's clear front layer, stays healthy through two processes: cells multiply, and cells stick to each other. Wound repair needs both, finely balanced.

Mice with a basonuclin null mutation, no working copy of the gene, let the pair test its role in living tissue. Basonuclin was already tied to ribosome gene control in skin type cells. Its absence impairing homeostasis and wound repair shows a growth regulator's reach. Eye surface healing is a daily clinical concern, from scratches to surgery.
plos-pone-0001187:
Chronic cocaine abuse is blamed for brain changes that make staying abstinent so hard. Deborah Mash and colleagues measured gene expression in the hippocampus of cocaine abusers, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The hippocampus is a brain region central to memory, including the persistent memory of the cocaine rush that can trigger relapse.

The authors report genes that regulate remodeling of the extracellular matrix, the scaffold around brain cells. Changes in that scaffold could physically alter connections between neurons. Their findings link the molecular side of addiction to the stubborn learning that keeps pulling former users back.
plos-pone-0001287:
The visual world is split in two: each half of the visual field is processed by the opposite side of the brain. Cristian Carmeli and colleagues studied interactions between the hemispheres in the visual areas, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Connections between the two sides are abundant near the representation of the visual midline.

The authors describe a novel interhemispheric interaction: modulation of neuronal cooperativity in the visual areas. In other words, activity in one hemisphere tunes how neurons in the other fire together. Coordinating the two halves is essential for a seamless visual field, and this is one of its mechanisms.
plos-pone-0001387:
Peng Gao, Zeyu Xin, and Zhi-Liang Zheng published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how plants balance carbon and nitrogen foods. Plant cells must keep these two in step to grow well. How plants sense that balance was poorly known. The team worked with Arabidopsis, a small plant used in labs world wide.

The authors pinpoint a gene that makes a protein which tags other molecules. They show this gene is key for the plant's response when food balance shifts. Loss of the gene throws the response off. The finding names a core part of how plants tune growth to the food they can get from soil and air.
plos-pone-0001487:
Wei Li and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that maps the human set of E3 ligases. These enzymes tag proteins for removal or for a change in job, and the tag step gives the system its aim. The team listed about 617 such enzymes and their partner parts in the human genome. Most were barely studied.

Among them they found a new enzyme on the cell power unit, which they named MULAN. It shapes how those units move and signal. A full map of this enzyme family gives labs a shared base. It should speed the hunt for drugs that steer protein tagging in disease.
plos-pone-0001587:
Balakrishnan Ramakrishna and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE trial on a drink mix for severe diarrhea in adults. Standard sugar salt drinks seldom cut stool loss beyond what vein fluids and germ drugs do. A starch that resists gut enzymes had shown promise as a swap for sugar. The trial pitted the two mixes head to head.

Adults with acute watery diarrhea got one mix or the other at random. The team weighed stool loss, time to recovery, and safety. Diarrhea still kills widely where care is thin, so a better drink has large value. Even a small gain per case adds up at that scale.
plos-pone-0001687:
Tapio Mappes and co-authors ran a field experiment on how selection shapes life-history choices in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Negative frequency-dependence favors rare types: when a strategy is uncommon, it does well, which keeps variety alive in a population. Population density can also shift which strategy pays, driving cycles in type frequencies over time.

The team tested frequency- and density-dependent selection together in the field rather than the lab. The full text gives the setup and the animal groups tracked.
