It also shows how success changed as types grew common or rare and as density rose or fell. Field proof matters here because lab cages strip out the crowding, predators, and seasons that make these forces real.
plos-pone-0001787:
Brian L. Fisher and M. Alex Smith revised the trap-jaw ants of Madagascar in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Species inventories are essential for documenting global diversity and for conservation planning. But inventories help only if the taxonomic work of describing and identifying specimens keeps pace. The revision covers two ant genera, Anochetus and Odontomachus, famous for their snapping jaws.

Working through Malagasy species, Fisher and Smith sorted which are distinct, described them, and built identification keys. The full text gives the species accounts, images, and distribution records. Madagascar's ants are found almost nowhere else, so a clean revision underpins every later study of the island's forests and their protection.
plos-pone-0001887:
Nickolay Neznanov and co-authors compared how two viruses react when a key cell machine is blocked, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The machine is the proteasome, which chops up worn proteins, and many viruses lean on it to copy themselves. The two test cases were vesicular stomatitis virus and poliovirus.

The team added drugs that stall the proteasome and watched each virus grow. They report a split result: the drugs strongly curbed protein making by the first virus, while the second fared in a unlike way. That split shows virus families lean on host tools to unlike degrees. It also warns that a drug aimed at one virus may fail on the next.
plos-pone-0001987:
Annalise Paaby and Paul Schmidt studied a gene tied to aging in fruit flies, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The gene, methuselah, was found because mutant flies with a faulty copy live longer than normal. It codes for a cell-surface receptor, and it became a lead candidate for how aging is set.

The pair asked what the natural variety in this gene does in wild flies. Does each form change lifespan, or death rates with age, in a real way? Lab mutants can mislead, since their effects may not match those of common forms. Testing real variants shows whether the gene matters outside mutant lines.
plos-pone-0002087:
Aisha Farhana and co-authors unraveled a two-way iron gate in the tuberculosis bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Iron is scarce inside a host, and TB bacteria use siderophores, small iron-grabbing molecules, to steal it. That uptake is a principal survival strategy and a virulence factor, so its mechanics are a prime drug target.

The team report a novel exporter-importer system in Mycobacterium tuberculosis and show its role in trafficking iron. A gate that both sends the grabbers out and brings loaded ones in is a neat piece of logistics. Blocking it could starve the bacterium in the lung.
plos-pone-0002187:
Stéphanie Bedhomme and co-authors watched fruit fly mating behavior change fast once a conflict was removed, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Males and females often gain from different mating patterns, a tension called intralocus sexual conflict. It can keep each sex from reaching its own best outcome.

In an earlier study the team had removed female selection pressure in the fly Drosophila melanogaster, freeing males from that conflict. Here they report that reproductive behavior then evolved rapidly. The experiment shows in real time how a tug-of-war between the sexes can hold evolution back, and what happens when the rope is cut.
plos-pone-0002287:
Fabian Saenz and co-authors showed that a malaria protein is required for the parasite to enter mosquito salivary glands. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Malaria spreads when sporozoites, the parasite's infective stage, mature in the mosquito gut and then invade its salivary glands. That invasion is thought to depend on parasite surface molecules.

The team studied MAEBL, a protein related to ones the parasite uses to enter cells. They found its transmembrane form is essential for invading Anopheles salivary glands. A step the parasite cannot skip is an inviting target for interventions that stop malaria before it reaches a person.
plos-pone-0002387:
Cabantous and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Stéphanie Cabantous, Yvonne Rogers, Thomas C. Terwilliger, among others. Its subject is new Molecular Reporters for Rapid Protein Folding Assays. The GFP folding reporter assay [1] uses a C-terminal GFP fusion to report on the folding success of upstream fused polypeptides.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002487:
Pechous joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Roger D. Pechous, Travis R. McCarthy, Nrusingh P. Mohapatra, among others. Its subject is a Francisella tularensis Schu S4 Purine Auxotroph Is Highly Attenuated in Mice but Offers Limited Protection against Homologous Intranasal Challenge. Francisella tularensis is a Gram-negative coccobacillus that causes the febrile illness tularemia.

Subspecies that are pathogenic for humans include those comprising the type A (subspecies tularensis) or type B (subspecies holarctica) biovars. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002587:
Abrantes led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Patrícia Abrantes, George Dimopoulos, Ana Rita Grosso, among others. Its subject is chloroquine Mediated Modulation of Anopheles gambiae Gene Expression. Plasmodium development in the mosquito is crucial for malaria transmission.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002687:
A 2008 study by David S. Boukal and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up does Sex-Selective predation stabilize or destabilize Predator-Prey dynamics?. Authorship is credited in the record to David S. Boukal and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Little is known about the impact of prey sexual dimorphism on predator-prey dynamics and the impact of sex-selective harvesting and trophy hunting on long-term. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002787:
Basarab G. Hosu and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was reversible disassembly of the actin cytoskeleton improves the survival rate and developmental competence of cryopreserved mouse oocytes. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Basarab G. Hosu, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Effective cryopreservation of oocytes is critically needed in many areas of human reproductive medicine and basic science, such as stem cell research. It goes on to note a further point. Currently, oocyte cryopreservation has a low success rate. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002887:
Wayne P. Wahls, Eric R. Siegel and Mari K. Davidson reported in 2008 on where breaks form in DNA during meiosis in fission yeast. Long non-coding RNAs are transcripts that code for no protein, and their jobs were long unclear. In meiosis, a protein called Rec12 cuts DNA to start recombination, the swapping of DNA between chromosomes.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors show that hotspots for that swapping are directed to places that express non-coding RNA. That links an enigmatic RNA class to a core step in making sex cells. Geneticists get a new clue to why recombination favors some genome sites over others.
plos-pone-0002987:
Elizabeth Musgrove, C. Marcelo Sergio, Sherene Loi and co-authors mapped gene networks tied to estrogen, c-Myc, and tamoxifen response in 2008. Estrogen drives cell growth in normal breast and in breast cancer. Drugs targeting its receptor work, but cancers often resist them from the start or over time.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team identified functional networks of genes responding to estrogen and to c-Myc. They then related those networks to response to tamoxifen therapy. The aim is a mechanistic grip on resistance, so treatment can be matched or combined more wisely. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003087:
Werner Scherbaum, Christian Ohmann, Heinz-Harald Abholz and co-authors randomized blood glucose self-monitoring schedules in type 2 diabetes in 2008. Advice on how often to self-monitor varies widely among physicians treating the disease. The trial enrolled patients with stable metabolic control on oral drugs.

Two testing regimens were compared in a multi-centre randomized controlled trial. Published in PLOS ONE, the design gives the frequency question a direct experimental answer. Finger-stick testing costs money and comfort, so knowing the useful frequency helps patients and health systems alike. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003187:
Manasee Mankar, Radhika S. Joshi, Prajakta V. Belsare and colleagues propose a social view of obesity in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fat storage has classically been seen as a means of storing energy. Obese people have been theorized as metabolically thrifty, saving energy in times of plenty to guard against future scarcity. Recent research, though, highlighted many brain, behaviour and social aspects of obesity.

The authors develop the idea of obesity as a perceived social signal. Readers get an alternative frame to the simple energy storage story. It invites tests of how body size sends social information and how that affects behaviour.
plos-pone-0003287:
Boaz Kigel, Asya Varshavsky, Ofra Kessler and colleagues test tumour suppressing signals in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The class-3 semaphorins include seven family members. Six of them bind to neuropilin-1 or neuropilin-2 receptors, or to both, while the seventh, sema3E, binds to the plexin-D1 receptor. Sema3B and sema3F were earlier described as tumour suppressors.

The title reports successful inhibition of tumour growth by specific class-3 semaphorins, linked to tumour cells carrying the right semaphorin receptors. Readers learn that the signal works only when the tumour carries the right receptor. Matching signal to receptor could guide future cancer therapy choices.
plos-pone-0003387:
Justin M. Percival and colleagues studied weak muscles in mice for this 2008 paper. Healthy muscle holds an enzyme called nNOSμ at the fiber surface. There it makes nitric oxide, a gas that helps muscle work. The enzyme stays put by attaching to the dystrophin protein complex.

Mice bred without that enzyme developed a muscle disease called myopathy. Their fibers showed damage and their strength was reduced. The loss shows the enzyme is not a minor extra in muscle. Its absence alone is enough to make skeletal muscle fail. Healthy fibers need that gas signal in the right place at the right time.
plos-pone-0003487:
Emilie Bonnet and co-authors tested a vitamin fix for memory loss in rats in this 2008 study. Rats deprived of vitamin A lost ground on spatial memory tasks. New neurons are born in the hippocampus across life and aid memory. Retinoid signals from vitamin A support that birth process.

Giving retinoic acid restored new neuron growth in the deprived rats. Their spatial memory deficit reversed along with it. The work ties vitamin A signaling to adult brain repair. It also links diet to the health of memory circuits. Vitamin A lack is common in poor regions, where diet gaps hit children hardest.
plos-pone-0003587:
Daniel Wegmann, Isabelle Dupanloup, and Laurent Excoffier linked splicing to gene use patterns in this 2008 paper. Alternative splicing creates much of the protein diversity in complex animals. It is likely central to the complexity of higher eukaryotes. Most studies had focused on the molecular machinery that triggers splicing.

The team found the width of a gene's expression profile drives its splicing. Genes used across many conditions splice in more varied ways. How broadly a gene works may shape how many forms it takes. The link connects gene usage to protein variety.
plos-pone-0003687:
Emiliano Merlo and Arturo Romano published this memory study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A memory tied to a place can fade when the place is visited again without the reward or harm that formed it. That fading, called extinction, can also fail, and the old memory can return.

The authors show that extinction requires shutting off NF-kB, a factor that switches genes on. Blocking that factor's activity was part of how the memory lost its force. The result presents forgetting as an active shutdown in the brain, not a passive decay over time.
plos-pone-0003787:
Isabella Santi, Alfredo Pezzicoli, Mattia Bosello, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Group B Streptococcus uses enzymes called pullulanases to break down alpha-glucans, sugars it meets in the human host. Such enzymes may help the bacterium adapt to host niches. Genome reading turned up a new candidate.

The team characterized a newly found pullulanase that sits on the bacterial surface. Antibodies against it could block the breakdown of alpha-glucans. A surface enzyme that both feeds the bacterium and draws immune fire is a candidate piece for future vaccines.
plos-pone-0003887:
Waraphon Phimpraphi, Richard Paul, Bhee Witoonpanich, and co-authors studied malaria risk in Thailand in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article looks at a Karen population living where malaria is common. Past work on host genes mostly sought single genes that protect against malaria. Less work weighed genes against shared living conditions as a whole.

The team estimated how much of the risk for two malaria types runs in families. They covered infections by Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. Splitting risk into family and non-family parts guides future gene hunts. It also shows how much prevention must target homes and surroundings.
plos-pone-0003987:
Jérôme Beaufays, Benoît Adam, Catherine Menten-Dedoyart, and co-authors described a tick saliva protein in 2008. Ticks secrete many proteins while feeding on blood. Lipocalins in saliva help mute the host's inflammatory response. The team had earlier found fourteen new lipocalin genes in Ixodes ricinus.

Their PLOS ONE article characterizes one of them, called Ir-LBP. It binds LTB4, a signal that draws neutrophils to injury sites. By soaking up that signal, the protein interferes with neutrophil function. Such proteins help ticks feed undisturbed for days. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004087:
Philippe Bossi, Frédérick Gay, Imène Fouzai, and co-authors studied smallpox vaccine response in France in 2008. In March 2003, France built a bioterror preparedness program. It formed a national team ready for revaccination against smallpox. Team members had been immunized earlier in life.

Their PLOS ONE article asks which factors predict response to the vaccine. Age, health, and clinical traits were compared with outcomes. Knowing who responds well sharpens outbreak response planning. Such data are rare because routine smallpox vaccination ended decades ago. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004187:
Piotr Religa and colleagues published this transplant study in PLOS ONE in 2009. After a heart transplant, the new organ's arteries can thicken from inside, a problem called transplant arteriosclerosis. The thickening is built from smooth muscle cells that come from both the donor organ and the recipient's own body.

Using 124 heart biopsies, the team assessed how clinical factors relate to the presence of these host-derived cells in the graft. They also weighed the roles of inflammation and a cell-attracting signal called MCP-1. Understanding where the invading cells come from matters for keeping transplanted hearts working longer.
plos-pone-0004287:
Gaby Doxiadis and colleagues published this primate genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In humans, the MHC class I B locus is single and highly variable, linked to a microsatellite called MIB. Rhesus macaques differ: their haplotypes carry unique combinations of multiple B genes, each with its own level of variation.

The team used microsatellite analysis and the localisation of retroviral sequences to reconstruct this region's history. They describe a compound evolutionary history for the macaque Mhc class I B region. Understanding it matters because macaques are central models for immune research and vaccine testing.
plos-pone-0004387:
Empathy is the shared feeling that arises when one being senses another's distress. It can lead to comfort, care, or watchful concern. QiLiang Chen, Jules Panksepp, and Garet Lahvis asked whether genes shape that response in mice. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper compares mouse strains with different genetic backgrounds.

The authors report that empathy in mice is moderated by genetic background. Some strains responded more strongly to distress in others. That pattern points to inherited differences in social feeling. Mouse work cannot settle questions about human empathy. It can show where biology may play a part. The study gives later research a model for testing those genetic effects.
plos-pone-0004487:
A gut bacterium clings to the bowel wall using a hair-like factor that grips a fatty molecule, report Lena Jansson, Joshua Tobias, Catharina Jarefjall, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium is enterotoxigenic E. coli, a cause of severe diarrhea. Its first step in causing disease is to stick to the lining of the small intestine.

The sticking factor is called colonization factor antigen CS6, one of the most common of its kind. The team shows that CS6 recognizes sulfatide, a fat-and-sugar molecule on cell surfaces. Naming the exact grip helps explain how the bacterium gains its foothold. It also suggests ways to block attachment, a strategy that could prevent infection without antibiotics and without killing the bacterium outright.
plos-pone-0004587:
Children with high and low math ability use their brains differently when judging amounts without counting, report Yulia Kovas, Vincent Giampietro, Essi Viding, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Estimating numerosity, how many things there are, can be done without symbols like numbers or counting words. Several brain areas serve this numerical approximation in adults.

Most earlier studies examined adults and ignored individual differences in mathematical ability. This study examined non-symbolic estimation in children at both ends of the ability range. Comparing the two groups shows which brain systems track skill early in life. That could inform how math difficulty is spotted and supported before children fall far behind in school.
plos-pone-0004687:
Xi-Song Ke and colleagues mapped chemical marks on DNA in prostate cancer for a PLOS ONE study in 2009. More proof shows that these marks help drive cancer by turning genes on or off. Some marks tend to silence genes, and those shifts may guide how a tumor grows.

The team scanned the whole genome for two key marks on a core DNA protein. They compared patterns in cancer cells with those in normal cells. A clear mark pattern could serve as a sign of prostate cancer change. It may also hint at new ways to treat or track the disease.
plos-pone-0004787:
Cynthia Worobey and colleagues examined gene variants and risk of faster kidney decline in women, in PLOS ONE in 2009. A reduced filtration rate predicts heart disease and death in large populations. Genetic variants, particularly in genes of the renin angiotensin system that controls blood pressure, and Fluids, may influence how fast kidney function falls over time in adults.

The team examined relations between specific variants and decline in women. Knowing genetic risk could flag women who need closer kidney checks. It also clarifies how blood pressure pathways affect the kidney. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0004887:
Michael Treadway and colleagues studied early adverse events, HPA activity, and rostral anterior cingulate volume in depression, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prior studies independently reported links between major depressive disorder, elevated cortisol, early adverse events, and region specific grey matter decreases. Relationships among variables were unclear, prompting a combined study measuring trauma history, stress hormones, and brain volumes in depressed patients and controls.

Early adversity links hormones and brain structure jointly. Mediation patterns suggest developmental embedding of stress. Treatment may need trauma informed approaches. Biomarkers cluster in exposed subgroups. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004987:
A spinal cord injury destroys tissue and blood vessels. Recovery needs new vessels and surviving support cells. Hyuk Min Kim and colleagues tested a delivery strategy in rats. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used neural stem cells to deliver VEGF at the injury site. VEGF is a vessel-growth factor.

The delivered VEGF boosted growth of glial progenitor cells. It also increased angiogenesis, the sprouting of new vessels. More tissue was spared around the injury. The study shows stem cells can double as drug couriers. That dual role is attractive for spinal repair. It combines cell therapy with targeted factor delivery.
plos-pone-0005087:
Th17 cells defend against germs. They also drive autoimmune diseases. Salim Bouguermouh and colleagues studied what controls their development. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They focused on CD28, a co-stimulation signal on T cells. CD28 is involved in the start and progress of autoimmune disease. Its role in Th17 fate was unclear.

Stimulating CD28 down-regulated Th17 development. A soluble antibody against CD28 suppressed the cells' formation. The co-signal acts as a brake on these double-edged cells. The finding could guide therapies for autoimmunity. Calming Th17 cells without crippling defense is the goal. This study names a knob that turns them down.
plos-pone-0005187:
Doctors who treat tuberculosis watch how patients' immune cells respond to the germ during therapy. The key test tracks interferon gamma, a signal released by T cells that have met the TB germ. Sauzullo and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that treatment itself can shift those readings.

The team measured the T cell response both in patients and in lab tests as treatment went on. Their results help explain why earlier studies of these tests disagreed with each other. For clinicians, the work clarifies what a rising or falling test result means while a patient is on TB drugs.
plos-pone-0005287:
ANCA-associated vasculitis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system inflames small blood vessels. In animal models, T cell subsets marked by CD45RC levels shape who gets sick. Ordonez and colleagues defined the human versions of those subsets in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Expression of the CD45RC isoform split human T cells into functionally distinct groups. Those groups were distributed differently in healthy people and in patients with the disease. A marker that sorts patients' T cells cleanly could aid diagnosis and point to the cells driving the illness.
plos-pone-0005387:
Genes are built from exons, and alternative splicing includes some exons often and others rarely. Isoforms are not random mixes, so splicing frequency must be regulated somehow. Song and colleagues compared exons with different splicing frequencies in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their component analysis searched for features that distinguish frequently spliced exons from rare ones. Candidate elements and splicing signals emerged from the comparison. Knowing what sets an exon's usage rate helps explain how cells produce the right protein mix from one gene. One gene can make ten or more forms of a protein. So the rate at which each part is kept or skipped is a code in its own right that this work helps to read.
plos-pone-0005487:
Peter Dalin, Oskar Kindvall, and Christer Björkman studied insect pests in willow plantings for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many farmers and scientists believe that single-crop fields suffer worse pest outbreaks than mixed wild land. Yet hard proof of that belief was scarce.

The team counted a leaf beetle pest over seven years at many sites, in both plantings and natural stands. Control of the pest by its enemies was weaker in the single-crop willow fields. The long record gives rare solid evidence that growing one crop alone can let pests escape their natural checks.
plos-pone-0005587:
Evgeny Kobrinsky and co-authors studied how helper subunits arrange calcium channels in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Calcium channels of the Cav1.2 type are central to how heart, muscle, and brain cells use calcium signals. The main pore part of the channel is guided by smaller helper subunits made by four genes.

The team asked how those helpers change the layout and grouping of the channels in the cell surface. Layout affects how strong and how local a calcium signal is. The findings refine models of signalling in the heart and brain.
plos-pone-0005687:
Katherine Dick Krueger and co-authors mapped gene markers in a small family affected by ALS in 2009. ALS, or Lou Gehrig's disease, kills the nerve cells that control movement. Finding single-gene causes has taught science a great deal about such diseases.

The team used SNP markers, single-letter DNA changes, to trace which stretch of DNA the family shares with the disease. Small families give weak signals, so the mapping must be done with care. A found locus points to a gene whose normal job, once known, may explain why motor neurons die. Each such gene adds a clue for future treatments.
plos-pone-0005787:
Lucile Espert and co-authors compared in 2009 how a cellular housekeeping process behaves during HIV infection of two cell types. HIV infects both CD4 T cells and macrophages, entering through different co-receptors for its X4 and R5 strains. The housekeeping process, autophagy, eats worn cell parts and can also attack viruses.

The team found autophagy plays different roles in the two cell types and strains. In one setting it may help the virus; in another, hinder it. That split complicates any plan to treat HIV by tuning autophagy. The study maps the terrain such plans must cross.
plos-pone-0005887:
Ingmar Werneburg proposed in 2009 a standard system for staging vertebrate embryos across species. Staging tables describe embryo development for model animals, but each table uses its own landmarks. Comparing development between species then becomes guesswork.

Werneburg reviews the problems and offers a common framework based on shared events. A standard system lets researchers line up a chick, frog, and fish embryo by true developmental stage. That alignment is the backbone of evolutionary development studies. The paper is a call for order in a basic research tool, with a concrete proposal attached.
plos-pone-0005987:
Stress can be smelled, at least in sweat. Alexander Prehn-Kristensen, Christian Wiesner, Til Ole Bergmann and colleagues tested what that smell does to the brain in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study used sweat from people waiting for a hard exam, a group under real anxiety, and measured how others responded to the scent.

The title states the effect: the smell of anxiety can induce empathy in the person who breathes it. A chemical signal from a stressed body thus tunes a social feeling in another. The work joins a line of studies in animals and people showing that feelings travel by scent, without a word or a look being shared.
plos-pone-0006087:
Some of the best drug targets are proteins the body itself refuses to attack. Hongzhe Zhou, Yunbo Wang, Wei Wang and colleagues tackled that refusal in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents a way to raise monoclonal antibodies against highly conserved antigens, proteins so alike across species that immune tolerance blocks the usual antibody-making route.

Therapeutic antibodies are among the fastest-growing drug classes, and their success rests on getting a good antibody at the start. A method that beats tolerance widens the target list for the whole industry. The work serves drug pipelines that had written off conserved proteins as unreachable, some of them central to cancer and immune disease.
plos-pone-0006187:
What an animal eats sets its place in the food web, but diets vary inside a single population too. Brice Semmens and colleagues built a statistical method for measuring that spread in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They used stable isotopes, natural chemical tags in tissue, to trace what each animal had been eating.

Their layered Bayesian models separate variation between individuals, between subgroups, and between whole populations. Older mixing models mostly gave one average diet for a group. Seeing the full spread changes how ecologists judge competition and resilience. The method can be applied to many species where diet samples are hard to gather directly.
plos-pone-0006287:
Machine learning tools are popular for big biological data, but choosing among them is often guesswork. Tune Pers and colleagues tackle validation of learning methods in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Few theoretical results guide which tool fits a new problem with thousands of measurements per sample.

The authors frame validation as a game of prediction from high-dimensional data. Their strategy aims to compare methods fairly before trusting their forecasts. Fair comparison matters because flexible tools can fool their own tests. The work lays early groundwork for a theory of machine learning assessment.
plos-pone-0006387:
Drug-resistant staph infections threaten communities worldwide, and one toxin is a prime suspect in severe cases. Ching Wen Tseng and colleagues studied Panton-Valentine leukocidin, a toxin of community-associated MRSA, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Epidemiologic data suggested the toxin contributes to severe human infections, particularly in the young.

The toxin contributes to inflammation and muscle tissue injury, the team reports. Direct evidence strengthens the case against this virulence factor. It supports efforts to neutralise the toxin in severe infections. Understanding its damage helps doctors judge which cases may turn dangerous.
plos-pone-0006487:
Juliana Jaramillo and colleagues measured heat tolerance in a major coffee pest for PLOS ONE in 2009. Coffee is predicted to be severely affected by climate change. The coffee berry borer, Hypothenemus hampei, is the most devastating pest of coffee worldwide. Knowing how much heat the borer can stand helps forecast where it will thrive as the world warms.

The team determined the borer's thermal tolerance in the lab. They then used it to predict climate change impacts on this tropical pest. If warming helps the borer more than the crop, losses could grow. Such forecasts help growers and governments plan defenses early.
plos-pone-0006587:
Stefano Focardi, Paolo Montanaro, and Elena Pecchioli tracked how fallow deer search for food in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lévy flights are random walks whose step lengths follow distributions with heavy tails. Clusters of short steps are connected by rare long leaps. Such patterns appear in many foraging animals.

The team tested whether fallow deer use adaptive Lévy walks in foraging. A Lévy pattern can be an efficient search strategy when food is patchy. Showing deer adjust the pattern to conditions supports its adaptive value. The study links a mathematical idea to real animal movement data.
plos-pone-0006687:
Zabrina L. Brumme and colleagues traced how HIV escapes the immune system in PLOS ONE in 2009. HIV-1 varies widely from person to person. Even so, its changes under immune pressure follow broadly predictable patterns. The immune proteins called HLA molecules shape which viral changes succeed. Different HLA types push the virus down different escape routes.

The authors studied subtype B virus and three of its proteins. The proteins were Gag, Pol, and Nef. They mapped sites where HLA-linked changes appear in the virus. Those maps show the pathways immune escape tends to follow. Such knowledge can guide vaccine design, since a vaccine must handle a moving target.
plos-pone-0006787:
Jia Zeng, Iana Angelova Parvanova, and Jonathan C. Howard studied an always-on immune protein in mouse liver in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most immune effector molecules switch on only during infection. The protein Irga6 is a resistance GTPase acting inside cells. Earlier evidence said it appears only when induced. The liver broke that rule with strong constant expression.

The team traced the expression to a dedicated promoter. A promoter is the DNA switch in front of a gene. This one drives steady production in liver without infection signals. A standing defense in the liver makes biological sense. The liver filters blood rich in gut microbes, so readiness there is valuable.
plos-pone-0006887:
Peter B. Adler, James Leiker, and Jonathan M. Levine ran a climate experiment on a prairie plant community in PLOS ONE in 2009. Climate change affects species directly through their physical environment. It also affects them indirectly through changed interactions. Competition and predation can shift with warming. Recent work shows indirect effects may amplify or cancel direct ones.

The team separated direct and indirect effects in the field. Prairie plants responded through both routes. Ignoring interactions would misstate the community's future. Species may decline from lost partners rather than heat itself. The experiment argues climate forecasts must include the web of interactions.
plos-pone-0006987:
Marieke Bax, Sandra van Vliet, Manja Litjens, and colleagues studied how dendritic cells travel in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dendritic cells are the immune system's strongest antigen presenters. Young ones patrol the body's edges and capture invaders. Mature ones then migrate to lymph nodes to alert T cells. A signal pair, CCR7 and CCL21, guides that trip.

The team examined a sugar coating on these cells called polysialic acid. They found it interacts with CCL21 and adjusts how well the cells migrate. Fine-tuning migration could help vaccine design, where getting dendritic cells to lymph nodes is the key step.
plos-pone-0007087:
Yuliya Karpievitch, Elizabeth Hill, Anthony Leclerc, and colleagues compared data classifiers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many biology experiments produce cluster-correlated data, where measurements come in related groups. Ignoring that correlation can mislead a classifier. It may overfit training data and report error rates that are far too rosy.

The team compared random forest classifiers built for such data. Their study used an implementation called RF++. Honest error estimates matter in fields like mass spectrometry diagnostics. A classifier that looks perfect in training but fails in the clinic helps no one. Their comparison shows how to test more carefully.
plos-pone-0007187:
Corine H. GeurtsvanKessel, Ingrid M. Bergen, Femke Muskens, and colleagues studied immune cells during flu infection in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Natural killer cells normally kill infected cells and release interferon signals. A newly described group of these cells also seemed able to present antigens, like dendritic cells do.

The authors compare conventional and interferon-producing killer dendritic cells during influenza virus infection. They ask whether both types can present antigen to other immune cells. Their answer helps immunologists sort out overlapping jobs among the cells that first meet the flu virus.
plos-pone-0007287:
Andrea Sartore-Bianchi, Federica Di Nicolantonio, Michele Nichelatti, and colleagues searched for colorectal cancer treatment markers in 2009. KRAS mutations occur in many metastatic colorectal cancers. Those mutations block response to EGFR-targeted antibodies such as cetuximab and panitumumab, two standard targeted drugs for this cancer.

Yet fewer than a fifth of patients with normal KRAS respond. The authors analyze multiple molecular alterations beyond KRAS. They aim to predict clinical benefit from EGFR-targeted monoclonal antibodies. Their multi-determinant approach could spare non-responders ineffective treatment. It also sharpens how oncologists select therapy by tumor profile.
plos-pone-0007387:
Katarzyna Bozek, Alexander Thielen, Saleta Sierra, and colleagues analyzed HIV surface sequences at large scale in 2009. The V3 loop of HIV-1 is critical for coreceptor binding. It is the main determinant of whether the virus uses the CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptor to enter cells, a choice tied to disease stage.

The authors perform a large-scale, data-driven analysis of V3 loop sequence space. They compare CCR5-tropic and CXCR4-tropic viruses. They report different evolutionary patterns for the two types. Those patterns may help predict coreceptor use from sequence, informing treatment with coreceptor-blocking drugs.
plos-pone-0007487:
Valorie Salimpoor and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on why listening to music feels rewarding. Music has no clear survival value, yet people seek the pleasure it gives again and again. The authors proposed that the reward is tied to emotional arousal. They measured listeners' physical responses while music played. Chills and body changes served as signs of that arousal.

The rewarding moments tracked the degree of arousal closely. When the body buzzed more, listeners reported more pleasure. That link held across the people tested. The result grounds a slippery feeling in measurable physiology. It also helps explain why music can move us like far more concrete rewards. The study feeds a growing psychology of why humans keep music so close.
plos-pone-0007587:
Jeremy Terrien and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on energy saving in the gray mouse lemur, a small primate of Madagascar. Many small mammals let body temperature dip each day, a state called daily heterothermia, to save energy and water. Cooling saves energy, but arousal, the rewarming, costs it back. The trade-off tightens in winter cold. The team studied aging lemurs exposed to cold.

The major constraint was not the cooling itself. It was impaired control of body cooling and rewarming in the aging animals. Older lemurs paid more to manage the cycle. That shifts the picture of heterothermia's costs toward control, not just temperature. For aging animals, the machinery of the daily dip becomes the burden. The study speaks to how aging reshapes basic energy strategies in primates.
plos-pone-0007687:
Maximo Brito and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns HIV prevention in the Dominican Republic. Trials elsewhere had shown that male circumcision can lower a man's risk of catching HIV. Whether men and communities would accept the practice was a separate question.

The study asked people in the Dominican Republic for their views on circumcision as a prevention tool. Their answers show how much support exists and what concerns stand in the way. Public health teams need that kind of local evidence before they can plan a program that people will actually use.
plos-pone-0007787:
Christine Palmer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies immune cells from people with Crohn's disease. Crohn's is a chronic gut disorder with patchy, deep inflammation. The team had earlier shown that patients' macrophages, a key immune cell, work defectively.

After stimulation, macrophages from patients died less readily than normal ones. They also made fewer reactive oxygen species, the chemicals used to kill germs. Both flaws could let bacteria linger in the gut wall. Lingering bacteria would keep the inflammation burning. The study sharpens the picture of Crohn's as a failure of first-line defense.
plos-pone-0007887:
Laura MacConaill and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It brings fast mutation testing to real tumor samples from patients. Finding key gene changes in a tumor can predict how the illness will go. It can also point doctors to the right drugs.

Broad testing of this kind was not yet a routine part of care. The team set up a genotyping platform and checked it on clinical samples. Their pipeline reads critical mutations across many genes at once. Routine profiling could match patients to targeted drugs sooner. The study is one step toward that standard in cancer care.
plos-pone-0007987:
Jean-Pierre Bayley and colleagues tested a tumor gene in mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. Faults in the gene SDHD cause human tumors called paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma, which grow near nerves and glands. The gene also does daily work in the cell's energy chain.

Mice bred without the gene, even in a sensitized strain, did not grow those tumors. The clean result cuts against a simple story in which losing the gene alone starts the cancer. It warns that mouse models can miss what drives a human tumor, and that other steps must join the gene fault.
plos-pone-0008087:
Jeffrey Kwong and colleagues checked whether statin drugs guard older people against flu in PLOS ONE in 2009. Statins lower cholesterol and also calm inflammation, which led some to hope they might soften flu's toll. The team ran a population cohort study of elderly patients through flu seasons.

People on statins had somewhat fewer flu hospital stays and deaths than those not on them. The gap was modest, not a cure. Still, in a bad season even a modest guard matters, and the result supports trials of statins as backup during flu pandemics when vaccines run short.
plos-pone-0008187:
Elena Gabrielli and co-authors wrote about antibody regions in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Antibodies carry small parts called complementarity-determining regions, which grip targets. Past work showed peptides from these regions can act on their own. They can fight microbes and viruses and even harm tumor cells. This holds regardless of what the full antibody targets.

The study tested how these region peptides bridge two arms of immunity. One arm adapts to specific threats, while the other reacts fast and broadly. A bridge between them could inspire new drug ideas. The authors present evidence for that link in their experiments.
plos-pone-0008287:
Carole Deyts and colleagues studied Huntington's disease in mouse neurons in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Huntington's disease stems from an expanded polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin protein. The faulty protein is expressed throughout the brain. Yet striatal neurons suffer more than other brain cells. Why they are so vulnerable is a common hypothesis topic.

The team tested dopamine D2 receptor stimulation in striatal neurons. It worsened the dysfunction caused by the expanded protein. The effect ran through Rho/ROCK-II activation inside the cells. That pathway could be a target for protecting the striatum.
plos-pone-0008387:
Garima Khare and her team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about an enzyme of the TB germ. New strains of the germ now shrug off the best drugs in use, so the hunt for new drugs is a dire need. The enzyme, FadD13, is part of a set of genes the germ needs to cause disease and to stay alive in host cells. Its job is to wake up fatty acids so the germ can use them for food and growth.

The team mapped which parts of the enzyme count most and which fatty acids it likes best. A firm grip on those two points lets drug teams build a key to block it. If such a block works, the germ may starve or fail to cause harm. The work aids the search for new TB drugs.
plos-pone-0008487:
Wai Lok Sibon Li and co-authors test gene coevolution in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Genes whose proteins work together face shared constraints. To keep their partnership, they tend to evolve in step. Past studies checked this by comparing branch lengths in gene trees. A branch length shows how much a gene changed along a lineage. Linked genes should show matching patterns of change.

The authors measure how branch lengths covary across many gene pairs. Pairs of genes with related functions show stronger covariation. The result backs the idea of coevolution among partners. It also gives a way to spot functional links from sequence data alone.
plos-pone-0008587:
Ernest Adeghate and co-authors study a sleep-related receptor in the pancreas in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Orexins play a critical role in sleep and wake states. They also regulate feeding behavior and reward processes. The pancreas regulates food metabolism and energy balance. That function is deranged in diabetes. The team examine the orexin-1 receptor in pancreatic islet cells. They test if it co-localizes with pancreatic hormones there.

They find the receptor sits with those hormones in islet cells. It also modulates outcome in streptozotocin-induced diabetes in their model. Streptozotocin is a toxin that destroys insulin cells to mimic diabetes. A sleep and appetite receptor thus influences diabetic course.
plos-pone-0008687:
Michael Landrum, Ann Fieberg, Helen Chun, and colleagues studied adults carrying two viruses at once. Their 2010 PLOS ONE article follows people infected with both HIV and hepatitis B. Blood markers show whether hepatitis B is active, quiet, or cleared. Doctors did not know well how HIV changes those markers.

The team looked back through cohort records for patterns in the blood tests. They searched for traits linked with each marker outcome. Clearer patterns could sharpen screening and vaccine plans for co-infected patients. The work also helps doctors judge who needs closer watching for lasting hepatitis B infection.
plos-pone-0008787:
Ruth Ellis, Laura Martin, Donna Shaffer, and colleagues ran an early safety trial of a malaria vaccine. Their phase 1 report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The vaccine targets MSP1, a protein on the blood-stage parasite. Two versions of the protein were mixed to cover its common variants. Volunteers had never had malaria, giving a clean readout. An added booster ingredient, CPG 7909, was tested in one arm.

Adults received the vaccine with or without the booster. The team tracked side effects and antibody responses. Phase 1 success means the vaccine can move to trials where malaria circulates. Malaria still kills hundreds of thousands yearly.
plos-pone-0008887:
Francine Einstein, Reid Thompson, Tushar Bhagat, and colleagues read DNA tags in newborns who grew poorly in the womb. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Intrauterine growth restriction means a fetus grows slower than it should. Those babies face higher risks of diseases like diabetes decades later. Early womb conditions can leave lasting marks on gene control. Cytosine methylation is one such lasting mark.

Newborns after growth restriction showed disturbed methylation patterns. The dysregulation appeared right at birth, before lifestyle could act. Womb stress may thus set disease risk from day one. Early marks could someday identify children needing preventive care.
plos-pone-0008987:
Jane Greatorex and co-authors tested everyday cleaners against the pandemic flu virus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus was influenza A/H1N1, the strain that swept the world in 2009. In a pandemic, most sick people are nursed at home, not in hospital. Homes need simple ways to keep the virus from spreading between family members.

The team tried a range of common household cleaning agents on the virus. They measured how well each product cut the amount of live virus. Some ordinary products worked strongly; others barely dented it. The ranking gives households practical guidance for flu season cleaning.
plos-pone-0009087:
Julian Lim and co-authors kept volunteers awake and tested their eye for objects, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sleep deprivation dulls attention, a fact shown in many behaviour tests. Most past work blamed the brain's front control areas. This team looked instead at the ventral visual cortex, the object-recognition stream.

Brain scans showed sleep loss weakened top-down biasing there. The visual cortex responded less selectively to the objects people sought. Attention failures after lost sleep start earlier in the brain than assumed. The finding matters for night workers who must spot hazards reliably.
plos-pone-0009187:
Tzu-Ching Chang and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines Rho kinases, enzymes that control how cells contract and stick. Those forces help decide whether a cell stays the same or turns into a new type. The team suspected the kinases also steer embryonic stem cells.

Working with a mouse embryonic stem cell line called CCE, they tested how the kinases affect self-renewal and nerve cell development. The effect depended on how densely the cells were plated. In crowded and sparse dishes, the same signals pushed the cells differently. That density link matters for anyone growing stem cells in the lab.
plos-pone-0009287:
Michele Mishto and co-authors published this multiple sclerosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Multiple sclerosis involves immune attacks on the brain and spinal cord. Cell shredders called proteasomes chop proteins into the fragments that immune cells inspect. A variant in one shredder part, LMP2, caught the authors' attention.

They found that the 60HH variant of LMP2 changes how fragments of myelin basic protein are produced. Myelin is the coating that MS attacks. In Italian women, carrying this variant lowered the risk of developing multiple sclerosis. A small change in the shredder thus seems to change which targets the immune system sees.
plos-pone-0009387:
Mary Bath published this fertility study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Frozen mouse sperm is a workhorse of genetics labs, but thawed sperm often fertilizes eggs poorly. Dead sperm in the mix seem to release factors that block the living ones. Removing calcium from the medium, oddly, had been shown to help.

Bath tested what the damaged sperm release and what can offset it. The antioxidant glutathione stimulated the fertilizing capacity of cryopreserved sperm. Understanding these blockers and boosters improves a routine lab technique. Better frozen sperm IVF means mouse colonies can be stored and revived more reliably.
plos-pone-0009487:
Meredith Ezak and Denise Ferkey studied smell and behavior in a tiny worm in PLOS ONE in 2010. The worm, C. elegans, avoids a strong odor called 1-octanol. A brain chemical named dopamine tunes how strongly it avoids that odor. Worms that cannot make dopamine react too strongly. The team tested one dopamine receiver, DOP-3, for its role.

Without DOP-3, the worms' avoidance changed, showing the receiver lowers sensitivity to the odor. So a single receiver can dial a simple behavior up or down. Worms give a simple system for studying how dopamine shapes the senses. Lessons from it may apply to larger brains as well.
plos-pone-0009587:
Frank Baur and co-authors showed that a quiet gene switch is vital in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. The switch, Sp2, belongs to the Sp family of transcription factors. Its close kin Sp1, Sp3, and Sp4 bind DNA and turn genes on. Sp2 breaks the family pattern and does not bind DNA in the usual way. That made its true job unclear.

Mice that lack Sp2 fail to develop normally. Cells taken from such embryos also fail to multiply on their own. So the odd family member is in fact essential. The study forces a rethink of how this switch works, since it acts without the family's standard trick.
plos-pone-0009687:
The West African gaboon viper carries one of the most complex venoms of any snake. Sakthivel Vaiyapuri and colleagues isolated a new enzyme from that venom for a 2010 PLOS ONE report. They named the enzyme rhinocerase, after the horned gaboon viper subspecies it came from.

Serine proteases are enzymes that cut other proteins at set points. The team purified rhinocerase and tested what it cuts and how it acts on blood-related targets. Knowing each venom part in detail supports better snakebite care. Venom enzymes also sometimes become leads for new medicines.
plos-pone-0009787:
Sooty mangabeys are monkeys that host SIV, the monkey relative of HIV, without falling ill. Namita Rout and colleagues examined a rare immune cell type in these animals. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The cells are CD4 positive natural killer T cells, or NKT lymphocytes. The mangabeys had very few of them, a paucity the team measured directly. That scarcity matched a lack of NKT cell loss after SIV infection. Hosts that avoid immune damage may hold lessons for HIV care. That pattern sets natural hosts apart from species that sicken.
plos-pone-0009887:
Chlamydia bacteria invade human cells by rearranging the cell's inner skeleton. Jessica Thalmann and colleagues traced how one bacterial protein drives that rearrangement. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bacterium studied was Chlamydia trachomatis, serovar D.

The skeleton in question is actin, a protein that forms moving cables inside cells. Evidence pointed to CT166, an effector protein the bacterium injects, targeting Rac. Rac is a switch protein that tells actin where to rebuild. Knowing the hijack steps exposes points where infection might be blocked. Chlamydia is a common sexually transmitted infection. The work stayed at the level of cells in culture.
plos-pone-0009987:
Growing human liver cells outside the body long enough to study is hard. Martha Harding and colleagues built an implantable gel that keeps young liver cells alive in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The construct is a vascularized protein gel, laced with blood vessels once implanted. Mice normally resist hepatitis C infection. It supports human fetal hepatoblast survival; hepatoblasts are the young cells that become liver. The setup also supports infection by hepatitis C virus in mice. A living liver test bed could speed hepatitis research. That pairing had blocked hepatitis C work for years.
plos-pone-0010087:
The authors were Barbara Ingold, Eva Simon, Ute Ungethüm, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study hunted for new drug targets in stomach cancer. They focused on G-protein-coupled receptors, a large family of cell surface switches. Such receptors are strong candidates for cancer prevention and treatment strategies.

Comparing tumors that had spread to lymph nodes with those that had not, they singled out CXCR4. That receptor appeared in blood vessels feeding the cancer. Blocking it might slow new vessel growth, so the authors raise it as a possible antiangiogenic target.
plos-pone-0010187:
Julia Wenger and Elena Naumova mapped flu timing across the United States in a 2010 study. In temperate regions, flu epidemics return each year and peak in winter. Federal health agencies document onset times and circulating strains in detail. Their PLOS ONE paper focused on older adults, a group at high risk from seasonal flu each winter.

They asked how synchronized flu seasons are across the country in that age group. Strong synchronization means one national timeline can guide vaccination and hospital planning. Weak synchronization would argue for local timing, since peaks would arrive at different weeks in different states.
plos-pone-0010287:
The authors were Madhuri Salker, Gijs Teklenburg, Mariam Molokhia, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study reframed repeated miscarriage as a failure of embryo selection. Recurrent pregnancy loss means three or more miscarriages in a row. It is usually blamed on faulty embryos or on uterine factors. Those factors are poorly defined, leaving many couples without a clear explanation.

The team tested whether the womb lining, the endometrium, fails to prepare properly. A poorly decidualized lining, they argue, cannot vet embryos or support the right ones. That failure would let poor embryos implant briefly, then lose them, again and again.
plos-pone-0010387:
Hirotaka Masuda and co-workers described stem-like cells in the womb lining for PLOS ONE in 2010. The lining, called the endometrium, regrows itself every month during a woman's fertile years. Such regrowth hints that stem-like cells live there. Cells that stray and implant elsewhere cause endometriosis, a painful condition affecting about one in ten women of fertile age. The team isolated a special side group of lining cells.

That side group behaved like stem cells in tests. It could be the source of the lining's monthly renewal. If so, it may also seed the stray growths of endometriosis. Finding the source cells gives that disease a possible root cause to target. It also opens ideas for rebuilding damaged womb lining.
plos-pone-0010487:
Daniel Smith and colleagues measured how a widespread ocean bacterium copes with iron shortage in PLOS ONE in 2010. Iron is scarce in much of the ocean, yet marine life needs it. The bacterium studied, known as Pelagibacter ubique, is among Earth's most abundant organisms. The team starved cultures of iron in natural seawater. They then read responses at both the gene and protein levels.

Responses at those two levels did not always match, which is itself informative. The bacterium tightened its iron use and adjusted key processes. Ocean microbes drive global carbon and nutrient cycles, so their limits matter planet-wide. Iron fertilization debates in climate policy also hinge on such responses. This study gives a molecular view of scarcity at sea.
plos-pone-0010587:
Robert Brooks and Alexei Maklakov compared obesity patterns across countries in PLOS ONE in 2010. In many nations women are more likely than men to be obese. The authors asked what tracks that gap from place to place.

They found the gap grew where the average number of children per woman was higher. Where fertility was low, male and female obesity rates sat closer together. The authors link the pattern to the physical costs of reproduction. The result offers an evolutionary angle on a modern health problem, alongside diet and activity.
plos-pone-0010687:
Douglas Heimburger and colleagues followed adults starting HIV treatment in Lusaka, Zambia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Death rates run high in the first weeks of antiretroviral therapy in much of Africa. Clinics with few lab tests need simple signs that flag who is in danger.

The team tracked blood phosphate, a cheap and common test, from the start of treatment. Low or falling phosphate marked patients more likely to die early. The link held even after other risk signs were counted. A low-cost flag like this could steer food support and close watching toward the patients who need them most.
plos-pone-0010787:
Nancy Thorogood and Carolyn Brown studied X chromosome shutdown in hybrid cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Female mammals silence one X chromosome in each cell early in development. A RNA called XIST coats the silent X and helps lock it down. The locked chromosome gains many marks of silent chromatin.

In hybrid cells carrying XIST, some X chromosomes kept marks of active chromatin anyway. Those chromosomes lacked full gene and repeat silencing. So XIST presence alone did not guarantee shutdown. The leak is scientifically useful: it separates the steps of coating, marking, and silencing that are usually tangled together.
plos-pone-0010887:
Hilgo Bruining, Leo de Sonneville, Hanna Swaab and co-authors published this autism study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Autism spectrum disorders vary widely from person to person, and so do their genetic causes. The authors asked whether groups sharing one defined genetic cause would also share a tidier, more uniform pattern of autistic traits.

They compared the symptom profiles of autistic people with one of two genetic syndromes, a deletion on chromosome 22 or Klinefelter syndrome, against a large mixed autism sample. Standard parent-interview scores were analyzed for how alike symptoms were within each group and whether groups could be told apart. Bruining and colleagues use genetics to slice a broad diagnosis into cleaner subgroups. Such slicing could sharpen research on causes and help tailor support to each subgroup's profile.
plos-pone-0010987:
Ewart Kuijk, Jeffrey de Gier, Susana Chuva de Sousa Lopes and co-authors published this reproduction study in PLOS ONE in 2010. NANOG is a master factor of pluripotency, the stem cell state, and textbooks restricted it to early embryo cells and the germ cells that precede sperm. Since sperm production ends in a cell that can start a whole new organism, the authors checked whether NANOG appears during spermatogenesis.

Across several mammals, including mouse and human, they detected the gene's message and protein in testes. Surprisingly, the signal sat not in the most primitive cells but in pachytene spermatocytes, cells in the middle of the sperm-making process. A reporter mouse confirmed the pattern. Kuijk and colleagues argue NANOG's job extends into sperm formation itself, hinting at safeguards for the genome passed to the next generation.
plos-pone-0011087:
Marshall, Bradshaw and Johnson reported bacterial genetics work in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was the germ that causes botulism, a rare but grave food borne illness. The germ makes a powerful nerve toxin, and its toxin genes were the focus of the study.

The team found toxin genes carried on plasmids, small DNA rings that can move between bacteria. That movement, called conjugation, means toxin making ability can spread to new germ cells. The finding raises fresh questions for food safety and germ tracking. It shows why watching gene movement matters, not just watching single strains.
plos-pone-0011187:
Wu, Zhou, Fu and colleagues modeled cooperation in PLOS ONE in 2010. In many groups, helping others pays off only if enough partners help back. The team studied networks whose links change at random over time, a closer match to real social life than fixed networks.

Even on such shifting networks, cooperation could take hold and persist. The structure of who meets whom, and how often that changes, shaped the outcome. That helps explain why helpers endure in nature and in human groups. The results inform game theory and social science models of trust and teamwork.
plos-pone-0011287:
Rassy, Bobes, Rosas and colleagues dissected a tapeworm vaccine in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cysticercosis, caused by tapeworm larvae forming cysts, harms pigs and people in many poor regions. A vaccine called S3Pvac has been tested against it in pigs. The team characterized the vaccine's components in detail.

Knowing exactly what the vaccine contains helps design broader shots against related tapeworm diseases. A working animal vaccine also breaks the cycle that infects people. That double benefit protects herds and human health together. The study gives tropical medicine a defined plan for the next vaccine generation.
plos-pone-0011387:
Li Guo and Zuhong Lu asked in 2010 whether a byproduct of gene silencing is truly waste. When cells make microRNAs, tiny molecules that tune gene activity, the process yields a main strand and a partner strand long treated as scrap to be destroyed. If the partner were pure waste, evolution should have let its sequence drift freely over time.

Tracing the partner strand across species, the authors found signs that its sequence has been kept similar over long spans of evolution. That conservation suggests the strand does useful work as a regulator in its own right. The finding expands the cast of gene regulators biologists should track. It also warns against dismissing any RNA strand as junk before its history across species has been checked.
plos-pone-0011487:
Gustavo Palacios and co-authors linked in 2010 a mysterious salmon disease to a newly found virus. Farmed salmon had developed inflammation of the heart and skeletal muscle that threatened the aquaculture industry, and no cause had been proven. The team searched diseased fish tissue for viral material and identified a novel reovirus present in the sick animals.

Naming the culprit gives fish farmers what they lacked: a target for diagnostic testing and containment. Breeding stock and fry can be screened, and outbreaks can be confirmed quickly instead of guessed at. The discovery also adds a new virus to the watch list for marine disease, where farmed and wild fish meet. In an industry feeding millions, tying a costly disease to a testable agent is the first step toward controlling it.
plos-pone-0011587:
Wayne Delport and co-authors tested computer models used to read evolution in DNA, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such models compare rates of silent DNA changes with rates of changes that alter proteins. That ratio helps scientists judge where natural selection has acted across a genome.

Simple models assume one shared rate, while multi-rate models let different sites evolve at different speeds. Delport and colleagues benchmarked these multi-rate models against each other to see which perform best. Their results guide researchers toward models that add real insight, and warn against extra complexity that brings little gain.
plos-pone-0011687:
Robert Marshall and colleagues checked water policy claims in the dry American Southwest, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A sound water plan should supply both homes and nature. In practice, the authors note, plans in the region focus mostly on feeding fast town growth, with Arizona named as a state where growth has run ahead of supply.

Marshall's team set official claims side by side with real supply and use data. Their check asks whether current plans in the region can truly be called sound for the long term. The answer matters far beyond Arizona, since many dry regions make the same claims while demand keeps rising.
plos-pone-0011787:
Shengxi Guan and co-authors retuned a DNA-cutting enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme BtsI recognises a specific DNA sequence and cuts nearby. It has two subunits: one carries the recognition domain and part of the cutting machinery, while the other completes the cut on both strands.

The authors altered the enzyme's sequence specificity, changing which DNA words it accepts. Retuned cutters give laboratory scientists custom DNA scissors for genetic engineering. Small engineered changes in the recognition part can thus create tools with genuinely new powers for building and editing DNA.
plos-pone-0011887:
Duane McKenna and Brian Farrell used nine genes in 2010 to test the family tree of insects that undergo complete metamorphosis. This group, the Holometabola, covers beetles, flies, butterflies, bees, and more. One order, the twisted-wing parasites called Strepsiptera, has defied placement for centuries because its body plan is so strange.

Adding the nine-gene evidence strengthened the main branches of the holometabolan tree while offering fresh views on where Strepsiptera belongs. A firmer tree matters because nearly everything said about how insect traits evolved depends on who is related to whom. Settling the odd order's place removes a long-standing wobble from that framework.
plos-pone-0011987:
Yutong Sun and Harvey Lodish reported in 2010 that a hormone made by fat tissue helps restrain tumor growth. Adiponectin circulates in blood and had been tied to blood vessel growth with conflicting claims about its role. The team asked directly what happens to tumors when adiponectin is absent.

In mice lacking adiponectin, tumors grew faster, and the change was linked to reduced infiltration by macrophages, immune cells that can attack tumor tissue. Fat tissue is often discussed only as a cancer risk, so a fat-made hormone policing tumors complicates that story. The result connects body weight biology to the immune environment inside tumors.
plos-pone-0012087:
Renée Douville and co-workers reported in 2010 that two much-discussed variants of an immune sensor do not, in fact, change how people respond to bacterial signals. The sensor is TLR4, which detects LPS, a molecule on many bacteria, and also responds during respiratory syncytial virus infection. Its Asp299Gly and Thr399Ile variants travel together in many people and were suspected of blunting immunity.

Testing human immune responsiveness directly, the team found no impact of the variants on responses to LPS or RSV. Many disease-association claims had been built on the assumption that these variants matter. A direct functional test that finds nothing saves the field from another decade of explaining an effect that is not there.
plos-pone-0012187:
Manja Reimann, Constanze Friedrich, Julia Gasch, and co-authors presented a method for tracking the body's pressure reflex in PLOS ONE in 2010. That reflex, the baroreflex, steadies blood pressure by adjusting heart rate, and its strength predicts outcomes in heart disease. Standard tools measure it from natural wobbles in heart rate and pressure but cannot follow quick changes over time or between groups.

Their spectral method maps those changes as they happen, and they used it to compare women and men and younger and older people. Following the reflex live, rather than as one average number, can show when control is failing during stress or disease. Better measurement is the first step toward using the reflex in everyday cardiac care.
plos-pone-0012287:
Sarah Burl, Uche Adetifa, Momodou Cox, and co-authors tested what distorts the tuberculin skin test in Gambian babies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The skin test remains a frontline tool for tuberculosis diagnosis, yet a positive result in a very young child is hard to interpret. Nearly all these children receive the BCG vaccine at birth, and many meet harmless tuberculosis cousins in soil and water, either of which might fake a positive.

Comparing skin tests at four and a half months, they found recent BCG vaccination does sway the result, while the environmental cousins do not. That split tells clinics which positives to discount and which to trust. In high-burden countries, reading this cheap test correctly decides who gets treated in time.
plos-pone-0012387:
Wendy Aartsen, Koen van Cleef, Lucie Pellissier and co-workers delivered a glowing marker gene into mouse eyes in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Müller glial cells stretch across the whole retina and react strongly to injury, which makes them prime targets for gene therapy of blinding diseases. The team used a virus vector to switch on a green marker mainly in activated Müller cells.

After injection, the glowing cells lined up along retinal blood vessels, showing where the vector worked. That precise targeting is what eye gene therapy needs: reach the support cells without flooding the whole eye. The study supports using these cells as delivery routes for future treatments of retinal disease.
plos-pone-0012487:
Sarah Brennan, Qiuju Wang, Robert Tressler and colleagues blocked telomerase in multiple myeloma, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Most myeloma tumor cells cannot sustain endless growth; a rarer clonogenic pool reseeds the cancer. Telomerase, the enzyme that maintains chromosome ends, keeps such stem-like cells going in many cancers and is a prized drug target.

Telomerase inhibition hit the clonogenic myeloma cells through both telomere shortening and a second, independent mechanism. Hitting the reseeding pool is what a lasting therapy must do, since killing only the bulk invites relapse. The dual mechanism strengthens the case for telomerase drugs in this blood cancer.
plos-pone-0012587:
Boram Kim, Rui Kan, Lynne Anguish and colleagues studied a maternal protein in mouse eggs, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. MATER is a maternal effect gene: the mother's egg supplies its product, and embryos need it to develop past the two-cell stage. Inside the growing egg, a lattice of fibers called the cytoplasmic lattice stores materials for the embryo, and its construction was poorly understood.

The team found evidence that MATER helps form that lattice in mouse oocytes. A missing scaffold in the egg could explain some unexplained female infertility and early embryo loss. The work connects a single maternal protein to the physical architecture that makes development possible.
plos-pone-0012687:
Rolli, Rosenblatt-Velin, Li and co-authors showed that a bacterial flagellin can weaken the heart directly. In septic shock the heart often pumps poorly, and the cause may lie inside the heart itself. Their 2010 study exposed hearts to flagellin, the building block of bacterial tails, which immune sensors detect.

The heart tissue mounted an innate immune response and its squeezing power dropped sharply. That direct link helps explain why blood infection so often brings heart failure. Blocking the sensing step could become a way to protect the heart in sepsis.
plos-pone-0312887:
Khaled Shaeel Althabaiti and his team used a 2018 survey of Saudi homes. It held more than eight thousand grown-ups. The team asked who holds bought health cover, and how cover type links to clinic use. The facts form a base line from just before the land's big health revamp.

One in four held bought cover. The split by birth land was stark. Near three in four guests from abroad held it, next to one in eight Saudis. Rich, male, wed, and well-read folk held it most. Yet the bought-cover group used walk-in care less than the state group. The team flags a gap in reach.
plos-pone-0337387:
Isabelle Robène and seven colleagues build field-ready DNA tests for three devastating bacterial diseases of banana, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Moko, blood disease, and Xanthomonas wilt can each destroy plantations, and confirming them normally needs a laboratory. Their tests use a method that copies DNA at one steady temperature, run directly on banana tissue with a simplified extraction — no shipping samples away.

Across wide panels of related and unrelated bacteria, the tests hit their targets and ignored everything else, bar two explainable exceptions. Detection worked down to traces of DNA and in real field samples. Fast answers in the field mean infected plants can be removed before whole districts fall.
plos-pone-0340887:
Mahdi Moharami and co-authors simulated lane changes on roads that tilt sideways to both sides, a design used for drainage on suburban routes. They wanted to know whether such slopes make vehicles unstable. Using professional driving simulators, the 2026 study ran sedans, SUVs, and trucks across four slope angles in dry, rainy, and snowy weather, tracking steering, sliding, and rollover measures.

Steeper slopes nudged steering and rollover angles only modestly, and cars and SUVs stayed composed throughout. Trucks grew hard to control above ninety kilometres per hour on the steepest slopes, and snow amplified every risk. The authors conclude slopes up to two and a half percent are safe for ordinary traffic.
plos-pone-0341787:
Ibukunoluwa I Ibrahim and co-authors interviewed kidney stone patients in 2026 about why their care stalled. Claims data already show delays fall hardest on the underinsured and minorities, but the reasons live in patients' own accounts.

Twenty patients at a safety net hospital and an academic centre, all late for urology follow-up after an emergency visit, described their paths in English or Spanish. Median delay ran past three months. Themes pointed outward, to costs, confusing systems, and doubt sown by earlier encounters, more than to personal neglect. Fixing stone care delays means fixing the route in, not blaming those lost along it.
plos-pone-0344187:
Roxane Schaub and colleagues tested more than two thousand adults in the far Amazon towns where French Guiana meets Suriname. They checked each person for three kinds of hepatitis and for HIV. These river towns are hard to reach, so state health counts, drawn from the big towns, miss them. Each person also told the team what they knew and thought about these germs and how they spread.

Blood checks mixed quick antibody reads with direct hunts for the germs, and the counts were weighed to fit the towns' age and sex mix. A key mark of hepatitis B showed in about two of each hundred tested, while marks of past fights with the germ were much more common. Counts like these are what health chiefs need to plan shots and care where roads run out.
plos-pone-0345587:
Ahmad Zare, Elham Elahifard, and Zahra Asadinejad study when the seeds of a stubborn tropical grass weed wake up and sprout. Crowfoot grass invades rice and sugarcane fields and city lawns. Their 2026 lab study varies temperature patterns, light, seed age, salt, and water shortage to chart the weed's germination rules.

Light switched sprouting on, and day-night temperature swings beat steady warmth. Seeds stored a year sprouted best and fastest, near completely under the best mix. Drought and salt each cut sprouting, with strong doses stopping it fully. Knowing the seeds need light suggests burying them deep, mulching, and tricking them into sprouting before planting can drain the soil's seed store.
plos-pone-0345687:
Yakufu Niyazi led a team of eight authors surveying an unknown seamount in the southeast Pacific, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Seamounts are underwater mountains that host rich life, and this one had never been mapped. The team characterized its benthic habitat, the seafloor environment, and the biological communities living there, using automated and quantitative methods.

Niyazi's baseline survey documents a pristine deep-sea ecosystem before anyone disturbs it. Baselines matter because mining and fishing interests increasingly eye seamounts. Without a record of what lives there, later damage cannot be proved or prevented. Automated methods also let the team cover ground faster than manual sampling, a template for surveying other unknown mounts.
plos-pone-0347187:
Abdullahi Ahmed Tahlil and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One survey of undernutrition in pregnant women in Mogadishu, Somalia. The women were attending public hospitals for antenatal care. Conflict, poverty, and food shortages make expectant mothers there very vulnerable. Yet local proof was thin. The team interviewed and measured more than seven hundred women. They judged nutrition by arm size. They also asked about food access at home.

About three in four women were undernourished by the arm measure. That is a strikingly high share. Risk clustered with later pregnancy and first pregnancies. It also clustered with larger households, lower income, and no latrine at home. Severe food insecurity at home added risk. The authors say the scale of the problem demands action. Nutrition support should be built into antenatal care, with food aid for the poorest homes.
plos-pone-0347487:
Victor H Dominguez, Martin H Dominguez, and co-authors shared the design of a foot-pedal microinjector that any lab can build for about the price of a textbook. Precise injections of tiny volumes into living tissue are usually done with costly commercial rigs, putting virus delivery and genome editing out of reach for small labs.
