Their 2026 device is fully open-source, assembles in under two hours with ordinary tools, and needs no custom parts or soldering.

A footswitch frees both hands for the needle and the sample. The unit holds its own pressure control and can both draw up and dispense, with pulse-triggered shots reliably delivering nanoliter volumes within about fifteen percent error. The authors hope removing cost and complexity barriers spreads delicate injection techniques to more laboratories.
plos-pone-0347687:
Michael J. Ghedotti and colleagues dissected the light-making equipment of ponyfishes, small fish that glow using symbiotic bacteria housed in a throat organ. Their light escapes through windows in the body for camouflage and signalling, and some species blink rapidly despite hosting bacteria that cannot switch off. The 2026 anatomical study focused on one ponyfish tribe whose males bear clear flank windows.

The team gave the first detailed account of the organ's inner structure and found the blinking mechanism: sheets of transparent muscle slide tissue shutters across the light windows. Males carry bigger organs and windows, but females share the same blinking machinery. The anatomy explains a long-standing puzzle of fish behaviour.
plos-pone-0347987:
Dylan Lambert and colleagues test a chestnut wood extract against gut inflammation. Their lab study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The extract is rich in tannins. Those are the bitter plant compounds found in tea and wine. The team screened several plant extracts first. Chestnut stood out, and its chemistry held two dozen phenolic compounds.

In cell tests, the extract calmed two major inflammation pathways. It also shielded the gut lining from harm. Its action fought harmful oxygen molecules on one side. On the other, it curbed immune overreaction. The target disease is inflammatory bowel disease. The work is still at bench stage. But chestnut tannins now look like drug candidates.
plos-pone-0348087:
Yoshiaki Kabata, Ryo Terauchi, and Tadashi Nakano chart six years of eye injections used to treat retinal disease across Japan. These injections deliver drugs that block abnormal blood vessel growth in the eye. Their 2026 study mines the national health claims database from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-two, counting procedures, drug choices, regional rates, and monthly rhythms.

Total injections climbed from about six hundred thousand to more than nine hundred thousand a year. One drug stayed dominant, while newer options entered and diversified choices after twenty twenty. Rates per person rose everywhere, and gaps between prefectures narrowed slightly. Volumes showed mild seasonal swings and no marked pandemic dip. Planning eye services means budgeting for growth that shows no sign of leveling.
plos-pone-0348187:
Yo Ishigaki and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about Bangka Island, Indonesia. It maps how soils contaminated with TENORM, radioactive material found in nature and concentrated by industry, are spread through areas where people live. Bangka is known for tin mining, which can bring such material to the surface.

Knowing where contaminated soil lies under homes is the first step in judging residents' exposure. Radiation in soil is invisible, so surveys must stand in for the senses. Health and environment officials in Indonesia, and the communities themselves, are the readers who need this map.
plos-pone-0348287:
Alexander Mildener and colleagues tested four beluga whales at the New York Aquarium for mirror self-recognition, the ability to know that a mirror shows oneself. Only a handful of species have passed this test, including great apes, dolphins, elephants, and magpies. The whales, three adults and one youngster living as a social group, were shown a two-way mirror and a clear control panel.

Two whales, the youngster and her mother, spent time in self-directed behavior at the mirror, checking their own bodies rather than treating the image as another whale. The adult then passed a mark test, reacting to a mark she could only see in the mirror. The evidence adds belugas to the short list of animals with this form of self-awareness.
plos-pone-0348387:
Meeyoung Kim, Jood Dalbah, and Alham Al-Sharman test whether being a morning or evening person changes how much walking suffers when the mind is busy. Body clocks shift peak alertness across the day, and walking while thinking is a daily multitask. Several dozen healthy young adults rated their body clock type, then walked normally and while spelling backward, subtracting, or reciting months in reverse inside a motion capture lab.

Subtracting hurt walking speed most of the three tasks. Stronger morning preference protected walking speed during the spelling and month tasks, even after accounting for age, sex, body size, and base speed, but not during subtraction. Kim and colleagues suggest task type matters when clinics test walking under mental load, and body clock may belong in the chart.
plos-pone-0348587:
Sergei Scherbov and colleagues built the first complete set of life tables for all seventy-seven Thai provinces. They tracked how the survival gap between women and men changed from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-three. Civil registration data fed models of death rates at every age, computed separately for each sex and province, with national figures assembled from the provincial ones.

Thai women outlived men by seven years at the start, and the gap widened to nearly eight years at the pandemic's height, driven by heavier male deaths during COVID-19. Provincial gaps ranged widely, from under six years to over nine. Dirty air tracked with shorter lives across provinces in a moderate to strong pattern. The authors press for local, sex-aware policy aimed at male mortality and air quality rather than one national recipe.
plos-pone-0348787:
Jeffrey Wu, Gareth Peters, and Alex Franks present a statistical method for modeling counts that vary across both place and time, such as deaths in each county each month. Their procedure learns a graph of how neighboring areas connect, learns a repeating seasonal rhythm for time, and combines the two into one covariance structure. Area clustering keeps the computation manageable, and a fast approximation method fits the model.

They demonstrate it on monthly respiratory deaths across California, using deprivation indexes to shape the spatial graph and air quality measures to inform the time side. The result is a model that is both interpretable and lean, showing which places move together and which seasons bite, a useful shape for public health planning.
plos-pone-0348887:
Chukwunonso Geoffrey Okafor and co-workers survey Nigerian health workers on how well they understand teamwork styles in the care of older adults. Good elder care needs doctors, nurses, therapists, and social workers pulling together, but the labels for working styles blur. Their 2026 study questions close to two hundred fifty staff at a teaching hospital before and after showing plain definitions.

Awareness varied widely by style, with the deepest blending of roles the least known. Just seeing definitions shifted how staff judged their own hospital's practice. Pay gaps between professions, missing shared records, and too few specialists blocked deeper teamwork. Agreeing on what each style means is a first step toward care teams that truly merge their skills.
plos-pone-0349087:
Boris Lok-Fai Pun and colleagues surveyed three hundred and sixty-three university students in Hong Kong about their media habits and their readiness for work. Weekly hours spent with six media types, from newspapers to creator channels and forums, were set against three kinds of readiness. These were handling people and tasks at work, reflecting and learning, and planning a career.

Structured, feedback-rich media told a positive story. Newspaper reading and purposeful social media use tracked with stronger readiness scores. Entertainment-led habits pointed the other way: heavy use of forums and creator channels tracked with weaker readiness. The authors argue that what matters is not screen time as a lump but the shape of the engagement. Educators, they argue, can treat well-chosen media as an informal classroom for work skills.
plos-pone-0349187:
Nwanneka Chidinma Ghasi and Daniel Chukwuemeka Ogbuabor surveyed nurses in the four public tertiary hospitals of Enugu State, Nigeria, about violence at work. Four hundred fifty nurses described whether they had faced verbal, physical, or sexual violence in the past year. The study also gathered details about the nurses and their hospitals to find what raises the risk.

Research on this problem in sub-Saharan Africa is thin, even though attacks harm nurses, slow hospitals, and lower the quality of care patients receive. By measuring how common each kind of violence is and what predicts it, the study gives hospital leaders in the region evidence for staffing, security, and reporting changes.
plos-pone-0349287:
María Teresa Ballestar, Jorge Sainz, and co-authors used machine learning to sort Spanish public universities into types, asking how leadership profiles combine with institutional performance. Spanish rectors are elected by their own academics, staff, and students, making the country a natural laboratory for leadership effects. Their 2026 study assembled a database spanning teaching and research results, social goals, international reach, university traits, and rector characteristics.

An unsupervised clustering method found five distinct groups of universities, each with its own blend of performance indicators and management features. The authors present the clusters as evidence that university performance is a complex package, not a single league table, and that who leads belongs inside the picture. The full results section continues beyond the summary available here, detailing each cluster's profile.
plos-pone-0349387:
Zongshun Zhou and colleagues in China followed new leaves of the tea-oil tree through three growth stages in 2026. The tree yields a prized cooking oil, but harvests swing widely, and leaf growth may hold clues to better breeding.

Watching shape, internal structure, and gene activity as leaves spread, grew, and matured, the team saw green pigment rise and light capture genes switch on in step. Networks of genes tied leaf form to the making of oils and other compounds. The work lays out how a leaf becomes a working solar panel, giving breeders targets for steadier, richer oil harvests.
plos-pone-0349587:
Thin seams of wet mud between rock layers often decide whether a slope slides. Zumei Zha and co-authors tested how the strength of such muddy seams changes with water content and grain size, in a 2026 PLOS One laboratory study of remade soil samples.

As water rose, the stickiness of the samples first grew, then fell, then steadied, while the friction angle dropped the whole way. Adding coarser grains lowered stickiness but raised friction. Grain mix mattered far more than water in their analysis: how evenly grain sizes spread, and how the size curve bent, pushed strength in opposite directions. The results help engineers judge slope risk.
plos-pone-0349687:
Ye Deng and colleagues used gene databases to test whether flu infection and Guillain-Barré syndrome, a paralyzing autoimmune condition that sometimes follows infections, share a common biological pathway. Clinicians have long suspected a link between the H1N1 flu and the syndrome. The team compared genes switched on in each condition and looked for the overlap.

Shared genes clustered in immune pathways, and network analysis singled out three hub genes, TLR4, TNF, and ITGAM, as likely connectors. The study also mapped the small RNAs that regulate those hubs and possible drug interactions. Database work cannot prove the flu triggers the syndrome, but naming the shared machinery gives laboratory researchers a focused place to test the connection directly.
plos-pone-0349787:
Mohammed Saad Javeed and co-authors combined three kinds of deep learning into one system for understanding city transport data. Traffic networks pour out mixed streams of sensor readings, accident reports, and outside context, and sorting useful resources in real time is hard. Their 2026 design reads sequences forward and backward, weighs long-range patterns with attention, and maps road connections as a graph, all enriched with live data pulled from outside services.

Tested on a Barcelona accident dataset and a highway traffic volume dataset, the combined system classified transport resources more accurately than standard rivals and also spotted anomalies well. Removing either the outside data feeds or the graph component hurt performance, confirming both earn their place. The authors report fast enough responses for real deployment.
plos-pone-0349887:
Hina Hashmi and a large team wired a small quantum circuit into a classical neural network to catch faults on power transmission grids in real time. Grid faults must be found in milliseconds before they cascade, and renewables make flows twitchier. Their hybrid model reads sensor waveforms with a conventional front end, then classifies through the quantum layer. It was tested on two simulated standard grids and on about eight hundred real fault recordings.

Accuracy topped ninety-six percent on simulated faults and just under ninety-five on real recordings, beating the plain deep learning rivals they tried, with decisions inside three milliseconds. Removing the quantum layer hurt performance, their internal evidence that it earns its place. Quantum hardware limits and noise remain honest caveats, but the direction, quantum layers as specialist components, looks practical.
plos-pone-0350087:
Yan Duan and Yun Jiang led a team that built a new wound gel. Bad skin wounds stall when blood flow and growth cues run short. The gel blends two aids in one. Tiny carriers hold genes for two growth factors. They sit in a gel made from platelet-rich plasma. The team tried the gel on full-depth skin wounds in rats.

Wounds with the gel closed faster. Blood flow at the site ran stronger. Skin glands and fibers grew back in denser form. Tests showed the growth genes switched on as planned. Vessel, cell growth, and cell survival marks all rose. So did the early repair type of collagen. The team credits the blend, not one part alone.
plos-pone-0350187:
Rodríguez and colleagues tracked microbes through cheese making at a Danish dairy in a 2026 study. Small shifts in milk handling can change a cheese's taste and texture, which troubles makers who need steady quality. Three milk treatments were compared across fourteen steps of making and ripening a Swedish-style cheese.

One helpful lactic strain dominated the whole process, while other microbes stayed at very low levels. A spoilage germ with tough spores showed up in two treatments but was nearly absent when milk was finely filtered. A new gene-reading method also sped up spotting unwanted microbes early. Makers can use these findings to pick milk handling that guards flavor and safety.
plos-pone-0350287:
Md Habib Ullah Masum and co-authors designed a candidate vaccine on the computer against La Crosse virus, a mosquito-borne infection that can inflame the brain, especially in children. No vaccine or targeted drug exists for it. Their 2026 design stitches together immune-triggering fragments from three viral proteins into one multi-part construct, then runs the construct through a battery of structural and immune simulations.

The design scored as stable and well-formed, folded into a plausible shape, and gripped two immune sensor proteins firmly in docking tests. Simulated immune responses produced antibodies and memory cells, and the gene sequence was tuned for efficient production. The authors stress that everything so far is computational: laboratory, animal, and clinical testing must come before any real-world use.
plos-pone-0350387:
Two blood conditions look alike: carrying the beta thalassemia trait and lacking iron. Telling them apart matters for family counseling in Bangladesh, where carriers are common. Rumana Mahtarin and colleagues compared forty-seven ready-made formulas and twelve machine learning models on this task, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The test used about four hundred seventy people drawn from a larger screened group. Two new formulas blended the best older ones and performed strongly. A ranking method that weighs several quality measures at once picked overall winners. The authors aim for a cheap blood-count screen that clinics can run before costly genetic testing.
plos-pone-0350987:
Zhihao Xie and co-authors tuned how drones should fly to rebuild a traffic accident scene in three dimensions. Investigators photograph crash sites from the air, but altitude and photo overlap decide whether the model is true to centimeters or warped. Using a two-layer analysis that pairs a plain statistical model with a learning model, they tested twenty-seven flight setups against measured errors.

Altitude and overlap worked together rather than separately, and the two analysis layers agreed strongly, which supports the approach. A sweet spot emerged: flying low, roughly twenty to twenty-five meters up, with heavy forward overlap and slightly less side overlap gave centimeter-level accuracy with stable geometry. A trial at a real crash scene backed the recipe. For police and insurers, the settings turn drone photos into evidence-grade models.
plos-pone-0351087:
Diego Santana and colleagues describe a new treefrog species from Brazil's Atlantic Forest, found in the Serra da Mantiqueira mountains of Minas Gerais. The frog belongs to a small group whose members are split between the Atlantic Forest and the Amazon. The team combined body measurements, mating call recordings, and DNA barcoding to make the case that this population is its own species.

They name it Dendropsophus liliae. Small size, rounded toe discs, a spur-like heel flap, a dark red iris, and a white stripe running from snout to eyelid set it apart from its relatives. It is the group's most inland Atlantic Forest record. Finds like this keep rewriting the map of how the two great Brazilian forests exchanged species across drier land over deep time.
plos-pone-0351187:
Employees speak up more when they believe leaders can actually grow. Ziyi Zhang and Michael P Haselhuhn tested that idea across four studies, in this 2026 PLOS One paper on beliefs about whether leadership traits are fixed or changeable.

Workers who saw leadership as developable voiced ideas more often, mainly because they believed speaking up would work. The link ran stronger for suggestions aimed at improvement than for warnings aimed at avoiding failure. The authors extend mindset research, famous in classrooms, into the leadership arena. They suggest organizations that preach leader growth may unlock employee voice as a side effect.
plos-pone-0351687:
Miao Zhang, Huaian Qian, and Tengfei Ma present this 2026 PLOS One study of company data and honest reporting. They ask whether a firm's data holdings stop managers from bending real business choices to hit earnings targets. The authors used deep learning to read company reports. That gave a data score for Chinese listed firms from 2010 to 2023. They compared those scores with signs of earnings tricks run through daily operations.

Firms richer in data showed less of this trickery. The result held up under several checks. The authors trace two routes. Data tools curb managers' short-term thinking. Data-rich firms also draw more analyst attention, which tightens outside scrutiny. The effect was strongest in firms under earnings pressure. It focused on cost-side tricks. The authors argue that digital spending quietly improves the honesty of company reports.
plos-pone-0351987:
Mesafint Kebede and colleagues counted kidney failures after major vascular surgery at Ethiopia's largest referral hospital. The records covered seven years at Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital in Addis Ababa. Three hundred seventy-seven adults were included. Kidney outcomes were staged by international rules. The team then modeled which factors around the operation traveled with kidney damage.

Kidney dysfunction followed about one operation in five. That rate is heavy in a system with little spare dialysis capacity. Most published evidence on this risk comes from rich hospitals. A measured local rate does practical work. It tells the Addis Ababa team how large their own risk is, and it gives other hospitals in the region a first mark to beat.
plos-pone-0352587:
Rocco Miazzi and five colleagues review what is known about cocaine exposure before birth. Their 2026 systematic review searched two major databases through August 2025. Twenty-six human studies followed exposed children from infancy into early adulthood. Isolating cocaine's own effects is notoriously hard. Mothers often used other substances too, and poverty and unstable care shadow the same children. The reviewers weighed findings with those confounds in plain view.

Across ages, exposure tracked with a consistent pattern of harm. Babies showed smaller head circumference and motor delays. Older children showed weaker spatial, language, and executive skills. Brain scans found altered white matter and task responses. Growth lagged, and outward behaviour problems ran higher. Yet study quality varied widely, and imaging samples were small. The risk looks real and broad. Honest science must still keep separating the drug's fingerprint from the circumstances around it.
plos-pone-0352687:
Mastrangelo and colleagues, in a 2026 study, look for warning signs that a corneal transplant of a special thin kind will fail within the first years. The operation, used mostly for a swelling disease of the cornea, replaces only the innermost layer. Knowing who is at risk could guide who gets surgery and how it is done.

The team reviewed about one hundred seventy eyes at a regional hospital, followed for at least a year. About one graft in eleven failed. Four factors predicted failure: eyes that were unusually long, grafts from younger donors, trouble unrolling and placing the delicate graft, and major detachment of the graft afterward. Long eyes also had more placement trouble, which may explain part of their risk. Together the four factors explained only a modest share of failures, so much remains unpredictable. The authors urge extra care with long eyes during surgery.
plos-pone-0352787:
Zhao and Yang modeled a digital twin for a smart city drainage system in a 2026 study. A digital twin mirrors a real system live, letting managers test actions safely. Their five-part model adds data and connection layers to a three-dimensional city model, with a light framework for real-time scheduling.

Drainage is the test case, where live sensor data feed the twin and guide pumping decisions. Smart scheduling aims to prevent flooding and wasted energy. City twins attract hype, so working drainage pilots matter: drains are unglamorous, vital, and measurable. Success there would support wider twin use in city services.
plos-pone-0353187:
Lyman, Hanson, and Longo tested how rest breaks affect chest compression quality in a 2026 study. Rescuers tire quickly during resuscitation, and tired compressions grow shallow. Twenty-three young adults each performed nine minutes of compressions under four patterns, from short work-rest cycles to nonstop compressions.

Breathing effort, heart rate, and self-rated strain were tracked alongside compression depth, release, and rate. Comparing patterns shows where quality starts to slip as fatigue builds. Such evidence can guide team rotation rules, so a fresh rescuer steps in before compressions weaken. The lab setup limits direct claims about real arrests, but the fatigue pattern itself is useful for training.
plos-pone-0353287:
Miguel Valério, Fabio Tamburini, and Michele Corazza published this 2026 computational study of lunar calendars across East Polynesia, including Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island. Island communities kept lists naming about thirty nights of the moon. The team compared the wording and structure of forty-eight such lists from every major island group and built a family tree from the differences.

The calendars split into two families matching a proposed split in Polynesian languages. Valério reads the match as evidence that calendar traditions diverged alongside early voyages and language splits across the Pacific.
plos-pone-0353487:
Umair and colleagues, in a 2026 surveillance study, track which types of dengue virus circulated in Pakistan from 2021 to 2025. Dengue returns in seasonal waves, and its four types take turns dominating; a second infection with a different type can be more dangerous. Samples that first tested positive were sent to the national health institute for type testing.

Of more than sixteen hundred positive cases, about seven in ten were confirmed and typed. Type two caused the large majority overall, with type one a distant second and type three almost absent. Type one briefly took the lead in 2023, then type two returned to the top. Cases clustered in the months after the monsoon, and most patients were men in their twenties and thirties. Most reports came from two cities near the testing center, a bias the authors note. They call for year-round, wider molecular surveillance.
plos-pone-0353687:
Li and Pan, in a 2026 language study, test whether a famous idea about translation holds between two very different languages. The idea says traits of a source language shine through into a translation, more so when the source language carries higher prestige. It was built on close language pairs. These authors use a balanced two-way corpus of English and Chinese.

Statistical profiling found shine-through in both directions, but it was stronger when English was the source and Chinese the target, fitting the prestige account since English holds global prestige. Fiction showed the effect more than factual prose. Comparing with studies of closer language pairs, the authors suggest the prestige effect weakens as the two languages grow more distant in structure. They are careful to call that a hypothesis for direct testing, not a settled law, and they frame translation style as a tug among prestige, distance, and caution.
plos-pone-0353787:
Michael Grasdalsmoen and three colleagues use a huge Norwegian student survey to ask whether exercise protects against depression and anxiety, reporting in 2026. More than fifty thousand higher education students reported how often, how hard, and how long they exercised, and a subset completed diagnostic interviews a year later. That forward-looking design lets the team test whether activity today predicts mental disorders tomorrow, rather than merely tracking together.

Students who seldom or never exercised faced a clearly higher risk of a common mental disorder at follow-up than daily exercisers, in both women and men. Risk fell as weekly exercise hours rose, up to about ten hours, and consistency seemed to matter more than intensity or extreme volume. The younger student group showed the most graded pattern. The authors argue campuses should promote regular, attainable activity as part of mental health prevention.
plos-pone-0353887:
Mette Thrane Øhrstrøm and three colleagues follow Danish kidney transplant patients to see how often their original disease returns, in this 2026 PLOS ONE cohort study. The disease, IgA nephropathy, is the world's most common kidney-filter disorder and can destroy a transplanted kidney years later. The team tracked one hundred and eighteen first-time recipients treated at two centres between 1990 and 2020.

Biopsy-proven recurrence struck about one patient in seven, reaching roughly one in six by ten years after surgery. Younger diagnosis, fast progression to kidney failure, and receiving a kidney from a living or related donor each raised the risk. Recurrence sharply increased the chance of losing the graft, underlining the need for closer monitoring.
plos-pone-0353987:
Janbozorgi and colleagues ran a small pilot study, reported in 2026, on whether the time of day for exercise changes gene activity in the bones of diabetic mice. Diabetes can weaken bone and lower the activity of genes tied to cell repair. The team focused on four such genes in bone tissue.

Eighteen male mice were split into healthy, diabetic, and diabetic exercise groups. The exercise groups ran on a treadmill for eight weeks, five times a week, either in the light phase or the dark phase. Diabetes raised blood sugar and lowered the repair-linked genes. Training improved sugar control and partly brought gene activity back. Evening training gave the strongest recovery for two of the genes. As a pilot, the study is early evidence that when exercise happens may shape its benefit for bone.
plos-pone-0354487:
Mauricio Carvache-Franco led a team of four authors on this 2026 survey study of why people use Instagram. Nearly three hundred and seventy users answered questions about their motives, satisfaction, and loyalty, and statistical grouping sorted them into types. Four drives emerged: curiosity and documenting life, self-expression, socializing, and recreation.

Three user segments formed around those drives, differing in background, satisfaction, and loyalty to the platform. Carvache-Franco aims the detailed findings squarely at businesses that sell or communicate through Instagram and need to know which audience they are actually addressing.
plos-pone-0354587:
Duaa Abuarqoub and co-authors test in 2026 a nanoparticle delivery system meant to help stem cells from young tooth tissue become better insulin making cells for diabetes research. Such cells can be converted, but many die along the way. A growth boosting compound was packed into tiny polymer particles made with a microfluidic method and checked for size, charge, and stability.

Treated cells survived better, showed a higher share of healthy cells, and matured more fully, with stronger insulin related markers. In glucose challenge tests the cells released insulin in a controlled way. The authors present the loaded particles as a promising step toward cell based diabetes therapy.
plos-pone-0354687:
Pierre-Yves Robillard led a team of eight authors studying pregnancy risks in a very large birth cohort, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When the placenta grows a fetus too slowly, some mothers go on to develop preeclampsia, a dangerous rise in blood pressure, but most do not. The team asked what sets those cases apart.

Drawing on records from a long-running cohort of births, Robillard's group compared cases where both problems occurred with cases of slow growth alone. They searched for clinical signs that mark higher risk. A sharper watch list helps doctors focus close care on the mothers most likely to become ill, while sparing others needless alarm.
plos-pone-0354887:
Min Du and co-authors dig in 2026 for genes that raise risk of the most common skin cancer, working at the level of single immune cell types. Large genetic studies had found many risk spots, but averaging across whole tissue hid which cells each spot acts through. Their method joined cancer genetic data with gene control data from a dozen immune cell types.

Cell level analysis found far more linked genes than whole blood analysis, grouped in a few T cell, monocyte, and B cell types. Each type showed its own immune programme. Because the control data came from healthy donors, the authors call the findings leads needing tumour based checks.
plos-pone-0355187:
Mohamed Khalid AlOmar and colleagues improved computer prediction of how deeply buried pipelines have corroded, a measurement that decides when to dig, repair, or replace. Their 2026 study notes that training data for such models is lopsided: mild corrosion cases abound while dangerous deep cases are rare, so models learn to overlook exactly the failures that matter.

The team generated synthetic examples of the rare severe cases, then retrained four kinds of model, including a deep neural network and a gradient boosting method. Every model improved, and the deep network with balanced data cut prediction error by about a quarter. Better corrosion forecasts let pipeline operators spend inspection budgets where the metal is truly thinning.
plos-pone-0355387:
Héctor Hernández-Nuñez and seven colleagues examine how growing cocoa shapes rural life in Colombia, in a 2026 study spanning four departments. Households there have been redesigning how they earn a living, and cocoa has played a different part in each home's mix. The team surveyed and interviewed more than four hundred cocoa-growing households about their assets, strategies, and hopes for the crop.

Five household types emerged, from dedicated cocoa farmers to families mixing cocoa with livestock, coffee, or off-farm work. Santander's households were best equipped for cocoa, while those in Caquetá were least equipped. Families mostly planted cocoa because their land suited it, it paid, and it was easy to manage. Nine in ten saw a promising future in the crop, viewing it as secure income and a cushion for old age.
plos-pone-0355687:
Guanfang Weng and five colleagues redesign the product design process itself around artificial intelligence, using camping cookware as their test case, in this 2026 study. Interest in glamorous camping has raised demand for better cookware, and the team wanted sustainability built into the process from the start rather than checked at the end. They first structured user expectations through structured interviews and expert ranking methods, turning them into a requirements model.

Generative image tools then produced design concepts under structured prompt cards that encoded those requirements, and formal evaluation methods ranked the alternatives and measured user satisfaction. Function and safety, especially usability and ergonomic fit, mattered far more to users than emotional extras like personal flair. The authors report the AI reproduced schemes faithfully and sped creative work, while noting the framework's edge still awaits proof.
plos-pone-0356187:
Minlong Yan and coauthors published a 2026 landscape study in PLOS ONE on mapping feelings along a scenic road, treating emotion as flowing along a route rather than pooling in places. Most emotion maps chop space into plots or zones, missing how a drive or walk unfolds. Combining panoramic imagery, virtual reality sessions eliciting emotional responses, and spatial modeling, the team mapped emotions continuously along a famous scenic road in Wuyi Mountain National Park.

Feelings organized hierarchically, clustering along the main road and thinning into surrounding buffer land. Most strikingly, positive and negative emotions rose together in the most scenic core stretches, contradicting the assumption that a place feels either good or bad. Several landscape features mattered jointly, with sharp threshold effects rather than smooth trade-offs. The framework gives park planners a finer instrument: designing the emotional sequence of a journey, not just its stops.
plos-pone-0356387:
Jennifer Geis and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE exploring an unlikely liquid biopsy for prostate cancer: seminal fluid. The prostate contributes directly to semen, so its shed DNA should be enriched there, but collecting the fluid is awkward and had kept cohorts tiny. Nearly two hundred eighty men scheduled for prostate biopsy mailed in home-collected samples, and the team extracted cell-free DNA and read its methylation, chemical tags varying by tissue and cancer.

All samples held abundant long DNA fragments. Tissue fingerprints showed mostly sperm and white blood cell DNA, but prostate DNA was present at measurable levels. Simple clustering split men into two groups driven by sperm and white cell shares, confounding region-level summaries, so the team used fragment-level methylation features and found signals tied to clinically significant cancer. Seminal fluid, they conclude, is a workable, unconventional biopsy source worth developing.
plos-pone-0356487:
Meihua Sun and six colleagues catalog a family of hormone-response genes in tomato in this 2026 study. The genes, called B-type response regulators, relay signals for cytokinin, a hormone that drives plant growth, and may also mediate drought responses. The team searched the tomato genome and found ten family members. They mapped them across eight chromosomes, sorted them into three subfamilies by shared protein features, and charted where each is most active in the plant.

Some members dominated in shoot tips, others in roots, and one in fruit, while a few were barely detectable anywhere. Control regions of the genes carried drought and stress-hormone response elements, and both simulated drought and the stress hormone abscisic acid switched the genes down. Given the known opposition between cytokinin and that stress hormone, the authors propose these regulators as junction points in drought signaling, useful leads for breeding tougher tomatoes.
plos-pone-0356687:
Victoria C. Nolan, James Harrison, and Jonathan A. G. Cox published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE on a bee-free artificial honey that fights a stubborn drug-resistant bacterium. Mycobacterium abscessus causes skin, soft tissue, and lung infections and shrugs off many antibiotics, hitting the weakest hardest. Manuka honey works against it, but the team wanted a synthetic version easing pressure on the natural product, so they tuned their vegan recipe with key enzymes and components.

The adjusted artificial honey did more than slow the bacterium: it killed it outright in susceptibility tests. Two ingredients carried the killing power, the compound methylglyoxal and hydrogen peroxide, both familiar from natural medical honey. The authors present the result as proof that a fully synthetic, bee-derived-nothing honey can match the antimicrobial punch needed against this pathogen. A manufactured alternative could make honey-based treatments cheaper and free of supply worries.
plos-pone-0356787:
Yubin Xue, Hongwei Ma, Lin Yang, and Qiang Liu used Global Burden of Disease estimates to track hearing loss caused by otitis media. Otitis media is a middle ear infection common in childhood. Their study covered the whole world from 1990 to 2023. It compared countries by age, sex, and development level. It also separated how much of the change came from population growth, aging, and shifting illness rates.

Age-adjusted prevalence eased downward over the three decades. Yet it stayed highest in poorer regions and among children aged five to fourteen. Boys were affected more than girls. Most cases were mild, and no country showed a clear rise. The results point prevention efforts toward young children in low-income settings, where treatable ear infections still cost the most hearing.
plos-pone-0356887:
Wannes Nauwynck, Karoline Faust, and Nico Boon published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on screening microbes one cell at a time without exotic equipment. Individual cells in a species differ, shaping how communities survive stress, but existing single-cell tools are pricey or fiddly. Their workflow, DE-SWIRL, grows single cells inside uniform double-emulsion droplets made by a simple templating trick, then sorts the droplets with a standard fluorescence cell sorter found in many laboratories.

The team showed droplets of two sizes form reliably, with just under half surviving the process, and they worked out a gating strategy that keeps contaminating particles from corrupting the screen. From a synthetic community they pulled out chosen strains at near-perfect purity, and isolated droplet cocultures from a mixed community. Each run handles around ten million microcultures, making the workflow a cheap route to hunting rare, useful microbes in whole microbiomes.
plos-pone-0356987:
Yusif Gurbanli, Jaron Mohammed, and Francesco Travascio reviewed thirty years of attempts to rebuild the knee in three dimensions from ordinary flat X-rays, avoiding the radiation and cost of CT scans. Their 2026 systematic review gathered twenty-eight studies spanning shape statistics, deep learning, and image registration methods, comparing accuracy, image needs, and speed.

Accuracy improved dramatically over the period, with recent methods landing within roughly half a millimeter to a millimeter of CT truth, and two standard views often sufficed. Processing now takes from under a second to a few minutes. The review's complaints are about evidence quality: small patient groups, few diseased knees, and no shared public benchmark. Still, the trajectory points toward routine X-ray-based surgical planning.
plos-pone-0357087:
Jeremy T Claisse and colleagues produced fine-grained sonar maps of thirteen artificial reef complexes and shipwrecks off southern California, resolving the seafloor into hand-sized cells. Their 2026 study classified 154 reef modules and measured each one's footprint, volume, height, slope, and surface roughness, then asked whether those numbers reflect what the reef was built from.

They do. Quarry rock piles stood tall, steep, and rough within compact footprints, while scattered concrete pieces sprawled flatter with patchier roughness, and their fuzzy edges made footprints harder to draw. Because fish and invertebrates respond to exactly these structural traits, the maps let reef designers match construction materials to ecological goals and give managers a baseline for tracking change.
plos-pone-0357287:
Cecilia Rago led a team of eight authors describing virus tracking dashboards for England, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Family doctors and public health teams need current intelligence on respiratory viruses, not reports that arrive weeks late. The dashboards turn lab results into near-live views of where flu and related viruses are surging.

Rago's group set out how the dashboards serve both primary care and public health users. A GP can see local virus pressure before a clinic fills, and officials can target messages or resources. Timely displays proved their worth during past virus seasons. This work shows how routine lab data, well presented, becomes a daily decision tool.
plos-pone-0357387:
Jetson Lobos, Jeffrey Velasquez, and Fariborz Nasertorabi published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on making lab-made proteins and peptides easier to purify. Their approach tags a target protein with an elastin-like chain that stays dissolved when cool but clumps when warmed, so filtering can pull the product out without expensive chromatography columns. Two obstacles had slowed adoption: no standard gene cassette for the tag, and no clean way to remove the tag after cutting it free.

The team built a modular, ready-to-use cassette that works under mild conditions, clumping at temperatures only slightly above room temperature and at modest salt levels. After the tag is cut, its tendency to clump at higher concentration lets it be filtered away from the freed product. As a demonstration, they purified a small human antimicrobial peptide, noting the size gap between tag and peptide makes the trick work best.
plos-pone-0357487:

Missed check-ups during pregnancy raise risks for mother and newborn alike, and uninsured migrants face the steepest barriers. The review gathered fourteen studies from Canada, the United States, Iran, and Thailand since 2000, mapping interventions meant to open access, with their strengths, weaknesses, and costs.

A recurring story emerged around policy cuts: trimming services for uninsured migrants looks like savings, but costs resurface later and larger, landing on regional governments covering emergencies. The authors judge several of these shifts politically driven rather than economically sound. Helpful interventions ranged from dedicated clinics to coverage schemes, but coverage stayed patchy. As the first review of its kind, it maps what exists and warns against false economies in maternal care.
plos-pone-0357587:
Luis Pérez-Mañá and four colleagues grade what YouTube tells parents about controlling children's short sight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Myopia is spreading, treatments to slow it exist, and families increasingly learn about them from videos rather than clinics. The team searched in English and Spanish in February 2025 and kept two hundred thirty-five videos that met their rules, then had three optometrists score each one with three standard quality tools.

Quality and reliability swung widely from video to video. University and professional channels scored best but made up a minority of what parents actually find. Spanish videos edged English ones on one reliability scale, while English videos drew far more views despite no quality advantage. The scoring tools themselves sometimes disagreed with each other. The authors urge eye professionals to publish more evidence based videos, since the popular ones cannot be trusted by default.
plos-pone-0357787:
Jingqi Huang and Wasim Ahmad published a 2026 consumer study in PLOS ONE on how artificial intelligence hosts in live-stream shopping shows nudge people into impulse buying. Working within a stimulus–organism–response framework, they ran scenario experiments varying how human the AI host looked and how socially it chatted with viewers. They measured two inner states that might carry the effect: how much viewers trusted the host's competence, and how emotionally stirred they felt.

Both kinds of humanlike cues raised impulse buying through trust and arousal. Chatty, socially warm conversation moved viewers more than visual humanlikeness. The mechanism worked much the same for men and women, though it differed between product types and between viewers with more or less past AI experience. For sellers designing virtual hosts, the lesson is to invest in conversation style, not just a lifelike face; for regulators, the study names the levers of persuasion.
plos-pone-0357887:

Governments increasingly treat radicalization as a social care and public health problem, pulling social workers toward prevention work. Yet research on what social workers actually do there is scattered across countries and concepts, leaving practitioners unsure of their footing.

The planned review will be the first to systematically map that landscape: how roles are described, which theories guide practice, and what experiences workers report. It also aims to name the field's gaps, limits, and openings, separating what is known from what is merely assumed. Because extremism inflicts trauma across generations, a clear map matters for social work's development and for the wider prevention field.
plos-pone-0357987:

Pulmonary hypertension is the leading killer in this disease, so vascular insight has direct clinical stakes. Richard Price preached the sermon printed in 1787 as The Evidence for a Future Period of Improvement in the State of Mankind. Price was a Welsh dissenting minister, moral philosopher, and friend of the American and French revolutions. His sermons often carried his politics and his hopes into the pulpit.

The discourse reads prophecy and recent history together, arguing that the world is moving toward a better age of knowledge and liberty. Price points to the spread of learning and the fall of old tyrannies as signs of the design. The sermon is Enlightenment optimism at its most fervent, preached as theology. It shows why Price's admirers saw him as a prophet of progress, and why his enemies feared that his pulpit was really a platform for revolution.
price-review-principal-questions-morals-:
Richard Price, a Welsh minister and philosopher, published A Review of the Principal Questions in Morals in 1758. The third edition of 1787 is the text here, with its appendix and a dissertation on the Deity. Price defends rationalist ethics: moral truth, he holds, is perceived by the reason, as surely as any other truth.

His great opponent is Hutcheson's moral sense, which Price finds too blind and shifting to ground duty. Right and wrong, for Price, are real features of actions, known by the understanding. russell-studies-scriptures-vol2-1887:
Russell's Time is at Hand, in this 1889 edition of Studies in the Scriptures, Volume 2, works out the movement's Bible chronology. Russell counts the ages from creation forward through dates drawn from scripture and history. The 1914 prophecy stands at the heart of the book.

Charts and parallel dates between Israel's history and the gospel age fill the chapters. Bible Students treated the chronology as proof that they lived in the last days of the present order.
sayce-religion-ancient-babylonians-1887:
A. H. Sayce delivered his Hibbert Lectures in 1887 as Lectures on the Origin and Growth of Religion as Illustrated by the Religion of the Ancient Babylonians. Williams and Norgate published them at London the same year. Sayce, a pioneer Assyriologist at Oxford, read Babylon's hymns, omens, and myths from the new cuneiform finds.

He set Babylonian beliefs about gods, sin, and the soul beside the Hebrew scriptures he also taught. The lectures announced, to a wide public, what Assyriology meant for the history of religion. They were cited everywhere in their day and sparked fierce debate. Sayce writes as a scholar-explorer reporting from a newly opened world. Schottmüller walks through the charges, the papal inquiry, and the slow crush of the defense. He builds each claim on the trial papers his second volume prints. The story ends with the order suppressed in 1312 and its master burned in 1314. The book remains the great nineteenth-century history of the affair.
