Their first report finds fraud, self deceit, and scant that stands. The tone is dry and fair, which made its sting worse for fans. It is the first such verdict by a school in the United States. Its fame still lasts.
solinus-polyhistor-golding-1587:
Arthur Golding Englished Solinus's Polyhistor in 1587, the first English version of the ancient book of wonders. Golding was a busy Elizabethan translator, and this was among his most curious tasks. Solinus had gathered the marvels of the world from Pliny and other Roman writers.

English readers now met griffins, Amazons, and the wonders of the far East in their own tongue. Golding's plain, vigorous style suits the matter well. The book fed the Renaissance hunger for strange lands and strange peoples. It also helped stock the minds of the age that produced Shakespeare. In 1587, the fabulous East arrived in English print.
spr-proceedings-vol4-1886-1887:
Volume four of the Proceedings covers the years 1886 and 1887 in parts ten and eleven. London's Society for Psychical Research kept building its case files here. Thought reading experiments run alongside reports of crisis apparitions. A census of strange experiences was taking shape in these years.

Committees report in dry tables, then argue over what the numbers mean. Mediums who sat for the society include the trance speaker Mrs. Piper's circle and others. Physical wonders, like table movement, face exposure as often as praise. The volume captures psychical research in its earnest Victorian prime. Its records fed arguments for the next fifty years.
strindberg-the-father-1887:
August Strindberg wrote The Father in 1887, here in Edith and Warner Oland's English translation in print. The naturalist tragedy of the Captain's destruction in the battle of the sexes made Strindberg world-famous overnight. Its three acts compress a marriage's war into one house, one doubt, and one straitjacket at home.

Captain Adolf, a cavalry officer and man of science, fights his wife Laura over their daughter's schooling. Laura plants a doubt about his paternity, and the doubt eats his reason like a slow poison. Servants, a pastor, and a doctor are drawn in as Laura steers him toward the asylum's keepers. The old nurse tricks him into the straitjacket with a mother's soft voice and a nurse's hands. The Olands' version carried this fierce chamber tragedy to English and American stages alike.
system-und-folgen-illuminatenordens-1787:
System und Folgen des Illuminatenordens was printed at Munich in 1787, as the Bavarian state moved against the Illuminati. The book draws its case from the order's own printed papers, seized in house searches such as the raid on Zwack's home. It presents the state's reading in the form of letters.

Letter by letter, the writer lays out the order's grades, rules, and secret aims. He then warns what such a hidden system could do to church, state, and public trust. The book served as a guide to the seized archive for readers of the day. It shows how officials turned private letters into a public charge.
taylor-hymns-orpheus-1787:
Thomas Taylor, an English Platonist, turned the Hymns of Orpheus into English in 1787. It was the first English form of these old Greek hymns. Taylor was a lone, keen man who gave his life to the Greek sages and their gods.

The hymns praise the gods of Greece, one by one, in rich and high verse. With them stands Taylor's own long piece on the life and thought of Orpheus, the famed singer priest. The book is the root text in English for the rites that bear the name of Orpheus.
the-snare-pg2687: Sabatini sets a trap of love and politics in his 1917 romance. His hero dodges both with a swordsman’s grace. Dashing, clever, and romantic: the master’s lighter touch, the master's lighter touch, dashing and clever.
tob-0187:
Manly P. Hall read the world's fire myths as one symbol in The Initiates of the Flame. Prometheus stealing fire, the phoenix rising from ashes, and the burning bush all figure, for Hall, the divine spark awakening in human beings. The short work comes from his early years as an occult teacher in Los Angeles.

Hall proceeds by allegory and association rather than argument, inviting readers to see temples, altars, and volcanoes as chapters of one story about fire's sacred meaning. V1 evidence describes the result as occultism presented as comparative mythology, lit from within. Readers sampling Hall before his giant later encyclopedia will find his characteristic voice already formed: oracular, synthetic, and confident.
tob-10787:
M. M. Pattison Muir, a Cambridge chemist, told how the dream of transmutation slowly gave way to chemistry in The Story of Alchemy and the Beginnings of Chemistry. His route runs from Alexandrian adepts through Arab practitioners to Boyle and Lavoisier. The tone is lucid and unromantic throughout.

Muir shows real knowledge emerging from centuries of splendid error: furnaces improved, substances were identified, and vague spirits gave way to elements and measured reactions. He respects the workers while discarding their theory. Readers get a scientist's history of his own discipline's unlikely childhood, useful for understanding why chemistry's founders argued as they did.
tob-4087:
Seven Poems and a Fragment, a slim Yeats volume from 1922, gathers work from the years of Irish civil war and his life at the tower of Ballylee. Late Yeats in miniature remains unmistakable: history appears as nightmare, art as defiance, and old age as no excuse for softness. Seven poems carry that weight; the fragment trails off suggestively.

Private-press brevity is part of the point; such small books were made for collectors and friends of the Cuala Press circle. Yet the shadow is large, since these years produced some of Yeats's most haunted writing. Readers get a pocket specimen of the late manner, proof that scale and importance are different things.
tob-4187:
John Burnet's Early Greek Philosophy traces the first Western thinkers from Thales's water to Democritus's atoms. These Presocratics, working in Greek cities of Asia Minor and Italy, began explaining the world through nature rather than gods: air, fire, number, atoms and void. Burnet was a rigorous Scottish classicist who believed the fragments deserved exact, unsentimental reading.

His study set the standard for English scholarship on the Presocratics for generations, and his reconstructions still anchor debate. Readable despite its learning, the book follows arguments about change, being, and the kosmos as they pass from teacher to critic. Readers looking for where Western reason begins will find its birthplace mapped here.
tob-9287:
Buehler's translation of the Laws of Manu is the classic English form of ancient India's great law-book. Manu, the primeval lawgiver of legend, orders society by dharma: the duties of castes, the stages of life from student to hermit, and the king's justice. Georg Buehler rendered it for the Sacred Books of the East.

Marriage, inheritance, diet, penance, and the treatment of women and servants all receive rules. The code shaped Hindu law and custom for centuries, and modern India still argues with its legacy. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Buehler's version remains the scholars' standard.
tower-commission-report-1987:
President Ronald Reagan appointed the Tower Commission in late 1986 to examine the Iran-Contra affair. Former Senator John Tower led the board, which reported in February 1987 after hearing dozens of witnesses. The scandal mixed secret arms sales to Iran with illegal aid to rebels in Nicaragua.

The report traced how White House staff sold weapons to Iran, hoping to free hostages. Part of the money went to the Contra rebels despite a ban from Congress. It blamed a loose management style that left the president detached from his own aides' actions. Reagan accepted the findings and addressed the nation. The report remains the first and fullest official account of the affair.
tyler-contrast-1787:
Royall Tyler wrote The Contrast, and it reached the stage at New York's John Street Theatre on April 16, 1787. Thomas McKee's introduction calls it bright, humorous, and natural, with sharp satire on the follies of the day. The plot sets two suitors side by side for one young woman.

Dimple apes foreign fashion and polish, while the honest American colonel keeps plain manners. A blunt Yankee servant named Jonathan steals scene after scene. He became the first true Yankee figure on the American stage. Light and patriotic, the play announced that a home-grown theater had arrived and could please a paying crowd.
un-ga-res-a-69-87:
People driven from their homes in the June 1967 war are the subject of Resolution A/69/87, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls votes from 1967 and 1968 on their plight. It also weighs two reports on the year 2013. One came from the Secretary-General, the other from the head of the UN refugee agency for Palestine. Sorrow at the lasting human pain of that war and its sequels runs through the vote.

The 1993 deal on stopgap self-rule had set terms for letting the 1967 displaced come back. Those terms, the Assembly notes with concern, have still not been put into force. The text opens by stating again the right of all such displaced people to go back to their homes.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/87, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns persons displaced by the June 1967 and later hostilities in the Middle East. It reaffirms their right to return to their homes or former places of residence. Those are in the territories occupied by Israel since 1967. It presses for the return mechanism agreed in the 1993 Declaration of Principles to be used. It backs continued emergency help from the refugee agency UNRWA for those still displaced and in serious need.
un-sc-res-1287:
UNOMIG's mandate was renewed as the Abkhaz talks stirred on 31 January 2000. The ninth session of the coordinating council had met in Tbilisi on 18 and 19 January. The parties signed a protocol for the joint study of ceasefire breaches. They also agreed to renew talks on peace and on refugee return to Gali. The Secretary-General's report of 19 January guided the Council.

The Council extended UNOMIG's mandate for six months. The parties were urged to seize the chance offered by a new special representative's arrival. They had to deepen their engagement in the talks and honor the Moscow ceasefire in full. The Council restated that the population changes forced by the war were unacceptable and unlawful. Human rights had to be respected by both sides without exception. The Abkhaz side was pressed to accept the return of refugees to the Gali region as a first step.
un-sc-res-1387:
United Nations observers kept watch over the Prevlaka peninsula into 2002. On 15 January 2002 the Security Council authorized them to continue. The mission, UNMOP, monitored the demilitarized zone between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Secretary-General's January report guided the decision. Relations between the two governments were slowly improving. A joint border commission had been set up.

Both parties had to stop breaking the demilitarized regime. They had to work with the observers and keep them safe. The Council urged faster talks toward a settled border. It also encouraged steps to build confidence between the sides. The small mission guarded a dispute left over from the Yugoslav wars.
un-sc-res-1487:
Peacekeepers from countries outside the new world criminal court gained a shield in 2003. On 19 May 2003 the Security Council renewed a request to the International Criminal Court. If a case arose over United Nations work by staff from a non-party state, the court should not act. The pause would run twelve months from 1 July 2003. The Rome Statute allows such a request under its article 16.

The Council said it meant to renew the request each July. Member states had to take no action that clashed with it. France, Germany, and Syria abstained in the vote. The text renewed a 2002 measure that had eased the court's launch. It stayed controversial among the court's supporters.
un-sc-res-1587: Numbered 1587, this Council resolution is kept in the official wording copied by English Wikisource. Such texts are worked out line by line, because their words can place duties on member states. The entry gives that worked-out wording as it stands: findings first, then the decisions that rest on them, ready for close reading or for quoting in later work.
un-sc-res-1687:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed amid buffer zone strains on 15 June 2006. The Secretary-General's report of 23 May found the island's security stable and the Green Line calm. Building inside the buffer zone and new checkpoint limits on the force's movement caused concern. The committee on missing persons had resumed its work in August 2004. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay past 15 June.

The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions and voiced full support for UNFICYP. The Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces were called to restore the military status quo at Strovilia. Both sides were urged to take part in bicommunal talks on daily matters that touch both communities. The force's work to apply the Secretary-General's zero tolerance policy on abuse was welcomed. The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate for a further period ending 15 December 2006.
un-sc-res-1787:
The Counter-Terrorism Committee's executive arm gained a short extension from the Security Council on 10 December 2007. The General Assembly had adopted a Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, and a task force now coordinated the United Nations effort. The Council praised member states for working with the committee. It also reminded states that counter-terrorism steps must respect human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law.

The Council extended the Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate's initial period, set by resolution 1535 (2004), to 31 March 2008. The directorate's executive director had sixty days to propose changes to its organizational plan. Those changes would go to the committee for approval before the new deadline ran out. The text is a brief bridge measure. It kept the monitoring of resolution 1373 (2001) running while the Council decided how the directorate should be shaped for the longer term.
un-sc-res-187:
Nine days after Resolution 186 created a peacekeeping force for Cyprus, the Council pushed to get it onto the island fast. Cyprus, Greece, and Turkey had all addressed the Council. The Council said it was deeply concerned by events in the area. The Secretary-General reported that the force was about to be established. Its advance parties were already on their way. Resolution 187 was adopted unanimously on 13 March 1964.

The Council reaffirmed Resolution 186 of 4 March 1964. It repeated its call for all states to do nothing that could worsen the situation in Cyprus. The Secretary-General was told to press ahead with setting up the force. Member states were asked to help him in that work. The text is brief, and its point is speed. A force voted into being on paper had to become real on the ground before the fighting grew.
un-sc-res-1887:
Nuclear weapons are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1887, adopted on 24 September 2009. The Council met at the level of heads of state and government, a rare step. The vote was unanimous. Members pledged to work toward a world without nuclear weapons.

The text backs the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and all three of its parts. States must guard nuclear material so it cannot fall into the hands of armed groups. The resolution backs the goal of securing all at-risk nuclear material within four years. It urges tighter export controls, a halt to illegal nuclear trade, and steps to stop funds that feed such programs.
un-sc-res-387: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 387, this formal text is catalogued under the year 1976. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-687:
Iraq and Kuwait are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 687, adopted on 3 April 1991. The Gulf War fighting had stopped under a brief truce. Iraq still held Kuwaiti property and missing people. Its chemical, biological, and missile programs remained intact. The Council set the terms that would turn the truce into a formal cease-fire.

Iraq must accept the old border and destroy all chemical and biological weapons and longer-range missiles. A special commission, UNSCOM, will inspect and oversee that work. Iraq is liable for all losses from its invasion, and a compensation fund will pay claims. Observers will watch a demilitarized zone along the border. Once Iraq accepts every term, the cease-fire takes legal effect.
un-sc-res-87:
By Resolution 87, adopted on 29 September 1950 by seven votes to three, with one abstention, the Council acted on Taiwan. The government in Beijing had declared that the island faced an armed invasion. Who spoke for China at the United Nations was itself in dispute. The Korean War had made the question sharper still.

The Council puts off debate on the charge until its first meeting after 15 November 1950. It invites a speaker from the Beijing government to attend that debate. The invitation rests on the Council's rules for hearing outsiders. It settles nothing about which government holds China's seat. The delay let tempers cool while the facts were gathered.
un-sc-res-987: At number 987 in its series, the Security Council decision is catalogued here as a 1994 record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1287, adopted on 31 January 2000, returns to the Abkhazia conflict in Georgia. The Georgian and Abkhaz sides had met in Tbilisi days earlier and agreed on a way to jointly probe breaches of the 1994 Moscow ceasefire deal. The UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, and a CIS peacekeeping force kept the zone of conflict fairly calm, though the Council called it still unsettled.

The Council extends UNOMIG until 31 July 2000. It urges both sides to deepen their part in the UN-led peace process and to settle how powers are shared between Tbilisi and Sukhumi, while respecting Georgia's borders. It calls the self-styled elections and referendum held in Abkhazia unacceptable. It also repeats that all refugees and displaced people keep the right to return home in safety.

A small cape at Croatia's tip caused years of friction. Prevlaka guards the mouth of the Bay of Kotor. Croatia and Yugoslavia both claimed the ground. UN observers had watched its demilitarized state since 1992. Resolution 1387, passed with no dissent on 15 January 2002, kept those observers in place.

The watch would run to 15 July 2002. The Secretary-General's report of 2 January had urged calm. Both states had just agreed to form a joint border team. The Council told them to speed up a deal on the cape. Breaches of the no-arms zone had to stop. The observers from the UN and the NATO-led force nearby were told to work hand in hand.

A fight over the new world criminal court reached the Council in 2003. The court at The Hague could now hear war crimes cases. The United States, not a member, feared its troops abroad could be charged. In 2002 the Council had granted a one-year shield. Resolution 1487, passed on 19 May 2003, renewed that shield.

Twelve members voted yes. France, Germany, and Syria held back. The text asks the court to hold off for twelve months from 1 July 2003. No case could start against peace troops from states outside the court. The pause used a clause built into the court's own treaty. Critics called it a blow to justice. Backers called it the price of keeping peace missions staffed.

Somalia's arms embargo monitoring team is set up again on 15 March 2005. A Transitional Federal Government had been formed after national reconciliation talks, raising hopes of real governance. The previous Monitoring Group had reported continued flows of weapons into the country in February 2005.

The Secretary-General, working with the sanctions committee, is asked to set the Monitoring Group up again. Its task is to watch the embargo, gather evidence of violations, and recommend ways to make the ban work better. The continued flow of arms into Somalia is condemned, all states are reminded they must respect the embargo, and African Union and regional efforts to support the new government are backed.

Cyprus and its long-running peacekeeping force are the focus of Resolution 1687, adopted on 15 June 2006. The UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, patrols the buffer zone between the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot sides. The Secretary-General reported that the island stayed calm along the Green Line, though full peace talks were still stalled.

The Council extends UNFICYP's mandate until 15 December 2006. It asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. The text welcomes work on missing persons, mine clearing near Nicosia, and more than ten million peaceful crossings between the two sides. It urges both sides to avoid steps that raise tension and to keep talking.

Resolution 1787, adopted on 10 December 2007, concerns the machinery the Council built after the September 2001 attacks to police counter-terrorism duties. The Counter-Terrorism Committee, helped by its Executive Directorate, tracked how well states carried out obligations such as cutting off terror financing. The arrangement set by an earlier resolution was due to expire at year's end.

The Council extended that period until 31 March 2008. It also asked the Directorate's Executive Director to propose changes within sixty days, after consulting Council members, on how the body should be organized going forward. The text balances the extension with a reminder that counter-terrorism measures must respect human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law.

Resolution 187 is a UN Security Council follow-up on Cyprus, adopted unanimously on 13 March 1964, nine days after the Council created a peacekeeping force for the island. The Council had heard Cyprus, Greece, and Turkey, and the Secretary-General reported that the force was about to be established, with advance elements already on their way.

The resolution repeats the call on all member states to refrain from any action or threat that could worsen the situation in Cyprus or endanger international peace. It also presses the Secretary-General to carry on building the force and asks member states to cooperate with him. It kept diplomatic pressure steady while the first peacekeepers deployed.

A world without nuclear weapons is the stated aim of Resolution 1887, adopted on 24 September 2009 at a summit meeting. The resolution calls the Non-Proliferation Treaty the cornerstone of the non-proliferation regime. It voices concern about nuclear terrorism and urges use of IAEA safeguards. It notes US-Russian talks on a treaty to replace START, which was about to expire.

The Council says non-compliance with non-proliferation duties will come before it for judgment on whether such cases threaten peace and security. It calls on states outside the NPT to join as non-nuclear-weapon states, and on parties to pursue disarmament talks in good faith. It urges every state to refrain from nuclear testing and ratify the Test Ban Treaty. It asks the Conference on Disarmament to negotiate a ban on making fissile material for weapons. A state that leaves the NPT stays answerable for earlier violations.

Fiji raised its own flag on 10 October 1970. That same day, its bid for a UN seat won the Council's backing. The Pacific islands had been under British rule. Their leaders moved fast once freedom came. Resolution 287 passed with no votes against at the 1554th meeting.

The members told the General Assembly to admit Fiji. The Assembly did so three days later. Fiji was among the first Pacific island states to join. Its seat gave small ocean nations a stronger voice in New York. Sugar and tourism drove its economy. The one-line text hides a neat fact: few states have matched a birth date and a UN yes vote on the very same day.

South African forces invaded Angola in 1976, entering from Namibia, which South Africa held next door. The African Group of states brought the complaint to the Council. The invasion caused damage inside Angola, and equipment and materials were seized. Resolution 387 was adopted on 31 March 1976.

The Council condemned South Africa's aggression against Angola. South Africa was told to respect Angola's independence, sovereignty, and territory. It also had to stop using Namibia as a base for attacks. That ban covered attacks on Angola and on any other neighboring African state. South Africa had to meet Angola's just claims for full compensation for the damage done. The seized equipment and materials had to be returned as well.

The Gulf War is formally ended on strict terms by Resolution 687, adopted in 1991. Kuwait's sovereignty had been restored and its government returned after Iraq's invasion and occupation, but many nationals were missing and property unreturned. Iraq had used chemical weapons and ballistic missiles and was suspected of seeking nuclear materials.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council guarantees the 1963 Iraq-Kuwait boundary and orders its demarcation, and sets up a UN observer unit and a demilitarized zone along it. Iraq must accept destruction, under a Special Commission, of all chemical and biological weapons and of ballistic missiles with range over 150 kilometres. It must accept IAEA inspection and removal of its nuclear-weapons material, with monitoring after. Iraq is held liable for direct losses from the invasion, and a compensation fund and commission are created, financed from oil exports. A ceasefire takes effect once Iraq officially accepts the terms.

China's seat was fiercely disputed when Resolution 87 passed on 29 September 1950. The Communists had won the mainland civil war. Yet the Nationalist government still held China's UN seat. Beijing had complained to the Council about an armed invasion of Taiwan, called Formosa in the text.

Members voted seven to three to hear Beijing's side, despite the dispute over who represented China. They postponed debate until after 15 November 1950. Then a representative of the People's Republic would be invited to attend. The invitation rested on a rule allowing the Council to hear outsiders with useful information.

Fighting in Bosnia went on in the spring of 1995, despite the cease-fire agreements of December 1994. Troops of the United Nations Protection Force had come under attack, and some of them had been killed. The ban on military flights over Bosnia was also being broken. Resolution 987 was adopted unanimously on 19 April 1995.

The Council demanded that all parties stop intimidating or attacking UNPROFOR. The parties were held responsible for the force's safety. The Secretary-General was pressed for urgent proposals on how such attacks could be prevented. The Bosnian parties were called on to extend their cease-fire and their halt to fighting beyond 30 April 1995. Everyone was urged to return to talks. The goal was an overall settlement of the conflict, built on the peace plan of the Contact Group.
waite-real-history-of-the-rosicrucians-1:
A. E. Waite set out to sift fact from dream in The Real History of the Rosicrucians, his study of 1887. Waite was a young clerk with a sage's zeal. He read the old tracts, lists, and claims in full. Then he told what the proof could bear, and no more than that.

His tale is calm and spare next to Jennings's wild one. He traces the first tracts and the men back of them. Later scribes cite his work as their base. It is the sober root of all study of the band. Waite went on to write a shelf of books on rite and sign. This early work shows the care that made his name lead the field.
weishaupt-kurze-rechtfertigung-1787:
Adam Weishaupt founded the Illuminati in Bavaria in 1776 and was driven from his post when the state turned on the order. After officials seized the group's papers and printed them to shame him, he answered in print himself. Kurze Rechtfertigung meiner Absichten, issued in 1787, is that answer, a short book in his own voice.

Weishaupt replies point by point to the charges drawn from the seized letters. He says the papers were picked and arranged to make him look like a fraud and a corrupter of youth. He then sets out what he claims he truly meant the order to do. Few books from the affair speak so plainly for the losing side.
weishaupt-verbesserte-system-1787:
Adam Weishaupt published Das verbesserte System der Illuminaten, the Improved System of the Illuminati, in 1787. Bavaria had suppressed his order, and this German book is his definitive restatement of its graded structure. Weishaupt redesigns the society on paper, presumably for a future he still hoped might come.

The system lays out the order's classes and degrees in revised form. Instruction, secrecy, and the slow formation of members rule the design. Weishaupt writes as a founder correcting his own machine. The book completes the documentary triangle of the affair: seized papers, defense, and now the blueprint revised. The secret society, rebuilt in print, stands as the founder's last word on his creation.
wimmer-runenschrift-1887:
Ludvig Wimmer, a Danish scholar, wrote this study of the rune script in German in 1887. He was the lead rune expert of the Danish school of his day. The book asks where the runes came from and how they changed over time.

Wimmer set the rune rows in order by age and showed how each sign grew from older forms. He used stones from Denmark and the wider north as his chief proof. His scheme gave rune study a firm shape that held for the next age of work. Danish rune work still builds on the frame he set here.
yasna-mills-1887:
L. H. Mills translated the Yasna for the Sacred Books of the East in 1887. The volume, number thirty-one in the series, also holds the Visparad, Afrinagan, and Gahs. The Yasna is the chief liturgy of Zoroastrian worship.

Priests recite the Yasna's chapters while preparing the sacred haoma drink. The Gathas, hymns ascribed to the prophet Zoroaster himself, stand inside it. Those hymns may be thirty-five centuries old, among the oldest scriptures anywhere. Fire, truth, and the cosmic battle between good and evil fill the poetry. Mills spent his career on Avestan texts. His translation opened Zoroastrianism's central service to English readers.
ywain-and-gawain-schleich-1887:
Ywain and Gawain is a Middle English romance based on Yvain by the French poet Chrétien de Troyes. G. Schleich edited the English text in 1887. English makers reshaped the French tale for their own hearers, trimming it into a faster northern style.

Ywain fights at a magic fountain and wins a lady's love, then loses her through a broken promise. A lion he rescues becomes his loyal companion in exile. Fight by fight, he earns his way back to forgiveness. The romance pairs wild adventure with a plain lesson: a knight's word is worth more than his sword.
zola-soil-1887:
Vizetelly and Company issued The Soil at London in 1888 as a realistic novel. A frontispiece by H. Gray shows old Fouan warning a child to hold his tongue. The contents split the tale into five parts of five chapters each.

Fouan divides his fields among his children, and the gift turns poisonous. The family tears itself apart over every furrow of the loved land. Greed, lust, and violence follow, in scenes that shocked even Zola's fans. The French title is La Terre, the earth itself. Pitiless and earthy, the book shows rural France as a place where the soil seems to devour its people.
